InfoQ Homepage Presentations Opening the Black Box: Critical Explainability for AI Agent Tool Selection with Kiji Inspector

Hannes Hapke shares how Dataiku’s open-source Kiji Inspector applies Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) directly to decision tokens to expose why agents pick specific tools. Moving past superficial chain-of-thought narratives, he discusses causal ablation, layer activation extraction via patched vLLM engines, and production monitoring workflows for software architects and senior engineering leaders.

QCon AI is a practitioner-led event focused entirely on the engineering discipline required to scale these workloads safely. It provides direct access to the architectural playbooks and failure metrics that peer organizations use in production.

Presented by: David Iparraguirre - Senior Product Marketing Manager at Datadog, and Jessica Yang - Product Manager at Datadog

Presented by: Kiran Gangadharappa - Engineering Advisor at Harness, and Scott Davis - Senior Engineering Manager at Harness

For today, we want to focus on what we call the Kiji Inspector. It is a tool that is helping you to understand how agents "Think." The fundamental problem that we have with agents is that we don't know how they actually make their decisions. We have a number of tools out there. We have prompt engineering, behavioral testing, or probably the most sophisticated processes like chain of thought. None of them are actually providing you causality, they're often just giving you plausible explanations or plausible narratives of what the root cause could be. When we were asked to figure out how can we make sure that the model that is running an agent is picking the right tool, how do we know that it's thinking about the right context, we decided that we needed to look into the model.

The way we do this is by using sparse autoencoders. Before we get there, let me start explaining what an autoencoder is. This is a concept that has been around for a very long time, probably three decades by now. Autoencoders take a set of inputs, reduce this to a smaller latent space vector, and then reconstruct them through a decoder. The whole point of that autoencoder is that you want to minimize the error between the input and the reconstructed output. In an optimal system, there would be zero error, and the output here would be exactly as the input. Then you know that the representation of your vector z here in your latent space is most optimal. This has been used many times in various things like embeddings and vector searches and information compression, dimensionality reductions of various sorts of kinds. This is a really interesting way of forcing your model to reduce the amount of information to a smaller vector space.

The cool thing about this concept is that it's self-supervised. You don't need any labeling. You use the input as the output, that's your target, and then in between, that's what you would use in production. With sparse autoencoders, you would flip this concept around a little bit. Here in this case, we wouldn't create a bottleneck for the information, but we want to go wide here, with a little catch, and I'll explain the catch. Let's say you grab an activation from a model, or a hidden state, and you pass it through the sparse autoencoder, you can go wide in the information, and that means you force the model to pick certain features to represent the information. When you take a look at the activations inside of a model, there's something that we call polysemantic representation of the context, which means that one neuron that fires can have multiple meanings or topics it would fire on.

In our feature representation, if we want to understand the model, we need to separate them and put them apart from each other, and so that's why we're going wide in the feature representations here. Then again, we try to then have a decoder where we narrow that information piece again, and we try to reconstruct the activations that we used as an input. The catch here is that in this activation function, we are then forcing the model to only use a small set of features to be actually active, and the rest of them, roughly 95%, that's the ideal number, we want to force them to be zero. In that moment, we actually force the model during the training process to just be really selective on a handful of features, and then we can be absolutely certain that those features are representing the themes and the context of the model itself, what the model was thinking in this given layer at the processing of a certain token.

Then we can go one step further. Once you have those feature vectors you generated, those indices don't mean anything to us, to humans. What we can then do is, once we have a corpus, we can grab all the documents that fire highly on, let's say, dimension 3 and dimension 6, and then we can look at those documents and say, what do they have in common? It could easily be that they say like, the first one has something to do with Python, so then over the course of the entire corpus, we could say, those two features, they represent a programming language or an API vocabulary or things like this.

What we have tried to do in this project is combining a number of things and package them up so that everybody can use them in production. The first thing that we want to do is, sparse autoencoders have been around for a number of years now, and OpenAI published some research, and Eleuther published some research on this, but they focused on the entire LLM generation. What we changed here in our approach is we were only interested in the agentic decision-making. We focused on the decision token rather than the entire prompt, and then averaging those activations across the entire prompt. Then we put a bunch of concepts together. For example, Eleuther came out with this concept of token-level fuzzing, and so we added this to our framework so anybody who wants to use that framework and trains their own models, they can use that token testing. Then also we added causal validation testing as well so that you can make sure, is it actually causal or is it just correlation?

Then the other sweet thing, what we changed here in this project, what is novel, is that we're not just training on a number of prompts, but we created those pairs, training pairs. We have a given intent — I'll show you an example later — but for a given intent, you have something that we call the anchor that's the correct answer and the correct tool use, and then there's an adversarial reply, which is very similar, but very different. It's basically like look something up in an internal database versus look up something online. Two different use cases, very similar in the prompt response, but very different outcome in terms of the tool selection.

Looking at the training pipeline, let's say we have all these pairs generated, which I will show you how we do this. We then take our target model, and little caveat here, those have to be open-source models. We can't do this with OpenAI's models because we don't have access to their weights, but you can do this with any open-source model, and that's another novelty in our framework that we're not just focusing on Gemma models from Google or Nemotron models from NVIDIA. That tool, that framework here is working with various open-source models that are out there. You pick your subject model, that's the model you want to use the explainability for, and then you run all your prompts through the model itself, grab all the activations from the particular layers you want to watch. Then with those activations, you can train your sparse autoencoder as I just showed you with putting them in, widening them up, and then forcing the decoder again to reconstruct that activation.

Then once you have the model trained, you can do a contrastive analysis, and I'll show you this later, how we then figure out through those pairs of what's actually relevant in the context or not. Or you can go to a large language model and say, tell me what those documents have in common, and then you can generate those themes. This all happens in that package where we call the Kiji Inspector. You put in your corpus, you nominate those models, and out you get a feature definition of what those features mean when you run those LLMs and agent requests.

Earlier, I just mentioned you have to pick a certain layer. There's a little bit of an art what layer to pick rather than science. There's a little bit of an explanation here that if you're early in the stack, like maybe in the first third, the model hasn't fully conceptualized all the concepts of your prompt request. You're basically activating things that are highly relevant to the prompt itself. If you're further down the stack, there's a lot of intricacies of the model itself. Here in this particular model, we're looking at the Nemotron 3 from NVIDIA. That's an MoE model. That's because every different request goes through different routings, you have crazy errors. Learning something later on is very difficult. Also, the concepts you extract are so abstract in some cases that even for humans, it's impossible to understand what's going on. Then also for the models, it's difficult.

What we wanted to do is, for our particular experiments, we picked layer 20 because it is already down the pipe. It's like the model extracted some abstract concepts. It's not too far down the pipe that it would be too non-human understandable. In our open-source models, what we're publishing, we're publishing multiple layers. You can pick wherever you want to be in your model layer setup. Again, this is another representation of the training pipeline. Basically, you have your input. You calculate those representations. Then you do the reconstruction back to, in our case, it's 2688 dimensions. Then you calculate the loss. It's a very standard autoencoder model architecture. The key thing, and we show this in the following slide, we're using a particular activation, what we call the Jump Regularized Linear Unit. I will explain this here why this is in this particular case.

Then, how do we actually focus on the decision token? The way we do this is by forcing the agent to respond to a given prompt and says, I will use blank. Whatever tool, whatever the model then responds is expected to be the tool name, because we've provided the selection of tools in the prompt itself. Then in the response, we would see what tool the model has chosen. We do this a million times. We generated a training set with a million samples, basically 500,000 pairs, good and bad examples. The pairs come in later when we try to evaluate the model. During the training process itself, we use them raw, and we have those 1 million samples. Why are we doing this contrastive pair design again? Here's a little example. Let's say you have a given intent, resolve a password issue, and you can have the request, how do I reset my password?

That would trigger the tool knowledge base. You could also say, I tried to reset my password three times, and that could be a completely different tool. It's very similar in the response or in the request, but it's a very different tool outcome in this particular case. Later on, what you will see is we will then use those pairs and figure out which of the features we generated are actually relevant for those given tools. When we generate the features for both tools, the dimensions where the features are different have mostly contributed to the decision-making between knowledge base versus ticket lookup.

I don't want to go through the math here, but there's an interesting concept regarding the JumpReLU. As you know, Regularized Linear Units basically are, anything negative is zeroed out and anything positive is the input. It's like a linear function, but it's not differentiable because of that bend. Here in the JumpReLU, that's another derivative of the ReLU activation function. It's basically the output is the input, but there's a threshold. The interesting thing here is when we train the model of, figure out which activation is actually relevant and not relevant, we can then tune that threshold during the training process as the output activation. That's another tweak we can have to teach the model which feature is relevant for which given activation. When we look at some results per layer, then we see some really interesting side effects of early on, the error is low, but the model hasn't learned much.

Later on, the error is crazy high because this is logarithmic. Then we have too many, basically we learn something, but the error is exorbitant high. That's why we ended up in our practical example, we ended up somewhere in between at layer 20. Again, if we look at some stats here, like total, I think we had like 2,600-and-something input features, we widened this to 10,000 dimensions. Of those 10,000 dimensions, a little bit above 80% of those dimensions are alive. That means somewhere through the training, they have been nonzero. Then only less than 0.2% are completely dead, meaning those features have never been used through the entire training process. Then when we do the testing later on, we actually figured out that out of those 10,000 features, 668 are actually highly relevant to all the tool selections we wanted to investigate. This is for a given model for a given layer and a given dataset. If you retrain this, you might see different results.

Then somebody could say, why do we have to go through all this craziness of sparse autoencoders and training another machine learning model in all these crazy setups? As you can imagine, it's a lot of computation there. This is basically a couple comparisons. If you take the activations and then train a linear model on this, could we then figure out is this tool correct or incorrect? If you compare this and a binary classification here, we get to almost 80% accuracy. It's not bad, but it's also not perfect. Then if you do some just accuracy versus F1 score, that's a little bit lower. Then somebody could say, what happens if we just take those activations with those 2,000 dimensions and we just cluster them? Could we from the cluster then figure out which tool is the correct one? You're better off flipping a coin than actually clustering.

I think that was for us the interesting thing to see with the sparse autoencoders. I'll explain what fuzzing is. We can bridge the gap between interpretability and also having some causality testable features. I just mentioned token-level fuzzing. That was introduced by Eleuther sometime back when they looked into sparse autoencoders for entire prompts. What they did was they took a look at the prompt and then swapped out individual tokens, and then looked at how is the activation affected by swapping out those tokens and how is the end result being affected by that. That's the same concept we provide in our tool case here, in our framework that people can use when they want to evaluate their sparse autoencoders. Then when you look at the individual features and the quality of them, we can see that for the majority of the features they actually correlate really well to what we predicted the outcome to be. Only a small number of them have very poor influence on the overall decision-making. Again, from those 600 features we selected, it felt pretty good. This is heading in the right direction.

Then, let's take a look at causality and those other things. That's always the big question. We started this project where like, can we explain how an agent selected a tool? At some point, we needed to take a look at, can we actually prove causality? Little side note, I'm not a statistician, so I would love to have a better conversation about this with somebody who is more experienced with this. What we have done is looking at the activations. While the activation in this given layer in the model was produced, we then zeroed out the top 10 activations in that given vector. Then we looked at, is the tool selection changing or not? This was our setup. It's a little bit of like wiring and intercepting all the activations and those types of things. Don't worry, through the framework, we provide the other tools where you can replicate that.

The way this works is for our experiment setups here, where we looked at various tools, we were actually able to show that if you do the contrastive ablation, that worked extremely well for a number of tools. There were certain tools where we couldn't prove it, but for the majority of the tools, it actually looked very promising. Just a couple results here, the p-score is very low, so we were pretty happy about this. Through those testing, we were able to show that 23 of those contrast types actually worked. That worked better than randomly flipping. We felt that this is also, again, heading in the right direction. Like, yes, those particular activations, those 10 dimensions we blanked out or zeroed out actually contributed actively to the tool selection.

This was a lot of theory and a little bit of math and all those types of things, but you don't have to do this yourself, and that's why we have the Kiji Inspector, and that's why we open sourced that at Dataiku. What we're trying to provide here with a toolkit and the framework is like, we wanted to provide a model-agnostic framework that everybody else can use in the industry. Companies like Google have published similar frameworks, but they're always very tool specific. For example, Gemma Scope is the explainability tool for Gemma 2 or Gemma 3 or Gemma 4, or there's no Gemma 4 expanded model yet. There is no training pipeline. There's a lot of repos floating around with scripts and everything, but it's not like something you can download and fork and run something end-to-end on your site for your particular models and your particular use cases.

Then we wanted to provide a full production setup. We see a lot of research in those cases, but we hadn't seen a good production setup where people can run vLLMs and also get the activations back. Because in most setups like vLLM or SGLang, you get the response back but those inference tools don't give you the activations of a particular layer back. We provide a patch to vLLM that allows you to do that, and we also give you the containers so you can run this in production. Then as I said, everything is fully open source. We provide Docker containers, there's a PyPI package as you will see, and then all the models we have trained are on Hugging Face. This is only a subset, the list is way longer of what we're providing on Hugging Face. With our large training set of those 1 million data points or 1 million samples and the 500,000 pairs, we recently just trained Gemma 4.

Who knows if Google actually comes out with their sparse autoencoders. We wanted to beat them, and so we have the sparse autoencoders for the Gemma 4 and then for the latest Nemotron models, the Nemotron 3, we also provide the sparse autoencoders. Unfortunately, we don't have infinite compute resources as Google, that's why we have to pick certain layers to support them. If you have specific reasons, and you want a particular layer of a particular model, let us know, we can probably help you there as well.

How would the inference setup look like? If you run for example an agent and says, analyze my Q3 report, you would go through a large language model. Again, it has to be an open-source model, because you have to host that model so you can patch your vLLM version. We're hoping to get this into vLLM at some point so that hosting platforms like Baseten and others can provide those features as well. Then, you not just get the response back but you also get the activation vector for a given layer for your response. Then that goes into your sparse autoencoder. From your 2688 dimensions, you would then go up to 10,000 dimensions. Remember most of the dimensions are actually zero. Then you can take a look at the top features that are active in this large vector, and then you can take a look at those indices and figure out what are the themes you have determined during the training itself.

Then you can take those themes and put them back into a large language model as an explanation. Now somebody might ask, what's the difference now between doing all of this and chain of thought? The key difference is this information piece was directly derived from the activation during the model when that token was generated. It is not chain of thought where it first goes through some reasoning steps and then tries to execute. In chain of thought it could say like, here are two things I want to do, and then it executes 15 other things. There's no connection between those two steps. Here, there's the direct connection between the activation at a given layer. It goes into the sparse vector, and then we have the connection to the feature map we generated during the training.

Now the actually fun part starts. In Hugging Face, you can define what we call forward hooks. When the model is being executed, in Hugging Face the model is not compiled so you can easily hook into the execution, and say, give me the vector of a given layer for that given input. Then, we can grab the layer from here. When it's being executed, we can then actually ship it back to the response and send it to the user. I can show you another setup we have where you can also work with compiled models so you get a better performance. Then you run the inference, you retrieve the vector, and that is your activation. You're ready to go to use your sparse autoencoder. If you use one of the models we already support, you can then use our Kiji Inspector. We followed the Hugging Face setup. You can say like, from pre-trained, you mention the base model and under the hood we figure out like, what sparse autoencoder it needs to download.

We go to the correct repo, and then we use the correct model for the correct layer. Under the hood we convert this into the correct feature vector and then also do the lookup of the features to the themes. When you run SAE describe, that's how you get the description and not just a random vector. This is how it looks like, and I will show you this, again, but this is a little bit better readable. The interesting thing is that when we look at the second feature that was firing, it was actually something related to dishwasher gasket issues.

Seems relevant to the prompt we have. If it would fire on something completely unrelated here then there would be a good sign to go back and say like, maybe there's something going on in the model or maybe my prompt is incorrect or something else happening. Let me show you here a little demo of how this would work and how you can actually use this in production. Again, this is the same code that I showed you earlier where we just stepped through. If you want to use a larger model you have to pay for the bigger GPUs nowadays. This is still giving you an overview of how this works under the hood. Here's a truncated information on the slide. You see some more information, and we also provide the bottom examples. Basically, here you see all the things that are least related to that request. Then you can go down, and you can turn this into a description and you can see what the confidence level is.

Here's another thing that I think could be really interesting for folks. As I mentioned at the beginning, we provide patches for vLLM. Here in this case is like you can also execute the whole thing in vLLM. When you do vLLM generate, you can then also get the same vectors back with the explanations. We tied this all together in vLLM. Then we have another interesting example I think that is a use case where we're stepping through a larger agent setup. Instead of going through the code I want to show you how the result could look like, and maybe that gives you a feeling of how you can use this in your product. We built the standalone demo of like, this is your home repair agent. It tells you if something is broken, can you fix it yourself? Should you call somebody else? It could potentially look up YouTube videos of how to fix it.

In order to make sure that we know what the agent is doing, for every agent step, we then also look up what the sparse autoencoder features are. Here in this particular case, this was the dishwasher example, it relates to a machine handling water I would think, washing machines, and there's something like old machine troubling. At least we know that the agent is heading in the right direction when it made the decision of like a dishwasher is leaking in this particular case. You can do this for every different tool call. This one is completely empty, it's a good example, because when we trained this there was not a tool call in the training set at all for YouTube videos. For us it will be a good sample of like, we need to add more real-world examples in our training set. I showed you this example. There's a couple more, there's a left example there as well where we show this in a live demo, you can follow along what the agent is doing in the frontend while the agent is figuring out what is actually happening. It's pretty fun to look at.

What are the particular use cases you can use for your applications and where you could use the Kiji Inspector. One thing is like you could figure out what an agent misbehavior would be. Anything that is like, has it picked the wrong tool, as I showed you earlier in the examples, that is a something. You can do it for audit compliance. Some companies looking at this and figuring out, it's like, if we have another track record, traces is one thing but explainability is another thing. When we do traces, we basically see what tool has been selected but we still can't explain why that tool was selected. Here we generate another set of logs and figuring out why the agent has particularly selected this tool that is shown in the traces. Then we can do validate of prompt engineering. If you're not quite sure, like you want to optimize your prompt for particular goals and you don't want to do this iterative loop, you can then also investigate like how is that tool responding to your given prompt based on the activations.

Then obviously monitoring production drift. If your data changes, let's say you test your agent with a set of prompts, you watch those activations, and then over time you can see if those activations change. That is a really good indication that the data that is going through that agent has changed. Maybe you should take a look at that as well.

Just to summarize this, what are the key takeaways? We have the chance to prove that sparse autoencoders can work to explain why the agent made a certain decision. We showed how the token-level fuzzing works, and as part of the package we can prove that tweaking those prompts lead to different activations. I also showed the causal evidence of the tool selection is affected by zeroing out certain activations in the model itself. Then we did some comparison with construction only baseline, meaning, because it's a decoder and there's a loss effect, if we take this out, then we can actually show that there's a causal effect in the sparse autoencoder.

I want to let you go with a couple limitations and also pointing out some future work. As I said, you do need the model itself. It doesn't work with closed source models. Hopefully at some point they give us similar tools on there, and that would be fantastic. The training is pretty compute intensive, especially if you want to create your own datasets. If you want to use the tool and you want to create your own training sets, come talk to us. We can share some more tricks and tips of how to run this effectively. As I mentioned earlier, it is a synthetic dataset. If anybody wants to use this and has some ideas of what is missing in the dataset and where should we go in terms of making it more real-world replicable, then let us know. We would love to collaborate on that as well.

There's a future work here. We want to support more open-source models and provide those models from the start through Hugging Face. Something that is on mind is currently Qwen. More multi-layer experiments. Currently everything is based on single layers. It could be really interesting if you take a layer from the first third and then a layer from the last third, and then combine those and see what actually happens. Then another interesting idea we had was like what happens if you do cross-model transfer. Basically, you train on a Gemma model. You take those vectors. You learn certain features. Is there something we can generalize then if we go to another model and so we see certain patterns. That is all future work. We haven't touched this yet. If anybody wants to collaborate on this let me know. Everything is fully open source. We live from contribution from others. This is not our project. It's a community project.

Participant 1: Is there anything that stops this from being applied to something by the training, of course, beyond tool calls. For example, if we were looking at safety alignment. The reason being that at least from the results of the causal inspection that you did, it seems to be possible to do some kind of steering after you train the model. Do you have any insight on any ways that we could possibly change something like this for alignment and then use that for active steering after deployment.

Hannes Hapke: I think there's nothing that I would say that it's not possible. One of the things we're looking into is the security aspects of like, can we detect malicious attacks in those activations? Yes, I think that's possible. I think from the research I showed earlier when I showed the clustering versus linear classification versus the sparse autoencoder, it was visible to me. I think to me that's sort of the proof that if you just look at their pure activations you can't figure out what is going on. You do need the step through the sparse autoencoder. Yes, nothing is limited to just a tool call. For us, it was like a feasible project scope. The team is pretty small, so for us it felt feasible. Yes, totally.

Participant 2: Do you have any real-world examples where using your approach gave you a different understanding of why a tool was selected versus using chain of thought tells?

Hannes Hapke: Yes, we have a bunch of anecdotal examples. We haven't summarized them yet into something scientific that we say here's my prompt and here's my analysis. Chain of thought was maybe a bit abstract. Then in the features, we could see like, this is actually looking for a particular problem. For example, this dishwasher repair thing, it picked water damage on an electrical equipment or something. It felt more precise than the actual chain of thought. There's a little caveat. The sparse autoencoder we trained for those examples, they were domain specific. Meaning that we were focusing on a very particular specific domain and that's what we built the training set for. There was a little bit of an unfair advantage. Also, it changes with model size. If you use a smaller model like the Gemma E4B, I think those interpretability tools have a benefit of it. Those were the two things where you could see the difference between the chain of thought versus the explainability tool.

Participant 2: For those who are stuck with the closed source proprietary models, could you imagine surrogate models working ok enough? Do you think that the closed and open-source models are similar enough with why they would make certain choices?

Hannes Hapke: I can't speak for OpenAI and others. I would think the models are bigger than what we see in the open-source world obviously. I think you have maybe a better chain of thought experiments. That's an interesting question. We should compare different prompts and run them through a large Qwen model versus a large like OpenAI 5.5, and then look at the thinking steps, and see, are they comparable or not? Generally, we will never see this technology in closed source models, because, A, I think all the companies are walking back their logics now, because through the logics you could figure out model internals. This is even more like internals. They never want to share this. The other thing is also like, yes, it's proprietary modeling. They don't want to really open source that or share that.

#9895. Link Previews and You

Why it took us so long to figure out link previews, and where we're going in the future with them.

If youâre an avid user of programs like Discord, you might be familiar with the venerable âlink previewâ. This is a little block that shows below a link, and hints at what might lie on the other end of that URL. These are a little messaging convenience that allows for many things, like conveniently sharing social media posts without logging into a platform and providing a description for a blog post. It encourages sharing: the open internet is built on a diversity of open websites, where people can freely view content without stepping into walled gardens and discourse chambers.

Discord, as a centralised platform, employs their servers to visit web pages for you, grab metadata from tags specified in markup headers, and caches that response. Clients then query that server to get a structured response on what a link preview should look like, and can easily render it without much hassle.

Signal has to go about this problem in a different way. Signal doesnât know what websites you send people in messages, and they donât want to. They also donât want users to be able to send each other websites that would reveal information about them. For example, letâs say I own evil.example, and Iâm listening closely for every connection to my servers. If I send you a link from that domain, your phone will try and find information about that webpage, and a poor implementation could leak things like your IP address, which is information that could be used to narrow the scope of a search into where you are currently located at.

To address these issues, MSC4095: Bundled URL Previews adds the ability for clients to attach previews directly to messages. This mirrors the Signal approach somewhat, as it makes the sender generate the preview.

Hold onâ the sender has to generate it? Weâre principally a web client. Most of our users would prefer to download our program, either on mobile, or on desktop, but we have web users we canât just abandon. The issue is CORS: a limitation that stops websites from just sending network requests to random websites. Essentially, we canât do this for all users unless we find a server.

This ended up with us having a server that generates link previews for web users, and a client that generates link previews, both with different behaviour. This is also complicated with homeserver previews, so we essentially had three different ways to get link previews.

We moved link preview generation into a separate library, which lets us do fun things. We can now make architectural decisions on where we do link previews without doing a ton of refactoring work.

One thing this allowed us to do is to think about how we handle social media previews better. We now have an OpenGraph extension specification for specifying a social media ânoteâ, as Matrix link previews are OpenGraph based. We have scrapers for handling major social media websites, Atproto, and the Fediverse, and we can work on making these better separately from the rest of our codebase and infrastructure. We now format notes separately from default previews, which is shaped more like a social media note.

We might look into eliminating use of the homeserver for generating link previews entirely, at least temporarily. If we can provide a meaningful benefit to how previews are generated, users might get frustrated with us at inconsistencies between previews coming from Sable versus their homeservers. In that case, we would like to create MSCs and work with the ecosystem. Our advantage is that as a new, fast-moving project we can figure out where things fail in practice, and then come to the wider community with a proposal thatâs been informed by real users.

Thatâs our attitude in general: weâre trying out things. Matrix has been slow-moving for a long time (weâve all heard complaints about it) and Sable hopes to be a client that sits far ahead of the specification, making experimental implementations and helping inform future movement for the protocol at large.

#9893. Training a coding model to paint watercolours with TRL and OpenEnv

On 23 August, Surya Narreddi posted a beautiful video of watercolours painted by a language model. The model writes JavaScript through p5.brush, a library that "adds natural drawing tools to p5.js". The video went viral fast, over 1.5M views at the time of writing.

The video came with a blog post explaining the training behind an earlier and narrower stage of the project, close-up flowers rather than the full compositions in the video, sadly without open artifacts yet. His site says a full technical report is coming, so ensure you follow him. The original idea is his, coming from the art and design side, where his skills are way beyond mine. My attempt is on the engineering side, reproducing the recipe in the open with every piece published.

Note: for the context behind the project, told by Surya himself, watch this video of his thesis.

In this article I try and reproduce his idea with TRL and OpenEnv. The reference pool dataset, the RL environment, the training scripts and the trained models, all open.

The whole pipeline runs on Hugging Face, end to end:

Once the two Spaces are up, the recipe is one command. Duplicate the environment and the scorer model, set two environment variables for the reward mix, and launch:

The rest of this article is the story of getting there, and every piece is in the repo.

I have followed the original blog step by step, and only changed something when strictly needed. Every idea of my own went into a list instead of into the experiment, and that list became "What I would try next" at the end, next to the full list of published artifacts. If you have already read his post, the framing and the reward design will be familiar. The new material is the open implementation, the hand-rated pool, and three reward mixes trained and compared, and it starts at The RL environment you need to build.

The paintings look loose, imperfect, handmade, at a moment when image models produce perfect (statistically average) pictures. My guess is that this contrast is a big part of why the video went viral. It reminded me of the early days of generative AI art, when the point was to explore the medium. DeepDream (2015) was a debugging tool that people turned into art, works like Edmond de Belamy (2018) came from artists probing what a GAN could do, and artists like Mario Klingemann spent those years making dreamy portraits with neural networks.

This project feels closer to those early days. In his thesis, Surya describes the path that led here. He started by prompting text-to-image models, where the prompt is the only lever you can pull, and more detail buys more control only up to a point. Training the model itself goes further. The other half of the idea is the medium. The model writes a program of about 150 lines of JavaScript that paints the image. That model output is code. You can read it, edit it and run it again, and the decision behind each brushstroke is visible. And the style comes from a restriction where the model is only allowed ten of the library's methods. More on that below.

In that same period, Anna Ridler photographed thousands of tulips, hand-labelled every one, exhibited the dataset itself as the artwork, and later trained a model on it. I found her work through the references AI agents brought back while building this project and loved it because this project does something very similar by curating a set of images by hand, and then training against them.

Most of the recent RL work on language models uses rewards you can verify. For example, math problems with a known answer, code that passes tests, or graders that are right or wrong and cheap to run. This project is closer to the older exception, RLHF, where the model learns a reward model from human preferences.

Here the reward is aesthetic preference. There is no correct answer. The real question of the project is whether you can do RL over taste.

The reward, as his blog defines it and as the RL environment I built implements it:

HPSv3 is an open 7B preference model. Give it an image and a text description, and it returns a score for how much a person would prefer that image. It was trained on a large set of human choices between pairs of images, so its score is an average of many people's taste. The pairwise judge is Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B-Instruct, a general vision model called through HF Inference Providers. The pairwise judge sees the candidate painting next to four references randomly selected from the pool, guided by a written description of what to weigh (bleeds, translucent washes, soft edges), each comparison in both presentation orders, and its score is the share of comparisons the candidate wins. Its only standard is the pool, so its score is my taste, as encoded in those ratings.

Those are the weights Narreddi converged on. The pool defines taste here. That moves the work from tuning hyperparameters to building the set that decides what is beautiful.

I trained three runs with this reward. They differ only in how the weight splits between the two model judges:

I started with hps-only to validate that the pipeline could learn at all. Once the reward was going up and the metrics were healthy, there was no reason to run it longer, so I launched the two longer runs instead. The question that the longer runs ask is how much of HPSv3's power can you hand to the pairwise judge? The more weight the judge carries, the more the reward means my taste instead of everyone's, and the harder it should be to climb. Incidentally, if you push it far enough or your style is too far from the average, the model could stop entirely.

Fortunately, it did not stop and both runs with the pairwise judge on learned too. The hand-rated pool can steer the policy, at least as far as the metrics and the final paintings show. The numbers are below.

Disclaimer. If we use a frontier model, it can already generate the JavaScript code that paints watercolour from a prompt. That's the starting point. The work here is about teaching a smaller model to do it combined with a person's own artistic preferences.

The environment wraps everything that sits between the model and the reward, including the JavaScript library that the model uses for painting, the system prompt that restricts it, the headless Chromium that renders each sketch, and the gate that rejects cheats.

The library does more of the work than it seems. p5.brush, by @acamposuribe, simulates a medium rather than drawing shapes: pigment bleeds past the edges of a fill, paper has texture, strokes have mass, flow fields drag brushwork around. When the model calls brush.fillBleed(0.25) it is deciding how far the ink runs.

Note. The author of p5.brush had been trying to teach a machine to paint long before any of this. In 2022 he made a generative art series that hides a diary about teaching p5.js to draw like a child: "It is barely able to use the crayons [...] It cannot follow simple commands. I'm done for today, very infuriating." The series was meant to have three pieces, and he made two. When Surya's video went viral, he quoted it, sharing that diary and saying this work is the third piece arriving on its own.

p5.brush exposes 47 methods. The prompt allows 10: scaleBrushes, noStroke, fill, noFill, fillBleed, fillTexture, beginShape, vertex, endShape and circle. What the other thirty-seven add, lines, hatching, custom brushes, would break the watercolour look. With these ten the model can only paint filled shapes, and the library adds the bleed to every one of them.

His blog post saved me a lot of time I could have wasted iterating on the prompt. A long API reference makes the model invent methods that do not exist, and his 200 GEPA iterations converged on a strict allowlist with no documentation. I saw the same failures and wrote the allowlist by hand. My only addition to that recipe is one sentence: paint each petal two or three times, a big pass first and a smaller, more opaque one inside it. This small change made my outputs a lot more colorful.

Note. If it's the first time you hear about GEPA, it is an automatic prompt optimizer. A language model reflects in plain words on where the current prompt failed and proposes a better one, and the loop repeats.

The gate is the final piece. The sketch has to compile, use the library instead of direct p5 calls, put real pigment on the canvas, and not try to trick the scorer, for example by writing text on the canvas.

The pool consists of 178 paintings divided into two tiers based on my personal preferences, love and okay. All of them are actually generated by a model. Four open-weight models, called through Inference Providers, wrote p5.brush sketches, each one working from a real, openly licensed photo of a hibiscus from iNaturalist. A vision model gave written feedback on every sketch, over three refinement iterations. Every final render was then rated one at a time, by me, and 178 made the cut.

Here I chose four different families of models to test their different styles. These four were the open models that produced a valid sketch every time in a quick reliability check, and two other candidates were dropped for failing it. If you want to produce your own pool, you might choose others.

The tiers do real work in the reward. When the pairwise judge draws four references, half come from love and half from okay, so the policy always faces some rivals it can sometimes beat, and a win pays the same against either tier. This is one of my few deliberate changes: the original compares against its top tier only, and I kept the easier tier in the draw so a weak early policy still gets signal.

No human-made painting is in there, which is a real limitation. p5.brush is a niche library, and the human work that exists in it with accessible code is a handful of pieces, nowhere near what a training corpus would need, as his blog also notes.

The interesting idea here, as I've already discussed previously, is that the model will learn to imitate what the pool contains. If we point the environment at a different dataset, the reward would automatically change without touching a single line of code. For the dataset I generated and openly share, I also include the source sketch.

If we look closer at the judges, the two of them answer different questions. HPSv3 decides whether it is a flower, and the pairwise judge decides whether it is well painted in the style I chose.

Before anything worked, there was a long stretch of flat reward curves. If you've tried to reproduce a research paper/blog without open artifacts, you probably can relate. Every run tested what I thought was a reasonable theory about what was wrong. A run takes a lot of time, so I queued the next one while still going through the last one's results. As always, starting from something easier that works and then building on top of that was the answer. A simple control task, with no browser and no judges, was the first attempt that learned, and the reason was that my learning rate was just too low.

Another change that cost me time to find was adjusting the LoRA parameters correctly. The usual target_modules list assumes a dense model, and Qwen/Qwen3.5-35B-A3B is a mixture of experts that names most of its projections differently, so the adapter was training ten layers out of forty. I solved this by changing it to all-linear, which reaches every linear layer. The routed experts in this architecture are fused tensors that even all-linear leaves frozen, but everything else gets an adapter, and that was enough to learn.

The fix was four changes in TRL's GRPOTrainer:

These four changes unlocked the first successful run (hps-only), with the reward clearly improving.

With that configuration, all three runs learn. Both judge runs were launched for 200 steps and stopped at 110, with the reward still climbing slowly. A step takes fifteen to eighteen minutes, and the comparison between mixes was already stable, so I stopped both to save compute. Mean group reward over the first and final third of each run:

The three curves line up with how much weight my taste carries. The more the judge weighs, the lower the start and the noisier the climb. judge-led spent its first thirty steps nearly flat before it moved. It is the same move that solved the debugging. Shrink the problem until something learns, then add the hard parts back one at a time.

The pairwise judge term itself climbed in the two runs that used it. The model wins more comparisons against the pool as training advances, which is the claim hps-only could not make. No group in any run collapsed to identical rewards, the GRPO failure mode that kills the gradient. For the curious, the per-metric curves (HPSv3, paint coverage, entropy) are in the repository as CSV.

The full launch command, the hardware and the two environment variables that turn this into the other two runs are in the recipe.

In every run, the first thing the model learned was to stop producing bad paintings, the near-blank canvases and shapeless washes that score under 0.3 in total reward. In hps-only, three quarters of the rise in the group mean comes from bad paintings becoming rare. In the judge runs the collapse is even steeper: rollouts under 0.3 fall from 99 to 16 across judge-led's thirds, and from 37 to 4 in hps-led.

This is why the obvious visual, the best painting of each step, shows almost no difference in hps-only. It moves +0.034 across the run while the median moves +0.155. The learning is visible in the middle of the distribution.

What the pairwise judge changes is the top. In hps-only, paintings got more reliable without getting better. The quality of the good ones added just +0.03 to the group mean, and once HPSv3 saw petals around a centre and a stem, it stopped asking for more pigment. With the judge on, the other half of the story appears. Better here means closer to the pool, so closer to what I rated as "good" or something I liked more. That added +0.12 in judge-led and +0.16 in hps-led, the best of each step rose too, and paint coverage doubled in both runs (0.11 to 0.23, and 0.13 to 0.30) where hps-only barely moved it. With a reference left to beat, a good painting can still get better, and the model starts being rewarded for using more pigment.

One more finding. The model ignores an explicit instruction, and it is right to. The system prompt asks for fifteen to thirty filled shapes. If we look at the real mean, it is between 7 and 9, and n_shapes barely correlates with reward in any run (+0.000, −0.14, +0.07). The policy is not rewarded for obeying that sentence, so it does not obey it.

There is also a ceiling on the hps-only route. If every rollout matched its good ones, that run's mean would sit at 0.771. Whether more steps would break it is an open question.

The paintings also show something that the tables miss. Within each run, they all look similar. As training advances, the rewards inside each group get closer together, and the median paintings in the opening video look like takes of the same flower. That is GRPO doing what it is designed to do with a pool built from one subject. The pool decides what counts as variety, the same way it decides what counts as quality. If the reward only pays for matching one flower, the model learns to paint that one flower. More diverse output would need a more diverse pool, and building one is more curation work. Surya's newer compositions are an example of this. Alex Yango's animal paintings are the same recipe with different choices in the pool. This is the biggest difference between an aesthetic reward and a maths grader. Behind the number there is a very human job, deciding what belongs in the reward set. Jason Liu's essay on taste says the general version in one line. AI shifted the bottleneck from making to noticing.

Surya closes his blog with some of his favourites. Instead of picking mine, below is a wall with the 178 paintings the reward scored highest across the two judge runs, the same number the reference pool holds, in no particular order. Open it and pick your own.

To choose, you looked at many and kept a few, and that is exactly the job that built the reward of this project. Every painting of every run, with its sketch and its reward, is in the rollouts datasets, and browsable in this gallery.

Since the reward was partly based on my taste, it is fair to close with my verdict as a viewer. To my eye, judge-led is the run that ends up the most diverse and the most artistically interesting. hps-led paints convincing watercolours, but its best ones share a soft, wet-on-wet look that is almost a style of its own. hps-only converges the hardest, and most of its paintings settle on the same colours. You can judge for yourself in the gallery, which has every painting of every run, sortable by step and by reward.

This project is mostly infra. A run needs a trainer, two Spaces, an inference router and a websocket to stay healthy for hours straight, and every piece that fails quietly turns into a wrong number somewhere else. Half the work is checking that the number you read matches what actually happened.

Failures of the infrastructure were entering the reward as zeros. A render that timed out or a scorer that did not answer scored the same as a bad painting, 0.0 inside the group. Across all my runs that was about 1.5% of rollouts, and in the worst run it reached 5.2%. That trains the model on noise, so those paths now return None and the rollout is excluded from the group.

I also found a bug in OpenEnv, and sent the fix upstream. The client keeps one persistent websocket, and a socket closed by the far end stayed cached, so every later call failed even though the environment was healthy. It cost me two half-finished runs to find it. The fix is submitted upstream, and the runs launched with it have been running clean since.

The reward of a step depends on which references it drew. The pairwise judge samples four references per step, so every step faces a different set of rivals, and some draws are simply harder. GRPO itself is mostly safe, because advantages are computed inside the group and a hard draw moves the whole group together. The curve I was reading was not safe, and some of what looked like a bad step was just a hard draw. The image above is one example. Step 12 scored half a point below step 11 mostly because it drew the hardest references of the run, while the paintings themselves look close.

Rounded numbers, and only for the runs that finished.

A step is eight rollouts and takes fifteen to eighteen minutes, of which 70 to 80% is rendering. A single render takes 69 to 96 seconds against a 90 second deadline. Part of that is expected, the Space has no GPU, so Chromium renders the WEBGL canvas in software and p5.brush's bleeds and textures are heavy pixel work. Even so, I expected it to be faster, and I have not found the full cause.

A scorer can cost more than the training that uses it: HPSv3 has to be up for the whole run, so pause the Space, or set its sleep timer, when the run ends.

Everything runs on HF Jobs, with the environment as a Docker Space and metrics in trackio.

The rule of this project was to reproduce the recipe with every resource open, not to improve it, so a list of untried ideas piled up along the way. These are the ones I would actually try, in order of how much evidence there is.

Multi-step, and letting the model see what it paints. This is the first thing I would try. The original blog trains single turn, so I trained single turn, and in this setup the model paints with its eyes closed. No image ever goes in, and the only feedback it gets is one number. The evidence that a feedback loop works is the pool itself. The reference paintings came from models iterating three rounds under a vision critic, and the later rounds are better. The material that defines the reward was made with a loop the policy never gets.

Smaller models. There is evidence that 35B is more than needed. In my side experiments a 4B already wrote valid sketches that passed the gate. If a 4B can learn this, the cost of the experiment drops by an order of magnitude.

Other ideas on the list are SFT on the pool sources before starting RL, rewarding pigment explicitly, moving the judge's reference mix from easy to hard as the run advances until only love remains, widening the ten-method allowlist for more visual range (my attempts on this crashed more sketches and broke the watercolour look), and checking how consistent the pairwise judge really is by scoring the same image twice.

And the method is not specific to flowers. Alex Yango painted animals with the same mechanism, and Brendan Hogan trained canvas animations against a pool of hand-rated clips. I had also played with something similar before using Simon Willison's pelican benchmark, where code is rendered to an image and scored.

And underneath all of it sits the question this project cannot close. 178 paintings made by models define what this trained model considers beautiful. The pool is the bottleneck, and it is the part of the pipeline with no principled answer.

For anyone reproducing this, there are two deliberate divergences from Narreddi's recipe, both argued earlier in the article:

The rest, all-linear for the LoRA, infrastructure failures returning None instead of 0.0, stopping the judge runs at step 110, are decisions I had to make along the way because his blog does not specify them. His implementation is not published, so I cannot tell whether they match his choices or diverge from them.

The per-rollout numbers in this article can be recomputed from the published datasets. Nothing here depends on any Space staying switched on.

The method and original idea are Surya Narreddi's. The library is Alejandro Campos Uribe's.

#9892. Mozilla leaves Solo website owners to go it alone as hosting shuts down

If you have one of these AI-generated homepages, you'd better download and save it quick

Solo, Mozilla's LLM-powered website builder and hosting service, is shutting down. All sites and data will be deleted on November 30.

Mozilla launched Solo in December 2023 as a "Mozilla Innovation Project," aimed at helping sole traders to build themselves a webpage for their services. Some 54,000 people used its LLM to build pages, and relied on Mozilla to host them – complete with custom domain names.

Well, not any more. Now the Soloist.ai homepage says: "We've made the difficult decision to close Solo. We have appreciated all of your support building and growing this product, and the feedback we've received from all of you. Solo will cease operations on Nov 30, 2026."

Users now have just over two weeks left to find a new home for their pages, although Mozilla says it first notified them on October 1. According to the support FAQ, users can download a ZIP containing an HTML export, contact form and newsletter submissions, and a CSV linking to their images.

The images themselves must be downloaded separately. Domains purchased through Solo Domains must also be moved to Name.com, with Mozilla handling the transfer after users create an account and supply its code. So much for having the fiddly bits taken care of.

It also points at a couple of other bot-based site-generating services – in case all this feels like a bit too much. We suspect that for the sort of technophobes that this was aimed at, it very probably will.

Mozilla told The Register: "Experimentation is an important part of Mozilla's mission to make the internet better and give people more choice and control online. Sometimes, that means making the decision to bring a product to an end. Solo will officially shut down on November 30, 2026. We initially notified customers on October 1, providing a 60-day transition period, and have been offering support to help them download their website data and migrate their domains purchased via Solo Domains to another hosting provider."

It seems that some 54,000 users were not enough to keep it going, and we can see that this would cost money to keep running. An HTML export is a start, though the FAQ doesn't explain how much work it will take to get a complete, functioning site running elsewhere.

Buried in the dark recesses of the web is this vulture's own nearly 30-year-old homepage, created using a mixture of Claris Home Page (which was excellent) and Microsoft FrontPage (ever so slightly less so). We saw what a mess machine-generated web content was back then, and thanks to LLMs, we suspect it is almost infinitely worse now.

Mozilla might have made a few bucks by finding a commercial partner to take on its users, and perhaps through them offer a paid site-and-domain transfer service. As we noted last year, it seems not to have negotiated anything with KaiOSTech, which maintains and sells what used to be the formerly FOSS FirefoxOS for use on low-end smartphones.

#9891. Give Your Coding Agents a Memory You Own

I work across several machines, and I switch coding agents depending on the task. Every one of them meets my projects as a stranger. The reasoning from “last Tuesday” disappears when the session ends. Each new agent, on each new host, starts from zero.

Earlier this year, Software Forgets: Agent Traces Are the Memory made the case that coding agents already produce the record we keep losing. As they search a codebase, try approaches, hit errors, read documentation, and change direction, they leave behind a dense account of not just what changed, but why.

While the diagnosis is correct, traces are only potential memory. The session logs of an agent are still just an archive. You cannot grep your way to “why did we move off the streaming parser?” across ten thousand turns. For an agent to use those traces while it works, they need indexing, retrieval, ranking, and exact provenance.

That is what funes provides. It is a durable memory layer for your agents (Claude Code, Codex, pi, and Hermes). It is built from the sessions already on your machine. It works locally and becomes part of your agent's normal workflow with one command. When you want it to, it can also travel to a Hugging Face dataset you own, private by default.

funes is a single binary. Its default inference backend has no ML runtime dependency, and embedding and reranking happen on your machine. Install it:

That one add command builds the first index, gives the agent recall and get tools, and installs the automation that indexes each completed turn. Indexing is incremental, with new runs adding new turns rather than embedding the whole history again. The older and deeper content can backfill in bounded steps.

From there, you just work. When a task touches a past decision, rationale, or finding, the agent can reach for recall itself. You do not need to remember the old session or paste its context into the new one.

With funes added, recall happens inside the conversation. The agent reaches for its memory on its own and names the session behind its answer.

recall returns the original text, not a summary, and shows exactly where it came from (the agent, timestamp, session, and turn). Each result includes a get command that opens the full turn and its surrounding context.

Underneath, one deterministic pipeline parses every supported trace into the same turn-and-block shape, chunks it, embeds it with a pinned local model, and writes it to a local Lance dataset. A query combines vector and BM25 search, fuses their rankings, reranks the candidates with a cross-encoder, reweights them by recency, and attaches neighboring chunks.

That design gives funes three important properties:

The agent as a stranger problem is already solved on one machine. But memory gets more useful when the next agent is running somewhere else.

To make a memory follow your work, bind one when you add funes to an agent:

The bind publishes your current memory there. funes then keeps it current, indexing each turn locally and publishing at session boundaries. The agent recalls from it throughout. Run the same command on another machine and the memory follows you there.

Underneath, the local memory is a Lance dataset, and the shared memory is a Hugging Face dataset (private by default) you own.

Before anything reaches the Hub, credentials have already been redacted during indexing. Publishing then scans every chunk again and withholds anything that still looks like a secret. The scanner behind this is documented in SECURITY.md, including what it does and doesn't cover.

When an agent reads a remote memory, funes caches the dataset files locally, so warm queries return to local speed. The Hub supplies the ownership, access control, versioning, and distribution it already supplies for other datasets. Your memory does not become an account in a separate memory service, and you do not rent it back through an API.

recall is shaped for agents. When you want to put a question to a memory yourself, use ask. It reads your local memory by default:

Or point it at a shared memory. We published a memory of funes development, so you can ask why funes works the way it does without creating a memory of your own:

funes ask is the read-only, one-question sibling of funes add. It recalls the passages, hands them to a coding agent, and returns a grounded answer that names its sources. It does not install an integration or change the agent's persistent setup.

A retrieval miss is not papered over. If the passages do not support an answer, the agent says so. You can rephrase the question or add funes to the agent so it can search the memory iteratively during normal work.

A shared memory is not tied to the agent or model that created it. Start a task in Claude Code, continue it in Codex next week, and the second agent can recall the first agent's reasoning. Use pi with a local model or one served through the Hugging Face router, then return to Claude.

Claude makes a decision; a hook indexes it; Codex recalls it in another session. The older hits in the demo are earlier recordings of the same experiment: an append-only memory remembered the rehearsals too.

Published memories carry a dataset card and the funes tag, making them recognizable and discoverable on the Hub. The Hub already hosts open weights and datasets. funes adds open working memory. It holds the decisions, failed approaches, and rationale behind a project, queryable by another agent and traceable to the sessions that produced them.

A long investigation bloats a session until each turn costs more to carry the context than to do the work. The usual answers are to let the agent compact and carry on, or to write a handoff and start fresh. Recall is a third, so we measured them against each other on the handoff-vs-recall benchmark: two tasks whose answer cannot be reconstructed without the session prior knowledge.

Compaction is what most agents do by default, and it was the only one of the three whose result divided: it arrived on one task and never arrived on the other. Where it failed, its summary had flattened the findings that mattered. Recall returns the passages themselves, so a finding does not have to survive summarization.

Recall was the cheapest of the three on both tasks, 8x cheaper than a written handoff on one and 4x on the other.

The lighter segment of each bar is the one-time charge for preparing the channel, the handoff or the compaction, paid before the first question is asked and counted once. A cross marks a channel that never arrives, and so has no cost per success.

“To think is to forget differences, generalize, make abstractions.” — Jorge Luis Borges, Funes the Memorious

Your agents already wrote the record. funes lives at github.com/huggingface/funes, one command away from turning that record into a memory the next agent can read, on whichever machine you happen to be on.

funes invents little of this. It leans on open-source embedding models good enough to run locally, on Lance's append-only datasets with cheap incremental writes, and on the Hub's caching and content-dedup for datasets. The work is in fitting them into a memory an agent can actually use.

funes is open source too. Open an issue for anything from an install snag to a recall that missed, or an agent you'd like supported.

Ran funes 1.3.0 on a machine with 19,195 coding-agent sessions already on disk (LongMemEval laid down in the real ~/.claude and ~/.codex layouts), 100 questions whose answer sits in exactly one session, scored by whether that session comes back. Disclosure: I maintain deja-vu, one of the tools in the same table.

Full index: 2h03m on an M4 pro laptop (308k chunks), 6.3s per query. With defaults: hit@1 9/100, hit@5 39, found@50 71. With --half-life 0: 19/46/71 — the 30-day recency half-life halves rank-1 on history older than a month, which is most of what's on a real disk; worth a mention in the docs. Once recency is off, the vector+rerank stack is clearly the best ranker in the table at rank five. The documented one-minute first pass leaves 218 of the 19k sessions indexed (0/100 answered), so the "about a minute" framing is really "about a minute until the embedding job starts".

For comparison on the same corpus, deja-vu (plain BM25 over 24 agents' files) indexes in 29s and answers in 24ms at hit@1 18/100, hit@5 35. Corpus, drivers and every row: vshulcz.github.io/deja-vu/guide/day-zero.html - happy to be corrected if a setting I missed changes the numbers.

longmemeval does not really need semantic search: BM25 already gives the same ratio you mentioned IIRC, so for this use case this is pretty much expected that it is not worth paying the cost of evaluating the embeddings (this extra cost you see at indexing and recall time). funes shines when the information is actually difficult to find.

#9890. Running a law firm on Free software (2026 edition)

Published on: 2026-11-06 12:18:47 by Neil Brown

I started running decoded.legal - a small English law firm, focussing on Internet, telecoms, and tech law - on Free software, both client and server side, around five years ago. I have used Free software in my personal life for a lot longer than that.

Back in 2022, I wrote about my experiences after the first year or so.

Someone asked me recently what I am doing now, and, while it is mostly the same, some bits have changed. So here is the 2026 update.

I am still using Debian, with GNOME, and it works well for me.

Iâm using it on a ThinkPad X1 Yoga Gen 6, as my primary machine, and, being a âYogaâ version, I rather like being able to fold the screen back and write on it to mark up documents. (Here are my thoughts on the different âActive Pensâ available for it.)

However, the machine itself seems to have a hardware problem with the Thunderbolt / USB-C ports (fine for power, very flaky for data), and so I might need to replace it. And I have no idea what laptop I might get.

Email (MUA): Thunderbird and mutt, depending on what I am doing

Document production: LibreOfficeâs Writer if I want a âWordâ document (e.g.Â I am exchanging documents with other lawyers), and I am using pandoc and typst to convert Markdown files that I tend to write in vim for some other bits. Iâd like to explore tex at some point, as I have a client who likes diffs to their .tex files, and that looks rather neat.

PDFs: evince for most reading; Xournal++ for marking up PDFs; PDFarranger and pdftk for interfering with PDFs

Local wiki / knowledge management: vimwiki

Client-side encryption of files before syncing them with Syncthing: Cryptomator

Fediverse: I tend to use the Mastodon advanced web UI or, when I want fewer images, the TUI toot.

Password manager: Bitwarden, using the vaultwarden server, with YubiKeys for managing more sensitive credentials

Markdown editor (for blogposts; I do presentations in vim or gedit): Apostrophe

Label printing: thereâs a great FOSS web UI for Brother (and perhaps other) label printers. I donât print many labels, as we aim to be paperless, but itâs convenient when I need to do so

Why so many terminal-based tools? The simple answer is that I am very comfortable in a terminal, and I like them. They have fewer distractions and, when compared with most GUI software, are just - IMHO - easier to use, especially when I donât need to move my hands away from the keyboard. So, while I donât use them exclusively, I use mutt, vim, ikhal, ncmpcpp, newsboat, toot, links, and various other TUIs, frequently.

Everything here - other than Signal - is self-hosted, and Iâm mostly using Intel NUCs now. I still have some Raspberry Pi devices, but fewer than I did.

(Again, this doesnât list everything; just the main applications.)

Invoicing and tracking payments: InvoicePlane, just for generating PDF invoices. Clients donât interact with it

âCase managementâ / âMatter managementâ: EspoCRM

VPN: WireGuard, using trailofbitâs algo ansible scripts on one machine, and PiVPN on another (albeit not on a Pi)

Vulnerability scanning: greenbone/OpenVAS

Website: it is a static site built via mkdocs, hosted on apache2

Fediverse: I am using the *glitch-soc Mastodon** fork

Knowledge management, and managing our law firmâs (numerous) policies and procedures: dokuwiki with the Markdown plugin

DNS: unbound, with Pi-Hole in front of it

Collaborative document editing: I donât.

Iâm using a Pixel running GrapheneOS for my mobile device.

Using Android doesnât thrill me, especially given Googleâs direction of travel, but at the moment - despite trying quite a lot of different OSs and devices, including postmarketOS and Ubuntu Touch, as well as SailfishOS previously - I have not found something that does what I need better than GrapheneOS.

Many of my clients use Microsoftâs software, or Appleâs software.

#9889. Meatbags suck at spotting lying LLMs, so let AI narc on itself

What, you didn't actually want to fact-check it yourself, did you?

The internet is full of schlock, from biased news and dubious hot takes to false factoids. LogicLens aims to separate fact from fiction using the very same technology behind some of that slop: AI.

It’s a simple premise, really: LogicLens, which lives in Chrome as a browser extension, or on iOS in the form of a mobile app called Receipts, combs through articles, social media posts, and other content to check it not only for factual inaccuracies, but also for bad reasoning. LogicLens and Receipts claim to identify logical fallacies, flag reports that misrepresent information, detect content that attempts to polarize an issue, and the like.

It also cites sources, so if, for example, you need to call someone out on their BS, you’ll have ammunition. Or, if you’re trying to fact-check something before sharing it, you can get a more accurate view of the situation, and maybe post something else instead.

Using the Chrome extension is as simple as clicking on its icon in the list of extensions in the browser. On iOS, the Receipts app is found as a share option. Once it starts, LogicLens scans an article, post, video, etc. to find potential issues of factual or logical inconsistency and flags them for review.

If the facts of the matter turn out to contradict your worldview, LogicLens’ creators say they’re not trying to be partisan - you may just not be as informed as you need to be, which hopefully their tool will assist with.

“We're not trying to be the referee of truth,” the company’s about page states. “Instead, LogicLens helps uncover the context, so you can decide for yourself without the spin."

Of course, AI is increasingly used for online analysis and content review, and LogicLens is no exception. LogicLens doesn't identify the AI models powering its service in its publicly available documentation, but AI is definitely the backbone of the system.

According to LogicLens, it's using an AI system that's “Research-backed and custom designed to outperform general models like ChatGPT & even trained experts.” We’ll leave that up to anyone willing to give the tool a spin to decide, but one thing’s for certain: The world needs something.

Large language models and image generation tools are increasingly being used to generate internet content slop, and not all of it is as harmless as poorly made commercials for drop-shipped garbage: Some of it is being used to craft very convincing misinformation.

A 2024 study found that AI-generated misinformation was even more convincing than stuff crafted by humans - and that was two years ago. Just think how much worse it’s likely become since then.

To make matters worse, concerns have been raised about critical thinking skills being on the decline, potentially making it harder for people to identify falsehoods on the internet. AI users are reportedly less likely to admit they don’t know something, even though use of AI has been found in studies to lessen brain activity, leading to poorer retention of facts and worse performance on tests.

Is using more AI the solution to the problem? In an ideal world, we’d all just put the computers down and go touch grass, but we’re not in an ideal world: We’re living in the age of AI.

LogicLens is free but requires sign-up and restricts nonpaying users to 15 analyses a day and 100 over the course of a month. A $4.99 monthly subscription removes those analysis caps.  ®
