#9860. One Compromised Laptop, Billions Lost: The Binance Attack-Path Warning

The record theft shows how weak system separation, inadequate controls, and untested attack possibilities can turn one breach into systemic loss.

Last week's $6.3 billion breach at Binance underscores why effective security often depends not just on what an organization's controls are designed to block, but also on what they are configured to allow.

Details from Binance's disclosures thus far show that a threat actor, whom the FBI has identified as North Korea's TraderTraitor group, compromised a developer's laptop to access an internal service container with the permissions to initiate withdrawal requests.

Using that access as a starting point, the attackers exploited additional points of compromise and an Ethereum account-delegation mechanism to gain transaction approval authority over a hot wallet. And in around 20 minutes, the threat actors drained billions of dollars in assets.

In the process, the attackers appear to have bypassed Binance's normal approval controls. The company itself has said there's no evidence the attackers used any leaked wallet keys to carry out the massive theft.

Related:Inside an AI Attack Against a US Retailer

"Binance's initial findings pointed to a compromised laptop belonging to an employee as the starting point. Its subsequent investigation has identified additional points of breach, showing the incident went beyond one device," the cryptocurrency exchange noted.

The incident, at least based on available details so far, has raised questions about whether Binance had sufficient independent safeguards to prevent a compromised system from approving and executing unauthorized withdrawals.

"At a minimum, a platform holding digital assets should have multiple layers of security so no single compromise, such as a hacked employee laptop, can authorize a transfer," says Tim Rawlins, senior adviser and director of security at NCC Group. "Those layers need to be independent of one another."

Funds, for instance, should be separated across hot and cold wallets to limit the impact of a compromise. Developers and administrators should have privileged access workstations to ensure systems they used for critical operations are separate from those they use for other activities such as email and Web browsing, he says. Also critical is 24/7 monitoring for anomalous behavior to help detect compromised endpoints and suspicious activity before attackers can exploit privileged access.

The focus should be on identifying single points of compromise, such as components or privileged roles whose compromise could give an attacker control over funds. "Protecting private keys is only part of the challenge. The systems that request and approve their use must also be secured. A properly secured system has layered, independent controls, hot/cold separation, and has been through threat modelling and end-to-end security testing," Rawlins says.

Related:Artex: The AI Pen-Test Tool Hackers Turned Into a Weapon

For now, much remains unclear about exactly how the unauthorized transactions occurred and what safeguards Binance had in place to protect against them. Following the attack, the cryptocurrency exchange moved quickly to freeze some $3 billion. It has also claimed to have replenished — though not recovered — approximately 95% of the affected assets, meaning it has used its own funds to replace the stolen assets.

Cryptocurrency exchanges face many of the same threats as traditional financial institutions. But unlike banks and other financial institutions, which have long been subject to regulations governing operational risk and security, crypto exchanges have not yet faced the same level of oversight, making them a popular target for attackers.

John Bruggeman, vCISO at IT services firm CBTS, says large cryptocurrenct exchanges like Binance have to know that they are constantly being targeted by threat actors. In addition to controls that protect the perimeter or authenticate users, these companies also need to know what trusted identities and systems can do, verify high-impact actions, and prevent one compromised component from becoming a path to valuable assets.

Related:CISA Announces Enhanced Reporting Form for Cyber Incidents

That means segregation of duties, management of private keys that authorize transfers, limits on the size of a transfer, MFA on the use of the private key monitoring, alerting for large transfers, and endpoint detection on all employee devices, Bruggeman says.

Also key is user behavior analysis for all users. Architecturally, organizations like Binance should have custody mechanisms for protecting the cryptocurrency and wallets themselves, transaction controls on how to move the cryptocurrency, some kind of rate limits on withdrawals, identity and access controls, and segregation of duties so no one user can initiate and also finalize a transfer, Bruggeman says.

The Binance breach is an important reminder of why all organizations need to test the path that attackers can potentially take after gaining initial access to an environment and not assume that individual controls, each working as they should, are sufficient protection, analysts said. "The entry point and the damage can sit very far apart, so stop grading your security by how well the front door holds," says Waseem Ahmed, head of engineering at Secure.com.

The traditional approach to security is to check whether a request is valid. It almost never checks whether the action behind it should happen, he says. Available information suggests the attackers used Binance's own signing system to sign the transfers, so they looked valid on the way out. It was the "correct math, wrong decision," Ahmed says.

Security has to move from proving identity to governing consequences, he says. That means putting a human approval gate in front of any action that moves money or data, with limits that count across every system at once. "And test the whole route from laptop to payout, not each box on its own," Ahmed advises.

The Binance attack scenario can play out in any enterprise, too. "Swap out the withdrawal service for a payment system, a customer database, or a deployment pipeline, and this is an ordinary enterprise breach," he says. "A clean report from every tool you own tells you nothing about whether someone can walk from a laptop to the money, because no single tool is asked that question."

Robert Coles, senior manager of threat intelligence security at Black Duck, says the broader takeaway for organizations isn't really about cryptocurrency or the attack on Binance itself. Rather, it's about the blast radius, or what happens after initial break-in. It's one thing, he says, for an attacker to gain initial access. But turning that into a theft of billions of dollars is another entirely.

"Every organization has critical systems and privileged accounts where a compromise can have a much bigger impact," Coles says. "We spend a lot of time asking how we keep attackers out. We should spend just as much time asking, ‘If they do get in, what stops them next?'"

Security teams must assume something eventually will get compromised and make sure that one compromise doesn't become a catastrophic business event, Coles noted.

The Binance breach, the biggest ever by magnitude, is by no means the first to affect a major cryptocurrency exchange. In February 2025, Bybit lost approximately $1.5 billion in cryptocurrency after attackers manipulated a transaction approval process involving an Ethereum cold wallet. In May 2019, Binance itself lost 7,000 bitcoin after attackers obtained user API keys and two-factor authentication codes to bypass existing security checks. In October this year, attackers compromised a third-party script on Polymarket's website and used it to move funds from some user wallets.

North Korean threat actors have been especially aggressive in targeting crypto exchanges and wallets in general and account for 76% of all the money that traders have reported as stolen so far in 2026. In six of the past nine years, groups from the cash-strapped nation have accounted for at least one-third of all reported cryptocurrency theft.

Illinois-based Jai Vijayan is a veteran, award-winning technology journalist with more than 25 years of experience covering cybersecurity. His information security reporting has explored everything from ransomware, nation-state threats, and identity security to AI risk, critical infrastructure protection, software supply chain security, cloud security and emerging enterprise technologies.

Over the course of his career, Jai has written news stories, feature articles, survey reports, white papers, and e-books for enterprise and technology audiences. He has also moderated panel discussions and executive roundtables featuring CISOs, security researchers, and industry leaders.

His work has earned multiple industry honors, including a Joint ASBPE Excellence Award for Best Coverage of Government IT, and a Joint Jesse H. Neal Award for wireless LAN security coverage. Jai holds a Master’s degree in statistics from Bangalore University, and studied broadcasting and electronic communication at Marquette University in Milwaukee.

#9859. Welcome RL Environments to the hub

Reinforcement Learning environments give new capabilities to agentic AI systems, and they’re a great way to measure and improve performance in your agents. Therefore, Hugging Face Hub now has a special place for RL Environments.

An environment gives an agent a task, responds to its actions with observations, and scores the outcome. The resulting rewards can measure an agent's performance during evaluation or provide a learning signal during training. For an introduction to this interaction loop, see our blogpost on environments. Within the environment, the agent will perform a set of tasks that are represented as datasets. Therefore, environments can be split into broadly two parts: tasksets and runtimes. In this release, we are focusing on the tasksets.

An RL environment on the Hub is a dataset repo that shows up in the new RL Environments filter. The Use this dataset button gives you the command to run it in that framework. There is no new repo type, no registry, and no sign-up. There are already environments in Harbor, Verifiers, and NVIDIA NeMo Gym.

Every RL paper or framework uses its own way to find environments. Custom hubs, runtime registries, independent task datasets, or a GitHub list of tasks with a custom loader. This means that many of the published environments are siloed: if you publish an environment for one framework, users of the other three can’t load it. If you want to train on an environment from another framework or a new paper, you’ll need to port it by hand.

We think this is the wrong shape. An environment is tasks, tests, containers, and a reward rule, which are data with a runtime on top. The Hub already stores data, versions it, gates it, previews it, and serves it to millions of people. It does not need a second system to hold environments. It needs a way to say "this data is an environment, and here is how you run it."

The frameworks keep doing what they are good at. The Hub does what it is good at, which is hosting, discovery, and versioning. Nobody has to own the catalogue. In fact, catalogues can run on other platforms too, powered by the hub.

The dataset repository hosts your environment files. The framework runs them locally or on a supported cloud backend. Hugging Face Jobs can run cloud workloads, and Hugging Face Sandboxes, built on Jobs, provide interactive command execution. The tags describe compatibility and generate loading commands; adding a tag does not start a job or sandbox.

The RL Environments filter. Go to huggingface.co/datasets?other=rl-environment. Every dataset with the rl-environment tag appears there, whatever framework it works with.

Framework tags. Four environment frameworks are registered as dataset libraries:

Each framework tag puts the framework's icon on the dataset page and adds a generated snippet to Use this dataset.

A dataset can carry more than one framework tag. That is the point. Tags describe compatibility, and compatibility is not exclusive. Each listed framework must support the files in the repository; adding a tag does not convert them.

Choose the example for your framework and run it in a separate Python environment with the prerequisites listed below.

Harbor can load task directories from a Hub repository. The oracle agent runs the task's reference solution, then the verifier scores the result. It does not call a model.

The viewer shows the task's reward, verifier output, and logs. This checks the task and its reference solution before you try a model agent.

The Harbor integration of verifiers v1 can run the same task directories in different runtimes, such as Docker. It also supports different harnesses, including a minimal bash harness.

Here repo is the full Hugging Face Git URL, while dataset is the name and version in that repo's registry.json. This loader uses Harbor's registry conventions, so a bare Hub repo ID cannot replace both values.

OpenEnv's Harbor integration can run the same task directories with an agent such as OpenCode and return the verifier's reward alongside the agent's trace.

The command downloads the dataset's tasks/ directories, runs one task in Docker, and writes the result. The default connection uses a temporary Gradio tunnel so the sandboxed agent can reach OpenEnv's model proxy. Read the verifier result and the number of model calls:

A reward of None means no verifier reward was produced; inspect error before interpreting the run as a model failure. This path expects Harbor task directories.

NeMo Gym supports evaluation and RL training: its environments collect trajectories and compute rewards, while a training framework updates model weights. For example, the Structured Outputs dataset pairs prompts with JSON schemas. Its verifier rewards schema adherence; it does not check whether the generated content is factually correct.

The best part is that this gives one repo and one discussion tab where people report broken tasks from all major frameworks. So when an author fixes a bad test, every framework gets the fix on the next pull.

Open your dataset card and add this to the YAML header:

That is the whole integration. Keep rl-environment, then list every framework that can load your files. If your environment works with a framework we have not registered yet, open a PR to the list of supported libraries.

We opened PRs to tag some of the environments people already train on. If you maintain one of these, merge the PR and your environment shows up in the filter.

The first version generates one default snippet per framework. Per-config snippets are next, so a repo with several task sets can show the right command for each. After that we will look at structural detection for frameworks with strict layouts. It would also be really cool build custom task UIs, we’ve been experimenting with this here:

The bigger goal is for framework tagging to be automatic everywhere. OpenEnv already does it on upload. If you maintain Harbor, Verifiers, Nemo Gym, or any other environment framework, add the tags in your push path. It is a few lines, and every environment your users publish becomes visible to everyone else.

If you train agents, go browse the filter. If you build environments, publish and tag them, whether they cover coding, tool use, games, robotics, or another task. Include the files, a working run command, and the rule that produces the reward so others can use them. If your framework is missing, contribute it to the list of supported libraries.

libcurl runs in an estimated thirty billion installations today. InfoQ Homepage Podcasts Doing The Right Thing: Accountability In The Age Of AI Coding Summary

In this podcast, Shane Hastie, Lead Editor for Culture & Methods, spoke to Hugo Venturini about who is accountable when AI writes the code, how AI is reshaping code review and traditional engineering roles, and how leaders build a culture of transparency and psychological safety.

Presented by: Kiran Gangadharappa - Engineering Advisor at Harness, and Scott Davis - Senior Engineering Manager at Harness

Shane Hastie: Good day, folks. This is Shane Hastie for the InfoQ Engineering Culture Podcast. Today I'm sitting down with Hugo Venturini. Hugo, welcome. Thank you for taking the time to talk to us.

Hugo Venturini: Thank you, Shane, for having me.

Shane Hastie: Now, we are sitting in opposite sides of the world. I'm in New Zealand and you are somewhere in Europe.

Hugo Venturini: Yes, right now I'm in Spain, in Valencia.

Shane Hastie: Nice. You've got a beautiful warm summer. I'm sitting in a pretty cold winter, but we'll get past that. My normal starting point with these conversations is, who's Hugo?

Hugo Venturini: So I'm a software engineer. I defended my PhD on the debugging of optimized code in 2008. And after that, I joined the industry as a software engineer and I climbed the ladder one step after the other. Senior then manager. I was a manager at Meta, Facebook at the time. I was accountable for the type checker and the compiler of the hack language. Eventually I decided to try to create my own company, grew it, then joined another organization, was the CTO of Qwant, the search engine, 90 people in the organization from network engineers to AI researchers. And right now, I work in a software company, startup company that deals with tooling for AI, to help AI do the right thing, so to speak.

Shane Hastie: The right thing. What do we mean when we say, "The right thing", today?

Hugo Venturini: Somebody's making a decision about what should be provided as a product to users. Somebody's about to write the code. Somebody will test it. Somebody will make the decision to release this to prod and somebody will use it. It can be all different people or it can be the same person at every step. Doing the right thing, to me, is solving the problem to a user. And then at every step, you got doing the right thing of that step. And for a code generation, it is generating the proper code to some extent.

Shane Hastie: Now, somebody made a decision, but all too often today we are seeing the addiction of, "Yeah, but the agent did this. The code generator did this".

Hugo Venturini: I think humans are in charge and humans should be accountable and are, most of the time, at least to what I can see, and that's the right thing. I'm not minimizing what it does, but AI is just another tool. It's a very powerful tool. And don't get me wrong, I still got these wow moments several times, not a day, but at least a week. And yet if it fails, the one conducting this great tool is accountable, is in charge and should answer what goes wrong. Doing the proper thing is doing what the human asks it to do. And when you want to generate code, code has to be to the colon, to the semi-colon, to the character. And if it does not, many times, the proper tooling can actually tell the AI how to loop and give the right feedback. So when it comes back to the human, a great deal of what could be automated has been automated.

Shane Hastie: One of the things that we are seeing, and various studies are pointing to this, the size of pull requests are getting bigger and bigger. I've heard stories of the 2000 lines, a senior engineer who's got a backlog of over 300 pull requests, each of which is hundreds of lines long waiting to be reviewed.

Hugo Venturini: First, the size of pull request is a problem which does not rise with AI. It was already existing before. And the first thing is asking yourself, "Should I review everything?" Sometimes you got all that boilerplate. We could already, before AI, automate the verification. Let me do this. If it compiles, that's already a good thing. If it passes all the tests you've created, if it behaves the way you wanted it, do you really need to review the code? That was already not the case before.

Second thing is, already before as well, and I've lived in an organization that was working like this, you don't have to go for a signature of a diff for every single diff you do. Eventually people are good enough, senior enough or do trust each other that says, "I can totally merge this diff without having anybody reviewed it. And if it goes wrong, I'm accountable for fixing it. That'd be okay, but I'm totally sure and people trust me to merge it already". And sometimes you've got the heart of the product which you want to create and you need to be able to review for two reasons. First, for quality. Second, for sharing the knowledge, of course. And sometimes it's really just boilerplate that you can totally merge it.

With AI, big reviews always, and you can still, I believe, not go for who's got the biggest review, but who's handy enough to get your AI to create the proper diff and the proper stack of diff. So you get only one to review what the heart of the product is. I think with AI, because of the wow effect, some people are playing this game of the wow effect with, "Look, I have rewritten this entire big product in only one diff", which is just for the show. Let's face it, nobody does this. And before, at the group of engineers, if anybody were doing this, we were all telling him or her, "Please, help us review your code". That's one thing. And after that, you got the number of diffs and that's another problem.

How do you review for number of diffs? I don't have any good answer and I'm really eager to have anybody telling me, "How do you do this?" Right now, what we've decided in my team is we don't review everything. We were not reviewing everything before and we trust people with our own good judgments that this needs not being reviewed and we only ask proactively, "This, I want you to review it". I give you two other reasons for that. And this, I can merge it already. And so this minimize number of diffs to be reviewed by other people. But that's an open conversation I'm sure we all want to have, like, "How do others do about this?" And please, tell me.

Shane Hastie: We'll leave that as an open question for the audience to respond. So what are the implications of this in terms of the broader elements of quality in our product? And we think of the architectural frameworks and so forth, how do we make sure that we are building the right stuff?

Hugo Venturini: I got a story about rising quality in an unexpected way, at least for some. I worked with Microsoft in 2014 when they decided to merge the software engineer branch with the testers branch. At the time, testers were doing two things. Some were not coding, some were coding, and the software engineers were writing software and handing it to the testers for testing and was going back and forth. By removing the official testing step by somebody else, it actually raised the quality of the software. And the reason I believe is because it made software engineers accountable for the final product, not one step of the chain.

Today, I got the feeling that we are removing the software and everybody's becoming a tester via your AI, because you command some software which is written and then people become software. But we are all, again, merging those two verticals as one. And the difference is, we don't see an increase of quality yet, and I believe it's because people are still blaming the AI and don't feel accountable for what the tooling is doing. And that's one thing we totally need to work on as leaders, as managers, as colleagues, as users. I've seen some software I've been using definitely lacking quality over the last month. And I read in the press that those people are massively using AI and I'm like, "Maybe I see something here". And I'd like to know what kind of feedback I can give to get them back on quality.

Shane Hastie: So with collapsing roles, so you mentioned the engineer, the tester. What about the architect? What about the product manager? What about the security tester, the compliance elements?

Hugo Venturini: The more people you have in an org, the more narrowed focus you have for people. When you're in a startup company, you are everybody. The tester, the PM, the architect, and sometimes the users, the dogfooter and the HR and the finance, you're everybody. And the bigger the org grows and the more people you need in every single verticals, and eventually you have a PM for the front end, a technical PM for the backend. You're going to have a handful of software engineer for the front, from the back, for the queues, and the more it grows and then it becomes like an army of people working on it. And with AI, we try to shrink it back again to when the industry was growing, to when the company was growing and we face sometimes some misunderstanding of people who have never been a PM, even a bad PM, but when you have to be a PM because you're a startup company, you eventually do the job.

And when the AI comes, it really helps you. When you've never been, but you can be and you're asked to be, that's something you have to learn. I believe that we need some more trainings or help for all those people because AI really, really empowers you, but it empowers you to do things that you're not sure how to do, and that's where AI barely helps you. It always answers the question you're asking, but if you're asking the wrong questions and being a senior is asking the right questions, the good question that helps grow, that helps define, that's being a senior. Senior is, with experience and knowledge, you actually ask the question that helps move forward to a solution. And I believe we need to help people being better at asking the right questions to the AI, if you really want it to succeed.

Shane Hastie: It worries me that the software engineer who's being used to being asked to build this and given some sort of a spec, whether it's a set of user stories, a screen mock-up or just a quick conversation, we're now asking that person to think of the right questions to ask. What is the implication of that? We've spoken about shift left and shift right for the last couple of decades. We're shifting further left, but have we and how do we empower and give the people who are being now asked to do the questioning to do that left shift to know how to do that work?

Hugo Venturini: People dare to do things if they know they will be accountable but not blamed for what happens. And that's an organization, that's a human part of your organization. If you empower people, but they don't dare, you're just not doing anything. And that comes back to the human, to managers, to organizations. How do you empower your people and give them not only the tooling, but also the state of mind of stepping out of your comfort zone? I'm a software engineer and as I said, I have to also explore a broader space. What if I don't dare? What if I can't? Because even though I got all the tooling I have, I fear it. I fear the organization I work with. And that's something which is... This is a hard part. I mean, human is the hard part of the software industry, right?

Shane Hastie: So this is culture. This is the Engineering Culture Podcast. How do I nurture that culture?

Hugo Venturini: I'm not sure that the recipe... Sorry, I know there's no recipe. However, I got some good examples where I believe it was the right move. The first thing is transparency and honesty. If you are honest with your team, most of the time people start being honest. I eventually became the CTO of a company which had a broken culture. People would lie, hide, steal, everything was wrong. And I was asked to fix the culture, so to speak. And very quickly I decided to lead by example. So I started to have a Q&A every week. You can ask me any question. If I can answer, I answer. If I can't, you have to keep me accountable for answering the next time. And you ask me the question again, and if I don't answer, ask it again until you have the answer. No judgment about it. Of course, first Q&A, I only got easy questions.

People wouldn't dare to challenge the head of the org. And I started to come with answers such as, "I don't know. I made a mistake. This is a good thing. Congratulations, but you don't name people. You only name solutions and product. You are accountable for what you're doing and you take the load whenever. And coming back with the last time you asked me these questions and I found the answer and it is unpleasant, but you need to hear it and we are all in this together and gathering the thing". Eventually after a few sessions, people started to ask me difficult questions and eventually we started to go with even more difficult questions by allowing for an anonymous board. So I asked my managers, "What about you ask them if they have questions and if they have it on there, write it down and you ask it. Even better, you give it to another manager so I cannot even guess which team it comes from, but I want the questions. I don't care who ask it, so please dare".

And they started to organize this so I could never guess from which part of the organization the question was coming, but I got the questions and eventually people started to vote for questions and it grew like this and it becomes very interesting. Eventually people would stack questions before the Q&A. What I noticed in the org is, when I arrived, people would lie to me and I would see it. And I was like, "Okay, you can totally confront the person, 'You're lying to me, that's bad.'" I said, "No, no, no. It's a cultural thing. How do I take it as a whole and shift almost the entire culture of lying, of hiding things by being transparent and explaining things and showing them that I can be accountable and move forward and fix things?" Being exemplary is when you can totally break things as long as you've fixed them before and you learn a lesson and you don't repeat your mistakes.

Being wrong and making mistakes is totally acceptable. What is not acceptable is repeating your own mistakes because you have not learned, so you have not grown. And this cultural thing of allowing people totally shift the essence of this organization, which went much better by the time, but you also have to be patient. When you write software, you see it right away under your hands, maybe a few hours later. With humans, you need to learn patience, but eventually you see results.

Shane Hastie: Beautiful story and a great example of shifting culture. What if I'm not high enough up in the organization to do this?

Hugo Venturini: Okay. First, there's nothing as just a team lead. You are a team lead. That's not just a team lead. And at every level you got something to contribute to and to help grow. I've seen it work in smaller teams. Eventually I was in a startup company, a startup. We were already at 1200 in the company, so it was scale up, you say. And I found two teams were already working like this at their level. They were already working on this transparency and we are a team, but also we also need to be accountable. And I've seen it work. It was less efficient in terms of, I would say, impact because it was at the size of the one team and not the entire org, but already very interesting. And the good thing is, managers also gather together. I mean, as a manager, you have a team, but you are part of another team which is a team of managers.

And that's the difficulty of being a manager that most people don't get. First is, you're not only manager of a team, you are now a member of two teams with sometimes different goals or opposite goals. As a manager, you need to think outside of your own team to help the org at the size of every manager. As a manager of a team, you need to help the team grow and sometimes you have to make decisions that won't please either the rest of the managers or sometimes your team, and it cannot only be one way. You have to think outside of your own team to make it grow and make it better. And that's maybe the most difficult part of being a manager. And at every level, you always have a way to influence right outside. If you start to do the right thing and you actually see benefits, you can talk about it to other managers and eventually they will follow you and do the same thing and eventually it will grow. Okay, this is wishful thinking maybe, but if you don't try, you know it won't work, right?

Shane Hastie: Yeah. If you don't even try, you're guaranteed to fail.

Hugo Venturini: The way I see it is, as a manager, I'm here to help people. So I would always, not maybe always phrase it this way, but I'd say, "Help me help you". So if you provide the right information to your manager, your manager would be able to help you. If you hide too much, if you're too secret on some part of who you are or what you do, it becomes a little harder. You're not only a machine coding or being an engineer, you're also a human. And sometimes you got ups and downs and if you provide some information to help your manager, your manager can also totally help you. And that works at every level.

As a CTO, I was at the COMEX and talking with the CEO, the CFO, and if you give them some hints that they can help you because you are in a down moment or hub moment or you are available to help them, you become a member of the team. And it's not a day by day. It's an average, it's going to be 50/50 in the end, but it doesn't have to be you always being 50% helped and being helpful every day by the hour, by the week, it's overall. But it's kind of hard thing because you don't know when it ends.

Shane Hastie: We are dealing with people.

Hugo Venturini: I like to help people. I like to see people grow. Most of the time, staff relationship in helping people, and that's all why I moved to the management and leadership roles because I believe that most of people are better than I am at what they do in their job. So if I can help them be even better, it cascades to the next person and the overall organization grows.

Shane Hastie: So the manager as amplifier.

And that's also why when you got toxic management, it's devastating for an org. The impact is easier when you got people reporting to you, but also as easier, it's easier to destroy everything or to grow better.

Shane Hastie: We've handed a lot and given some good advice around that transparency and bringing that into culture and the culture of accountability without blame. What is the really important question that I haven't asked you?

Hugo Venturini: We've talked about management and the impact that come with the role. Is it possible to have the same kind of impact without being a manager? I've seen individuals being able to do this, and I've been always very much impressed by their level of influence, and I'm not sure I've deciphered how they were working. What I've seen is, those people were technically very strong, very humble, and the common characteristic of those people were like, they were always, always listening more than they were speaking. So yes, it is possible, but I'm also leaning towards the conclusion that it's not everybody is able to do it. There's something natural in those people, and when you ask them, they're like, "I don't know. I got it by chance. For some reason people are listening to me". I'm like, "Oh, come on, dude. You know that's wrong. You work on your skills, but also you've met the right people". Everybody's been mentored. Nobody came naturally to this kind of position.

Hugo Venturini: That's the one thing is, you can totally grow. It is possible, and it can be a north star to have this kind of influence. And if you don't reach this kind of influence, maybe you're too humble to understand that you are actually at this level of influence, and it is more probable that it's your humility that forgives you to see it than the fact that you are not at this level of influence. But yes, it is possible. It is a very tough career. Some of the best leaders I've met as ICs, many, many of them tried being manager for a while and came back. And the easiest and best seniors, staff, principal engineers I've managed knew the role of managers and knew how to help me as a manager.

So I would say give it a go. It doesn't have to last for your life. I mean, you can totally give it a try for a moment. I was an IC at Microsoft, became a manager, was hired as an IC at Facebook, became a manager, eventually created my company, was an IC, then became a manager, and then was hired as director, a CTO. I've been an IC for a bit more than a year. Going back and forth gives you all the understanding of the scope of what is it to create the product that answers a user's demand. In the end, it's just about this, I believe.

Shane Hastie: That pendulum swing across roles. You got a lot of really interesting and meaty stuff there. If people want to continue the conversation, where can they find you?

Hugo Venturini: They can find me on X/XTwitter as monsieurv. It’s French. My alias is monsieurv. And on LinkedIn, by my name, Hugo Venturini. Please, please come and discuss it all. You agree, you disagree, you have another story, you have questions, you have things to raise questions from me, because I'm very curious. Please keep this conversation going. I think it's a fascinating space, and we decided to be in this space because it is fascinating because the meeting of software and humans is an ongoing conversation that's going to be for life.

Shane Hastie: Hugo, thanks so much for taking the time.

Hugo Venturini: Thank you, Shane, for having me in your podcast. Very, very interesting conversation.

#9856. 3AM Affiliate Embraces AI-Like Loops in European School Attack

Evidence suggests a model may have generated and revised commands during the ransom gang's breach, though researchers stopped short of claiming full automation.

A 3AM ransomware attack targeting a UK school estate may provide an early look at how cybercriminals could use AI as a force multiplier rather than a replacement for human operators.

Bitdefender today published research concerning a "hybrid AI ransomware attack" observed in the wild, attributing certain actions taken to human or agentic elements. On the surface, the attack is fairly straightforward. As a blog post explained, a 3AM ransomware affiliate attacked a school in the UK, "then used ordinary Windows tools to build domain trusts and reach other schools."

Attackers stole backup credentials, created rogue domain-admin accounts, established trusts between previously separate Active Directory domains, moved between schools, stole data, and deployed 3AM ransomware. In other words, the attack largely followed a familiar ransomware playbook, despite Bitdefender's claims that AI helped execute parts of the operation.

Related:Extortion Group Luna Moth Flits Into Law Firms a Second Time

Where the attack got more interesting was how, as the security vendor argued, it didn't fit neatly into pre-existing buckets for attacks involving AI. It wasn't exactly an AI-generated attack where the malware was fully or largely created by a large language model (LLM); it wasn't exactly an AI-assisted attack where human engineers built the tools while using AI to speed up work; and it wasn't exactly an AI-operated attack where the LLM orchestrates actions and runs the show, as it were.

In this case, Bitdefender argued an AI system appeared to handle repetitive command generation and troubleshooting while a human operator made high-level decisions.

Many elements of the attack were ordinary for ransomware, such as significant use of living-off-the-land (LOTL) techniques, where attackers abuse tools already present on the victim's machine rather than relying on malware — in this case PowerShell, Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI), reg, netsh, rundll32, and other domain and scheduling utilities preinstalled on Windows. The attacker also used "an Impacket-style remote-execution tool," as well as Mimikatz and a previously published Veeam script.

But despite the attack's ordinary nature, Bitdefender assessed that several things suggest the use of an agentic loop, the control structure that makes an AI agent work. Certain actions appeared to be taken by a program rather than a human operator.

"The commands carry the usual tells of a model: a call to the backup software's web interface (Veeam, a widely used enterprise backup product) on a port and with a login method that do not match the vendor’s documentation, a mistake typical of writing from memory rather than from the manual (Veeam REST API authorization), along with confirmation files, self-labeled output and numbered revisions of the same script," the blog post read. "The retries behave like a loop too."

Related:'AdFection' Turns Ad Impressions Into Zero-Click Spyware Delivery

In another example, researchers assessed that the time taken between PowerShell command attempts was shorter than a human would take if issuing them by hand, but longer than if an LLM was orchestrating by itself. The longer time taken between individual tasks but the shorter time between retries "is what it looks like if a person is choosing the next step and a model is handling the retries."

Bitdefender caveated its findings by noting that it was unable to access the machine the attacker worked from, so it couldn't document anything tangible involving the AI model itself. The research acts as an argument that this attack behaves like a human operating alongside an agent, which is a working model defenders may wish to plan around.

With that in mind, Martin Zugec, technical solutions director at Bitdefender, tells Dark Reading that "a hybrid model is more reasonable for financially motivated cybercriminals, technically and economically, than a fully autonomous attack."

Related:Biomemory Launches DNA Shield, First Commercial Product Built on Its Molecular IT Platform

But even as a one-off, the situation is notable because the primary victim was an organization in a critical sector, and Bitdefender's anecdote suggests the affiliate may have used an AI agent to scale the attack by handling repetitive troubleshooting and command generation, although the report stops short of showing AI-enabled capabilities the attacker otherwise lacked.

Moreover, other similar institutions could fall in the crosshairs. "From a domain controller it enumerated trust relationships between domains and searched SYSVOL (the shared folder where Active Directory stores logon scripts, readable by any domain user) for the names and subnets of other schools," according to the research blog post.

The good news is that because much of this attack followed the typical ransomware playbook, the defender recommendations that stop regular ransomware would also stop the attack described in this research.

Zugec adds that agentic loops are noisy from an indicator standpoint, as many of their actions are repetitive and brute force in nature. "An agentic loop doesn’t make an attack quiet; it makes it repetitive: the same command re-run, small tweaks, numbered scripts and probe files left on disk. Even the quickest retries took 40 seconds or more. 'Machine speed' is mostly a marketing phrase about very expensive incidents; in real attacks, especially with local models, we expect this slower and noisier pattern. Speed isn't the giveaway; repetition is."

The vendor recommends focusing on prevention: Keep admin credentials of different domains separate, treat backups as a possible target, restrict remote execution and administrative shares to known management hosts, block interpreters and shells on machines that never use them, and put endpoint security tooling on every machine.

"Prefer controls that work regardless of volume and speed," the blog post read, "because they stop an action the first time and the hundredth."

#9855. [$] C++26 contract confusion

The International Organization for Standardization (ISO) has blessed seven C++ language revisions since 1998. The language is mostly developed by ISO's Working Group 21, which considers proposed additions and amendments, integrates them into a document, and then presents that document to the main ISO body to be voted on as a standard. On October 23, for the first time ever, ISO declined to ratify a document presented by Working Group 21, leaving the future of the C++26 standard in doubt. The decision was driven by controversy around a proposed new "contracts" feature that would add pre- and post-conditions to function signatures.

#9854. LLMjacking Emerges as Thriving Cybercriminal Enterprise

Cybercriminals have turned reselling cloud access to LLMs into a lucrative business model, with some victims paying as much as $1 million in resource consumption before access was revoked.

Cybercriminals have created a thriving business model out of stealing cloud access to commercial large language models (LLMs) and reselling it to paying customers, with the resource cost for victims reaching high as $1 million before access to their LLM was revoked.

The practice, called LLMjacking, has been around almost as long as LLMs themselves. However, now it's become an illicit enterprise on the underground market, providing a lucrative source of revenue for cybercriminals while victims are left to absorb the high cost of model usage, according to a report published Monday by Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) and Mandiant.

LLMjacking can create a massive spike in computing resources in a matter of hours, differentiating it from its more well-known cousin, cryptojacking, which gradually consumes resources. This has made it an attractive revenue stream for "a diverse set of financially motivated threat clusters operating out of multiple regions globally," Google researchers shared in the report.

Related:Attackers Say 'Hello' to a Different Scale of Cloud Attack

"Across individual incidents, we observed fraudulent charges associated with resource consumption exceeding $100,000 USD in a single day, with cumulative charges at some organizations reaching $1 million USD before access was revoked," they wrote.

The report details how attackers gain initial access to LLMs and achieve persistence on targeted networks, and describes the service model around LLMjacking that has become a lucrative endeavor for cybercriminals.

To gain initial access to an organization's LLM, attackers typically identify publicly exposed LLM endpoints or obtain valid LLM application programming interface (API) keys, according to Google.

"The dominant initial access vector has been exposed or stolen cloud identity tokens — including identity and access management (IAM) credentials, service account keys, GitHub personal access tokens (PATs), and active session tokens — which threat actors leverage to establish an initial foothold into target organizations' infrastructure," the researchers wrote.

Some attackers also deliberately keep their initial activity quiet to gain access to an organization's LLM, according to Google. The researchers observed the use of minimal API requests, sometimes containing just one output token, to validate stolen credentials without generating significant consumption.

This sneaky way to gain and then sell access to the LLM could mean organizations are giving up valuable resources without even knowing, while the attacker is cashing in, notes Nick Tausek, lead security automation architect at agentic AI firm Swimlane.

Related:External Teams Chats Anchor 15-Minute Malware Delivery

"By the time someone asks why the cloud bill has exploded, the attacker may already have paying customers," he says. "Selling stolen model access gives criminals a reason to keep that access working for as long as possible, which makes the quiet activity before the spending spike especially important."

This notably represents a detection challenge for organizations that need to identify early indicators of compromised identities, unauthorized permissions, and suspicious access to AI services rather than just look for unusual consumption, he says.

The report outlines several examples of how attackers compromised and LLMjacked organizations, demonstrating that there is not just one route to take for successfully and illicitly gaining access to an LLM.

In the middle of the year, for example, a threat cluster tracked as UNC6993 compromised a cloud instance through a misconfigured service account key and used it to grant further access to an LLM API. Attackers also hosted a session hijacking page mimicking an application portal to join a group of LLM users.

"This page tricks users into navigating to the legitimate LLM service website, and pasting their raw JSON payload containing an active access token, which was then posted to the backend API to bypass password and multifactor authentication (MFA) controls," the researchers explained.

Related:TiDB Breach Exposes Flawed Cloud Security Assumptions

In another instance, a threat actor gained initial entry by combining a stolen personal access token (PAT) to access private code repositories and a suspected Web application vulnerability in a package running within a containerized cloud environment.

Similarly, a different threat actor used compromised cloud federation tokens to programmatically generate new access keys that allowed the attacker to bypass MFA protections, according to Google.

Once access to an LLM has been gained, it then needs to be sold for attackers to make money. The key to this part of the LLMjacking business model is what is called an LLM Mixer, which is an underground service that turns stolen access to commercial AI models into a subscription business, according to Google. These services aggregate compromised credentials, route customer requests through victim environments, and offer access to premium models at prices significantly below legitimate market rates.

As the researchers describe it, LLM mixers act as illicit middlemen, allowing cybercriminals to resell access to compromised enterprise LLM accounts without their customers needing their own legitimate API credentials or cloud infrastructure.

"In one investigation, GTIG observed two distinct operational clusters coordinating to compromise and monetize enterprise LLM infrastructure, demonstrating the sophisticated specialization emerging in this space," the researchers wrote.

Indeed, LLM Mixers are an important part of the emerging LLMjacking ecosystem because they provide the monetization layer that makes stealing enterprise AI access financially attractive.

Since LLMjacking relies on victims being unaware for as long as possible, the key to not getting dinged with a huge resource-consumption bill is to catch on as quickly as possible to the intrusion.

To do this, defenders should prioritize IAM and supply chain security, two of the most common pathways for gaining access to and abusing cloud services, according to Google.

Other best practices for preventing LLMjacking in a cloud environment include good credential hygiene by using a centralized secrets-management platform; least privilege by ensuring users and service accounts only possess the permissions necessary for their specific role and required tasks; and code monitoring by automating secret scanning within codebases such as GitHub and GitLab.

Routine configuration audits, rate limiting, network allow listing, budget alerts, and MFA are also good defense strategies, according to Google.

She specializes in news coverage and analysis, using her years of experience to look at the current state of cybersecurity with a critical gaze. #9853. Holo4: powering generalist computer-use agents

Holo4 is our new series of agentic models. It comes in two sizes: 27B dense and 35B-A3B Mixture of Experts. Both are available on the H Models API. We are also releasing an updated version of Holotron 3: Holotron4 Nano.

Holo4 builds on our previous model and interacts with software through any available interface: GUIs, code, MCP and APIs. It scores well on academic benchmarks, but we built it for real business workflows. It was trained through supervised and reinforcement learning on a large set of environments and tasks, including those generated by our Agentic Task Factory.

Holo4 clicks and types on a screen, writes and runs its own code, and calls MCP or API tools. It uses whichever fits the task. Most agentic models are trained for one interface only: GUI-focused models are blind without a screen, while models that prefer tool calling are stuck in front of an application that has no API. Real work is not siloed that way, and a single business task can require combining these different approaches.

Holo4 runs on desktops, on the web, on Android, in a code sandbox and against business APIs. It is the same model in each case and it is called the same way. You do not need to select a different model for each platform.

Holo4 models improve significantly over their Qwen base. Holo4 trails only the strongest closed models on long workflows: on OSWorld 2.0, Holo4 27B scores 61.7% against 81.8% for Opus 5.5, and Holo4 35B-A3B reaches 30.9%. However, it does so with orders of magnitude fewer parameters and at a much lower cost. We open-source every trajectory behind our scores on public benchmarks: replay each step at trajectories.hcompany.ai or download them from Hugging Face.

On the hardest academic benchmarks for desktop control (OSWorld 2.0) and API use (AutomationBench), Holo4 competes with frontier models at a much lower cost per task.

OSWorld 2.0. Costs are estimated from the input and output tokens of each agentic run. Holo4 is priced at H Models API rates (single run). Qwen3.8 27B: model card score, cost from the tokens of our run at Alibaba Cloud list prices. Qwen3.6 35B-A3B: single run in our harness, at Alibaba Cloud list prices with cache hits at 20% of the input price. OpenAI launch data supplies the GPT and Opus effort sweeps; other closed and open-weight points use the official OSWorld 2.0 leaderboard. Releases, harnesses and task subsets differ. The line connects non-dominated score and cost pairs among the closed models; Holo4 is excluded.

AutomationBench. Holo4, Qwen3.8 27B and Qwen3.6 35B-A3B: AutomationBench v1.0.6, scores and costs measured in our internal harness. Other models: public-set scores from the AutomationBench README, cost per task from the official leaderboard, which runs on the private set. We will report Holo4 on the private set once it is evaluated.

Trained on environments and tasks from our Agentic Task Factory, Holo4 models excel on professional software. The examples below show Holo4 27B alongside Qwen3.8 27B, its base model. Same prompt and harness for both models.

Build a 3D model of the Eiffel Tower in FreeCAD, at a scale of 1 mm to 1 metre, centred on the origin and aligned to the X and Y axes. Work to this design.

The tower is square in plan at every height, never round. Its half-width, measured from the central axis out to the corner, is 62.5 mm at ground level, 32.5 mm at height 57, 17.5 mm at height 115, and 9.35 mm at height 276. Between those heights the half-width follows a smooth curve that falls steeply near the ground and gently higher up, never a straight line.

Four identical legs, one per quadrant, each a square column whose outer corner follows that profile. Each leg is 14 mm across at the ground and tapers to 4 mm at height 276. The legs stand apart from the ground up to the first platform, and converge as they rise. Nothing fills the space between them: the tower is open, and you can see straight through it from every side.

Three platforms, each a solid square slab centred on the axis: 72 mm across and 4 mm thick at height 57; 40 mm across and 3 mm thick at height 115; 22 mm across and 3 mm thick at height 276.

A mast from height 276 to 324, square, 8 mm across at its base tapering to 2 mm at the tip.

Every part must be a closed solid with non-zero volume, and no part may fill the space between the legs.

Build a 3D model in FreeCAD of the H company logo: a solid filled disc beside a blocky sans-serif capital letter H, both extruded to the same thickness, the two shapes of similar height and set apart so they do not overlap, with the centre of the disc level with the middle of the H. Colour both shapes black.

Build a Pac-Man-style game in Godot and leave it running.

A rectangular maze of walls laid out on a grid, with pellets filling every open corridor. A player marker moves continuously along the corridors, eating each pellet it passes over and scoring a point for it. Three ghosts move through the same corridors and chase the player. If a ghost catches the player, the player loses a life and everything resets to its starting position. Score and lives are drawn on screen.

No one is going to play this. The player drives itself with a simple heuristic: at each junction it heads toward the nearest pellet, unless a ghost is close, in which case it moves away from the ghost. The game must run unattended and indefinitely, with no keyboard input at all.

When it works, start the game and leave it playing.

Holo4 27B (68 calls, 2.4M tokens, 268 lines)

Qwen3.8 27B (197 calls, 11.4M tokens, 327 lines)

Our internal set of agentic pipelines builds interactive environments and verifiable tasks from documentation alone, such as screenshots of real websites or open-source software. So far it has produced about 10,000 tasks across web apps, MCP servers and desktop environments, including hybrid environments that expose the same state through a GUI and MCP.

Alongside training, we rebuilt our harness, the loop that executes the model's actions and manages its context over hundreds of steps, using feedback from agentic performance on OSWorld 2.0. Agents tagged why each task failed and engineers reviewed their fixes. The largest changes were giving the agent a reliable memory that can keep track of hundreds of steps, and a shell on the desktop machine itself.

Opus 5 (70.2%) and GPT-5.6 Sol (66.2%) use max-effort partial rewards on the v2026.08.08 offline set from OpenAI's launch chart, as in the cost-performance plot. Other reference scores come from model cards and the official leaderboard. Task releases, subsets and harnesses vary.

Our post-training stack is designed to adapt to new foundation models and produce agents that generalize across interfaces and environments. As a member of the NVIDIA Nemotron Coalition, we applied our latest stack to the Nemotron 3 Nano Omni model as a follow-up to Holotron 3.

The same recipe turns Nemotron 3 Nano Omni into Holotron4 Nano, a generalist agentic model that significantly improves over the base model on GUI workflows and in environments exposing MCP, APIs or coding sandboxes.

Gains are absolute percentage-point improvements over Nemotron 3 Nano Omni.

These gains show that our recipe transfers well and can turn a generalist model into an agentic expert. Nothing in it is size-specific.

Both sizes are available today on the H Models API. Weights are on Hugging Face in BF16, FP8, NVFP4 and 4-bit GGUF, next to our small model, Holotron4 Nano.

We will release optimized DSpark drafter checkpoints in the coming days to further accelerate inference.

#9852. Introducing Polo: a Wayland MATE compositor

Kerem Söke has announced the 1.0 release of Polo, a Wayland compositor for the MATE Desktop Environment:

The idea is to keep MATE behaving as closely as possible to how it does on X11, rather than changing the desktop to fit a different compositor. [...]

Window management, metacity, workspaces, tiling, XWayland, clipboard and clipman support, multiple monitors, display scaling, hotplugging, screenshots, screen sharing, and session management are all working.

I've also added desktop effects: fade, zoom, zap, spin, squeemize, magic lamp, desktop cube, expo, and wobbly windows.

Söke is looking for people to test Polo, particularly on multi-monitor setups, and report back with problems.
