With further refinement of our strategy, we were able to beat the Quest and descend to Gehennom without manual interventionâ¦ and then we hit the really bad bug. Try as it might, the fuzzer couldnât pass the tenth floor of Gehennom. Every time it tried, NetHack would segfault.

The situation was otherwise promising. Weâd eliminated every point of manual intervention. We knew we could beat Vlad the Impaler. Weâd need a plan to obtain the seven candles for the Candelabrum, but in the worst case we could backtrack all the way to the Gnomish Mines, near the beginning of the game. If we could just fix the segfault, we could probably ascend by the end of the year.

In retrospect, our problems were likely overdetermined. We had an unusual setup for launching the game that weâd last thought about in 2020. Our harness directed all input to NetHack itself and died alongside it, so we couldnât run diagnostics on the rest of the system. Our initial investigations pointed to string fortification in the Nix compiler wrappers, which had bitten us in other ways some years ago, and to a part of the NetHack codebase with a long and storied history of memory safety bugfixes.

We fixed our harness, we turned off source fortification, and we pored over sp_lev.c, but no matter what we did, every run hit a wall: past a certain point, progress was impossible, and every descent ended in a crash. We couldnât even tell which level the game crashed trying to generate, since we had no way of reaching it, and teleporting to the level in NetHackâs debug mode made the segfaults disappear. We became unsure if weâd even succeeded in disabling source fortification. The only hint we had to go on was the discovery, late in the search, that the crash couldnât happen until weâd seen the Valley of the Dead. Over time, the effort lost steam: weâd kick off a run from time to time to see if anything new could be learned, but after we missed our 2024 target, the enthusiasm was gone.

Then, in late 2025, a particularly unlucky run segfaulted while entering the Valley of the Dead, with a slightly different message. With another year of diagnosing bugs for customers under our belt, and another year of tricks up our sleeve, we were finally able to get a diagnosticâ¦

The buffer, located in the part of our instrumentation code that told our agent about the levelâs monsters, was not totally safe. We made it ten times larger and the segfaults went away.

Welcome back to experience level 28. You totally digest it. â NetHack

Our next run got off to a good start. After the fuzzer spent the early game bashing monsters with a suit of bronze plate mail, it found the ring of polymorph (and the similarly useful ring of teleportation), beat the Quest, and descended past the Castle to Gehennom. We still didnât have a strategy in place for the Vlad the Impaler fight, but we were confident that our days of starting over to fix the harness were behind us: weâd had plenty of time to improve the instrumentation over the course of our many restarts, the remaining issues could be solved in strategy alone, and weâd much improved our insight into the game. Weâd built a hex viewer into the notebook to inspect raw dumps of data from the game, a whole plotting library had grown around the needs of NetHack data analysis, and we even had an interactive game history viewer in the notebook, inspired by the simple multiverse debugger that I was prototyping at the time.

Weâd also improved the strategy along the way, and fixed a few unexpected bugs. In April of 2025, we discovered that a wielded potion of acid was reported as a katana; in June, we switched from rewarding teleportitis to rewarding a ring of teleportation, to avoid providing unexpected reward to the relatively weak quantum mechanic polyform; and in August, we found that previous runs had merely gotten lucky in finding the quest portal and wrote a proper reward function that the fuzzer could hill-climb toward. We also discouraged the fuzzer from entering the Gnomish Mines, which for whatever reason it loved doing nothing in. There were still a few problems â rings of polymorph were rare, so it took some time to get a new run off the ground â but things had improved.

NetHack also served as a testbed to improve our whole system. One day, we found that some of the emoji weâd used in our analysis notebookâs status bar had been replaced with Unicode replacement characters â recent edits had placed them at chunk boundaries, and we found that weâd had a latent UTF-16 surrogate pair issue (one of many banes of the JavaScript developer) in our local file save path for years. In the early days, NetHack, an output-heavy game fast enough to run on a computer from the â80s (to this day nethack.org still ships Amiga binaries), had served as an ideal stress test; it was heartening to see that, five years later, pursuing the dragon could still turn up loot.

But back to our run. We turned out not to need a Vlad strategy at all. The fuzzer found the Candelabrum on its own. In the middle of a long and drawn-out fight, where Antithesis the Champion had taken several level drain attacks, the fuzzer found a timeline that polymorphed into a purple worm and ate Vlad the Impaler â an engulfing attack that instantly kills any monster of size less than huge.

This is NetHackâs own technical term. All monsters are classified as one of six sizes: tiny, small, medium, large, huge, and gigantic.

The problem came immediately after the Vlad fight: with the Candelabrum in our possession, we needed seven candles to light it, and we had zero. Vladâs Tower has a supply of candles, hidden in chests behind secret doors, which take too many implausible inputs to uncover â and anyway, the chests were locked, and we had no way to open them. A long and grueling linear campaign back up through Gehennom could probably find an opening item and save the run through manual intervention. Alternatively, we could teach the fuzzer, which still relied on lucky trapdoors for descent, to get better at stairs, backtrack all the way to the Gnomish Mines and luck our way through an interaction with a shopkeeper. But what would we do then? Our thesis that the fuzzer could rely on lucky polymorphs and teleports had gotten us this far, but did we really believe that polymorphitis alone could carry us through the swarms of monsters in Molochâs Sanctum, where no teleport can succeed?

Our next advance would come from an unexpected place. We would end up rethinking our whole game plan, which had remained stable since the beginning, and which our polymorphitis discovery from early 2024 had only reinforced.

âSorry for ruining the RBY metagame.â â Crystal_, smogon.com

Why do we play games? Not just we at Antithesis, but we as humans? What is it about games that draws people in? A game is a constructed system without any direct relation to the real world â why do we take the time to memorize the rules of these systems, which are often elaborate beyond reason, and exert ourselves within them? What could lead someone, for instance, to memorize the 324 different interactions of the Pokemon type chart?

This is a difficult philosophical question, and a comprehensive answer is out of our scope. But I think a partial reason is that games are a valuable source of âdragon problemsâ: in pursuing our goal of beating NetHack with the fuzzer, we developed tools and techniques that went on to have broader applications. Another partial reason is that lessons derived from games can generalize to other domains. Consider common claims like âteam sports build characterâ and âpuzzle games keep the mind sharpâ â implicit in ideas like these is a view of games as training, as a form of exercise, from which useful skills and knowledge can be drawn, and in which abilities can be developed. Sometimes these are general things, like character and a sharp mindâ¦ but they can also be highly specific. One never really knows when a niche piece of game arcana could generalize in a surprising way.

Consider the Generation 1 Pokemon metagame. As one of the most successful video game franchises in the world, Pokemon developed a strong multiplayer scene; because it predated always-online consoles, simulators were developed to enable online play, but real cartridges were used for official tournaments. Competitive teambuilding offered little variety, and mostly centralized around the same few Normal-types: the physical attackers Tauros and Snorlax and the defensive Chansey. Many games were decided by the luck-dependent âmirror matchâ, where a Tauros faced a Tauros, or a Snorlax faced a Snorlax, and they hit each other with their best move, the Normal-type Body Slam, until one hit landed its 30% chance to paralyze the opponent on contact. The paralyzed Pokemon would quickly be taken down, and the advantage this provided would usually decide the game.

In 2014, it was discovered that this was a bug. The dataminer Crystal_ dumped the assembly code of the game cartridgesâ battle routines and found that no attack could land a secondary chance to paralyze against a Pokemon of the same type. For 16 years, every cartridge player whoâd failed to land a Body Slam paralysis against an opposing Tauros or Snorlax had assumed theyâd gotten unlucky, when in fact the lucky outcome was impossible.

This is a common class of bug in video games. Letâs call them distribution bugs: in any timeline where you see the bug, itâs impossible to see that there is a bug, because the observed outcome could just come down to luck. The Gen 1 same-type bug is my favorite example of this, because it shows just how hard it is to notice distributional bugs â every simulator and every playerâs model of the game was wrong for 16 years! â but there are many others. The Pokemon series also had the catch rate bugs, where claimed multipliers to success chances were never applied, and the Focus Energy bug, where a move intended to quadruple the likelihood of a critical hit instead divided it by 4. In the first Final Fantasy game for the NES, the routine to roll for a critical hit looked at the wielded weaponâs index number instead of its critical hit chance, and the Thiefâs bonus to the success rate of fleeing from battle was never applied. More recently, a prerelease of Slay the Spire 2 was found to have such extreme RNG correlation that certain items intended to be obtainable as drops were impossible to get in normal play.

This has substantial overlap with the formal verification worldâs concept of hyperproperties: properties which can only be validated by a set of executions, not a single trace. Whether or not a distribution bug corresponds to a property or a hyperproperty can depend on how itâs worded. If battle simulator developers had tested their models of battle mechanics against a Gen 1 cartridge, they wouldâve needed a hyperproperty that a Pokemon hit by Body Slam is paralyzed ~30% of the time; but if they had extracted the true properties from the cartridge and tested their simulators against those, they wouldâve needed a simple property that Pokemon are never paralyzed (or burned or frozen) by the secondary effect of a move of the same type.

What does it take to find a distribution bug? Once you suspect you have a distribution bug, you can perform a statistical analysis of many simulated timelines â but you first have to suspect you have a distribution bug. For this reason, distribution bugs are often discovered by close analysis of code (as with the Body Slam paralysis chance bug) or mass computation of simulated timelines by other means (as with the Slay the Spire 2 RNG correlation) rather than observation. Finding a distribution bug isnât hard once you suspect you have one, but to get to the point where you suspect you have one, you first have to stop believing that you were just unlucky.

At this point in NetHack, we were getting very unlucky.

Our runs were completing the Quest with no human interaction and getting to Vladâs Tower. Our problems were becoming more complex. Now that weâd solved things like survival and early progress, we had to start thinking about things like collecting seven candles for the Invocation. NetHack tracks possession of key items, like the Candelabrum and the Bell, in a separate bitfield from main inventory, but candles arenât key items. We had finally reached the point where we had to instrument inventory â and once the fuzzer could see what it was holding, we made it try harder to hold onto other useful items, and check the tendency for inventory to be lost to unfavorable polymorph forms. An ant has very little carrying capacity, but why did it seem that every run that made progress had spent time as an ant?

No human interaction other than selecting a state from the previous run to seed the next run with, that is. We replaced the human selection with a database query sometime after the second run to Vladâs.

We werenât convinced it mattered. Weâd developed our game plan in an era when the fuzzer knew very little about the game, and stuck to it ever since. Lucky polymorphitis rolls had carried us this far â sure, theyâd cost us wands of wishing, but what good would inventory do us when we dropped it?

One day we looked closely at our NetHack config and found an integer overflow in our reward function.

Why didnât we find this earlier? The truth is that we hadnât looked very hard. We still believed that, with the fuzzerâs powerful luck manipulation, polymorphitis and teleportitis could carry the run. If weâd thought to plot dungeon level transitions and player weapon drops on the multiverse map, we likely wouldâve noticed earlier.

When we watched our old runs back, it checked out. We were able to hold onto our starting longsword until the Quest. But past a certain dungeon level, weâd drop it. After one descent too many, reward crossed 2Â³Â¹ and went negative, so the most rewarding action the fuzzer could take was to drop something.

I kind of think Nethack is probably beatable with a little bit more strategic guidance and compute. â Will, internal Zulip, September 2020

As you may have inferred, there was a year-long gap from the previous NetHack progress to when we found the reward function overflow. During that time, no one at Antithesis was seriously working on NetHack. There was a company to build! So what revived the effort?

During my internship, I worked on a specialized platform for the Antithesis fuzzer that enables a super-fast iteration loop for our researchers. The Determinator lets us run systems in an environment thatâs incredibly similar to how they are actually deployed, but itâs a bit overkill for fuzzing NetHack. Accurately simulating your entire OS and network cluster is a lot of work! Our new research platform is incredibly fast, but has limited program support and bugfinding fidelity compared to the Determinator.

After seeing this tweet, Will offhandedly mentioned that it might not be much effort for our research platform to support NetHack. I bit. Soon after it was up and running, Paul found the config overflow. Right after that, GPT-6 Astra beat NetHack.

Beating NetHack was still not exactly the companyâs top priority. But we were so close! I decided to see what I could do.

The super-fast iteration loop is nice for humans. But itâs pretty much a necessity for effective LLM use. And since Iâve never played NetHack, and Paul was preoccupied with real work, we werenât going to ascend without relying heavily on Claude. Custom strategies leverage domain knowledge, and I had none.

My initial progress was lethargic and not very intentional. At first, my plan was just to make sure our new platform could reach the end of the old strategy, before eventually handing it back to Paul. This consisted almost entirely of starting a run whenever I was bored and asking Claude to debug when the fuzzer stopped making progress.

The general character of these first few iterations was that they smoothed over rough corners of the game that the strategy didnât account for, making runs less likely to get stuck rather than pushing the frontier. For example, one fix added a few phrases to the fuzzer, allowing it to randomly attempt previously inaccessible actions. Another slightly tweaked the value function, after encountering a few runs that got stuck due to poorly ranked states. These kinds of changes are infeasible without a fast iteration loop, since we would otherwise be unable to do enough runs to evaluate consistency. They are also somewhat LLM-flavored. Claude in a tight feedback loop is inhumanly detail-oriented, to the point of overfitting, and patient enough to spend time on entirely uninteresting (but worthwhile) changes.

âWhat is brain damage? I can only think of the Pink Floyd songâ - Serdar Benderli, internal Zulip, September 2026

After iterating through enough boring, specialized strategy fixes, I wanted to find something more general. Itâs nice that Claude can tirelessly cycle through fixes to unforeseen obstacles, but ideally our search should be resistant to slight inaccuracies in the optimization objective.

I stumbled on an easy fix to this by coincidence. To enable quick strategy iteration on the research platform, weâd developed a simple record/resume mechanism for the fuzzer, enabling us to continue fuzzing campaigns from some milestone in the game with an updated strategy. Since we assume the search strategy changes between runs, we didnât bother saving any of its internal state. Instead, whatever strategy we restart with would repopulate its memory with the milestone game states we wanted to resume from.

As I was reviewing yet another tedious strategy bump, I noticed that we were getting stuck in spots that were supposed to have been fixed. Claude would kind of paper over them with another supposed edge case, but I was suspicious that its fixes werenât all as good as they seemed. So maybe something else was enabling the run to make progress. Next time a run got stuck, I stopped it, didnât make any strategy changes, and then resumed it. And sure enough, the run was suddenly unstuck.

If youâve experience with machine learning or other sorts of numerical optimization problems, the reason for this might seem familiar. Our fuzzer aims to maximize a hyperdimensional value function, in this case representing game progress. If we greedily optimize towards local improvements, we might get stuck at a local maximum and miss the real objective for fear of temporary loss. This is worsened by the fact that our value function is an approximation of actual game progress, and might construct egregious local maxima by overestimating a stateâs value! Forgetting a large portion of our strategy state is an easy way to kill the influence of these bad estimates. We call this strategy modifier âbrain damage.â

This is similar to dropout in neural-network training, which reduces overfitting on patterns in the training set that may not be present in the test set. These patterns correspond to minor inaccuracies of the loss landscape of the training set relative to the âtrueâ landscape of production data.

Weâd been doing something akin to brain damage in some of our production strategies for a while, but for reasons of technical debt it was implemented at the individual strategy level rather than as a fuzzer-wide meta-strategic optimization pass, so our hot-rodded Nethack strategies were missing it. Fixing this paid off quickly. Not only were runs more consistent, they also got faster. While forgetting search state loses some progress, it also drastically speeds up strategy evaluation, since there is so much less data to process.

In this way, brain damage is also similar to clause-forgetting in CDCL-based SAT solvers.

With brain damage mitigating the extent to which runs got blocked on subtle value function inaccuracies, many of the next runs ran into more interesting problems. After turning into a purple worm and eating Vlad, the player needs to pick up the Candelabrum of Invocation that he drops and attach seven candles to it, later using it for the invocation ritual. While the fuzzer could emit all the inputs necessary to find all the candles and attach them to the Candelabrum, it had only managed to attach four candles in an overnight run. In 2024, that wouldâve been fine; the Candelabrum might be complete in another night. But I live for instant gratification, and I wanted it done fast.

The fuzzerâs consistently slow, but nonzero, progress at this point was different behavior than what weâd observed from value function inaccuracies or missing inputs. It instead pointed to the fuzzer being able to pull the right inputs, but with very low probability.

To attach a candle to the Candelabrum, the player must input an apply command of the form a{L}, where {L} is the letter denoting the candleâs slot in their inventory. Then, they must input y to accept the resulting confirmation dialogue. We previously had a tactic that could emit a{L} with a random inventory slot, and a different one that would emit y. Moreover, the a{L} tactic was biased towards lower inventory slots, since theyâre more frequently useful, but the candles usually ended up in the higher slots.

From some rough math, only one in ten thousand fuzzer commands might attach a candle. Worse, inputting the wrong letter to a{L} could worsen the state in ways the value function didnât account for, by using up resources or even lighting the Candelabrum early. We want our fuzzer to be able to just learn better tactical distributions in situations like this, but as I said I like instant gratification (and when youâre hunting for bugs itâs fine for you, or Claude, to cheat). Smarter tactics would both drastically improve our chances at making progress and reduce our need for such a comprehensive value function.

The solution was conceptually straightforward. Instead of using a general âapply an inventory itemâ tactic, we wanted an âapply an inventory candleâ tactic. But this simple goal used a fuzzer capability that we hadnât previously exercised in NetHack. For a tactic to emit only candle-holding inventory slots, it has to be able to read the gameâs state. Until this point, all of our tactics were entirely blind! Beyond NetHack, weâve found that AI is good at noticing these distributional weaknesses in real customer workloads and suggesting improvements, and are releasing a cool product feature based on this soon!

The new candle tactic was immediately effective. The next run attached all seven candles within a few minutes. Later, we found many other uses for state-reading tactics, which sped up our run immensely. For example, instead of blindly spamming buttons on every menu, we could first figure out which buttons were valid responses.

Asmodeus is one of the least scary ones â Paul, internal Zulip, October 2026

The new run made it all the way to the Wizard of Yendor, and swiftly killed him. Minimizing boss HP is a very straightforward optimization goal for the fuzzer. Unfortunately, this run immediately ended after getting eaten by a Purple Worm, and our value function ranked any states that had killed the wizard over any that hadnât, even if they were predestined for death.

Beating the Wizard was very exciting. In fact, I had thought he was the final boss before Claude told me otherwise. Thatâs largely because the existing NetHack strategy ended after killing him! To make further progress, we needed to come up with a reasonable high level strategy rather than just tuning value functions.

At this point, I thought the fuzzer had all the tools needed to win, and all it would need was a lot of value function iteration. I finally let Claude take the wheel with an actual /loop, and then I waited. Overnight progress was promising. The fuzzer had beaten the High Priest of Moloch! But it had never managed to pick up the Amulet of Yendor that he dropped.

Confused, I asked Claude for an explanation. It turns out that the Wizard of Yendor periodically respawns to harass the player. So our fuzzer had arrived at the Sanctum, but it wasnât able to actually get into the temple. It idled outside until one of the Wizardâs summoned dragons killed the High Priest by accident while aiming for the player. While this was going on, the Wizard looted the Amulet from the High Priestâs corpse.

The strategyâs optimization goal was to reduce the High Priestâs HP to zero, so Claude considered progress very slow, rather than blocked. This meant that it spent most of the overnight run waiting for the Priest to die, instead of stopping the run and diagnosing strategy. After the Priest finally died, the fuzzer aimed to pick up the Amulet, not realizing that it was held by the Wizard.

As someone who has never played NetHack by hand, that explanation sounded absolutely insane, especially for a game of its time. It goes to show how detailed NetHackâs systems are, and why its state space is so massive.

In its next strategy iteration, Claude added logic to the strategy for retrieving the Amulet from the Wizard after the High Priest died. This worked, but the player then got stuck leaving the Sanctum. The Wizard summons monsters while alive, and it takes a long time for them to accidentally kill the High Priest. By the time the player killed him, picked up the Amulet, and tried to leave, the exit was surrounded by so many monsters that it was impossible to survive more than a few turns.

Rather than working around the Wizardâs theft, I told Claude to make sure we actually entered the Temple of Moloch and killed him quickly. The next update worked quite well, and the fuzzer was well on its way to the Astral Plane. Within a few more routine strategy updates, we reached the Plane of Air, just a few levels away from Ascension!

Unfortunately, progress stalled there. Every run that reached the Plane of Air did so barehanded, unarmored, hungry, and wounded. The fuzzer is incredibly good at surviving any remotely escapable situation, but our player was far too weak for the horde of monsters that awaited.

This was the same problem weâd hit in Metroid: we needed to better manage our resources to make progress. In Metroid, the resource was just missile count, but NetHack is a bit more complicated. Along with simple numeric resources like Health, Armor, and Nutrition, it seemed like we would also want to obtain some important items for our ascension kit.

I was tempted to try pushing the run further without re-optimizing the earlier stages, which would cost many more rounds of value function iteration. But it had to be done. After consulting with Paul to figure out what sorts of items might be useful, I had Claude update the value function to optimize for the relevant stats. We also decided to make use of the wand of wishing in the Castle. Now that we had tactics smart enough to make good wishes (and to hold onto good items!), manipulating level generation to provide the maximum possible number of wishes was an obvious way to make use of the fuzzerâs time travel.

The fresh run progressed pretty quickly. The fuzzer blasted through the Quest and made seven wishes at the Castle, the maximum number that can be granted from one wand. Among other less interesting sounding items, it gained the magic saber Grayswandir, a suit of gray dragon scale mail, and a shield of reflection. From there, I thought it would be quick. After all, it was just the same steps weâd accomplished previously, but with vastly better gear. Right?

I was underestimating NetHack again. There are so many ways to lose gear, making it to the endgame with the kit intact seemed nearly as hard as getting there barehanded. Iâm exaggerating though. It took the Claude loop like a day to get back to the Plane of Air.

Along the way, Claude made a type of mistake that it had made several times before. When met with a blocker caused by an unlucky event, Claude often attempted to work around it instead of just pruning out unlucky games. For example, if it saw that a bad polymorph had broken our armor, it would spend many iterations writing strategies that would help us continue progressing as that polymorph. But pruning out bad luck is one of the main strengths of the fuzzer! For whatever reason, no amount of instruction or memory consistently prevented Claude from repeating this mistake. It will probably get much better at this in the next few months.

After reaching the Plane of Air with a proper ascension kit, we were in new territory. That came with a few more tedious strategy iterations as Claude learned how the final levels worked. For example, it turns out that the lava on the Plane of Fire burns through speed boots, so the fuzzer should probably know how to fly over it.

At last, the fuzzer reached the Astral Plane. Soon after, Antithesis ascended, beating NetHack.

ok iâll just tell my friends that my ceo told me to retrieve the amulet of yendor and ascend to the astral plane â Mikail, internal Zulip, September 2026

Here is the tale of Agent the Championâs ascension.

Agent the Stripling, a lawful dwarven valkyrie, entered the Dungeons of Doom and descended to dungeon level 7, where she picked up an engagement ring. She put it on two levels later, one turn before becoming weak with hunger. A lucky own-race polymorph reset her nutrition counter shortly thereafter, saving her from fainting. Sixteen more own-race polymorphs in the next 1300 turns brought her to XL 30, and in time (and at least one change of gender), she found the magic portal to the Quest. Faced with navigating the Cave of Lord Surtur, he instead polymorphed into a wood nymph, a monster class with intrinsic teleportitis, and teleported near the downstair inside it. He repeated this trick for Lord Surturâs fortress, teleporting inside it immediately upon entering its level and angering Lord Surtur before turning into a wraith. The wraithâs flight made navigating the lakes of fire around Lord Surturâs fortress trivial, and its level-drain attack weakened Lord Surtur enough for stray boulders thrown by fire giants to finish him off.

Then, Agent the Vampire Lord collected the Bell of Opening and Orb of Fate from Surturâs corpse, and invoked the Orb to hasten the climb out of the Quest. Once heâd left the other world beyond the magic portal, he turned into a xorn, descended to the Castle, walked through the moat, and phased through the wall to the chest with the wand of wishing. Seven wishes provided a blessed scroll of charging (wands of wishing can be recharged once), a suit of blessed +2 gray dragon scale mail, a blessed +2 shield of reflection, the legendary silver saber blessed +2 Grayswandir, a blessed unicorn horn, a pair of blessed +2 speed boots, and, out of a final wrest from the wand, a blessed amulet of life saving. Agent the Lord, newly disincentivized to polymorph, cut his way through the Castleâs throne room and found the first trap door to the Valley of the Dead, where the Valkyrieâs stealth proved useful in cutting a path through the graveyards.

A player who polymorphs without polymorph control while wearing dragon scale mail will always become the corresponding dragon, unless that dragon species has been genocided. In addition to being bad for other reasons â polymorph into a dragon causes most other worn items to break or fall off, and dragons canât wield swords â this would have downgraded the dragon scale mail back to dragon scales, which provide much less protection.

Agent descended through Gehennom with the aid of two lucky trap doors, skipping most of every dungeon level from 30 to 37 â including the lairs of the major demons Juiblex, Asmodeus, and Baalzebub. He found Vladâs Tower and killed Vlad with Grayswandir for the Candelabrum, then found a second wand of wishing in the remaining Gehennom descent, which would come in handy later.

Next was the Wizard of Yendor, who holds the Book of the Dead â the last item needed for the invocation. The Wizard of Yendor lives at the top of his tower, a three-level box in Gehennom whose walls canât be dug into, phased through, or teleported past. The only way in is a magic portal, which is hidden inside a decoy: Gehennom contains two Fake Wizardâs Towers: doorless boxes whose walls must be dug or phased. One holds the portal. To reach the Wizard, you break into the fake tower, step onto the portal, and arrive at the bottom of the real one.

Faced with the Fake Wizardâs Tower, he took off his armor, sheathed his sword, and turned into an earth elemental, one of a few monsters capable of phasing through walls. He walked through the tower and into the portal, turned back into a valkyrie, and got stuck in an empty room for many turns, passing through a few useless polymorphs and at least one own-race gender change along the way, before turning into a xorn, another monster with phasing.

A polymorphed player reduced to zero HP reverts to base form. Agent the Xorn became Agent the Lady in the Wizard of Yendorâs inner sanctum, between a blue dragon and a biting vampire lord. She fled downstairs without killing the Wizard, who had been awoken by an unseen monsterâs aggravate spell and followed her downstairs â to the Towerâs treasure zoo, where, to escape the malevolent hug of a carnivorous ape, she invoked the Orb again to flee the Tower. The Wizard followed her out, and she killed him in Gehennom and obtained the Book of the Dead.

Upon finding the vibrating square at the bottom of Gehennom, Agent the Hero descended to Molochâs Sanctum to retrieve the Amulet, rushed into the graveyard that stands before the Temple, became blinded in the melee, and died.

But waitâ¦ Your medallion feels warm! You feel much better!

The amulet of life saving from the ascension kit came in handy. Our agent outran the rest of the graveyardâs hordes and promptly wished for another one, but forgot to put it on. He entered the Temple of Moloch, slew its High Priestess, and took the Amulet of Yendor.

He made his way out of the temple slowly and absentmindedly. A wish for a blessed ring of levitation was interrupted by a different tactic. The blessed ring of lev#force provided a topaz ring that he never wore. Then he remembered to wear his new amulet of life saving. Three turns later, held in place by another carnivorous ape, unable to escape the swarms that had been waiting for him outside, he died again.

Strategies can advise from any state they see. The blessed ring of levitation completed in one timeline, but the fuzzer branched from inside the wish and did something else. That lineage was the one that ascended. It may have been that obtaining levitation at this point was worse for the fuzzer, but it may just have been luck.

âGehennom on 5 zorkmids a day â more like 500 a day if you ask me.â â Tourist quest guide, NetHack

On the way out of the Sanctum, an unseen monster summoned Juiblex, a demon lord whose lair weâd skipped. He proved to be no match for Grayswandir and luck.

Agent the Hero exited the Sanctum and immediately wished for a ring of levitation. His position was difficult. The invocation ritual had created a moat and a ring of fire, which he would need to pass. Without a source of levitation, his only way across was a flying polymorph. He was under strict instructions not to permit polymorph while wearing the gray dragon scale mail, but heâd previously put on a mummy wrapping, an item which NetHack treats as a cloak. Cloaks are worn over armor; clothes must be taken off in order. He couldnât shed his mail, which he had a dedicated tactic for, without removing his wrapping, which he was never told how to do. So, a ring. He put it on and kept it on until the Plane of Earth.

Early in his ascent, trapped by a boulder that our levitating agent didnât have the leverage to push out of the way, he found the inputs to take off his wrapping by chance, then took off his armor again, polymorphed into a water nymph, and teleported past it. Weâd instructed the fuzzer to use polymorphitis on the climb purely for nutrition resets, but fuzzers can find creative uses for the tools theyâre given.

On the same dungeon level, he was mauled by a minotaur for almost half of his HP and zapped a third wand of wishing heâd found in the Sanctum for two blessed potions of full healing, one of which he drank immediately.

The climb up forced Agent the Heroine (the 10% chance to change gender applied again on level 38) to deal with the demon rulers sheâd skipped on the way down. Juiblex had been dispatched in the Sanctum, but two demon princes remained: Asmodeus, with a powerful cold attack, and Baalzebub, with a fearsome stunning gaze. Valkyries have innate cold resistance, so Asmodeus wasnât too scary; once our agent awakened him, he ineffectually harassed her all the way to the Plane of Earth. But thereâs no such thing as stun resistance. Baalzebub called for a different strategy, and the fuzzer found an interesting one.

To explain what happened, weâll have to get into a lot of the complexity of NetHack.

On turn 8348, our agent climbed into Baalzebubâs lair. On turn 8351, she found and opened the secret door from the downstair to Baalzebubâs chamber, where she spent a few turns being bitten by vampire bats. Turn 8355 is divisible by 15, which triggers a coin flip for the Amulet of Yendorâs clairvoyance effect. [CODE: src/allmain.c:331-333] The coin flip succeeds.

When a player attracts Baalzebubâs attention, he appears before them and asks for a bribe. All four demon princes who ask for a bribe â Asmodeus, Baalzebub, Dispater, and Geryon â are generated invisible, and peaceful unless the player is wielding Excalibur, which our agent never created. [CODE: src/makemon.c:1329-1334] Asmodeus and Baalzebub, who await the player in their respective lairs, are generated in the waiting state. [CODE: src/makemon.c:1399-1401]

When a peaceful bribing demon moves, he first checks for two conditions. If his HP is below maximum or he can see the player, he exits the waiting state. [CODE: src/monmove.c:387-390] He then checks whether the square he sees the player on is next to him, which his tactics make likely: all demon lords and princes want the Amulet of Yendor, making them covetous, and a monster in good health who covets the Amulet will try to teleport next to a player carrying the Amulet of Yendor on every move. If the player is not carrying the Amulet, different monster tactics apply â but our player was carrying the Amulet, so we donât need to get into them here.

The square that a bribing demon sees the player on may not be the playerâs true square. The player could be wearing a cloak of displacement, for example. If heâs wrong, he âwhispers at thin airâ; if the player isnât polymorphed into a demon, he then gets angry and removes his invisibility. [CODE: src/monmove.c:468-489] If he correctly identifies the playerâs square, he enters a long routine called demon_talk. [CODE: src/minion.c:228-317] If the player is wielding Excalibur, he gets angry without becoming invisible. Otherwise, he appears before the player â removes his invisibility â and, unless the player is polymorphed into a demon, asks for a bribe. If the bribe is paid, the demon vanishes; if not, he gets angry.

(There are two other cases. If the player offers something less than the amount demanded, a roll for charisma determines whether the bribe counts as paid or unpaid. If the player is helpless or has no gold, he skips the demand and just gets angry.)

Asking for a bribe opens a unique text prompt. Our fuzzer config has a tactic intended to deal with bribe prompts. For whatever reason, it never fired in this run.

Baalzebub has a stunning gaze attack. Because itâs a gaze attack, it only works if the player can see him. Unless the fuzzer can navigate the bribe prompt, which itâs unlikely to do correctly without special tactical handling â paying a bribe is slightly more likely than guessing a password, but theyâre the same class of problem â Baalzebub is guaranteed to be hostile. Life would be much easier for the fuzzer if its hostile Baalzebub could be made to stay invisible â but how?

What if Baalzebub just doesnât get a turn?

Turns in NetHack are determined based on movement points. (Think subpixels, but temporal.) Every action that takes time costs 12 points. When the player takes an action that takes time, the game subtracts 12 points from the player, then gives every monster with at least 12 points an action. If the player still has at least 12 points, the player acts next; otherwise, the game gives monsters actions until none has 12 points left. When neither the player nor any monster has 12 points, the game starts a new turn and gives every creature a new round of movement points according to their speed. [CODE: src/allmain.c:95-119]

Monsters can only receive movement points in multiples of 12. A monster with 12 speed will receive 12 movement points, a monster with 24 speed will receive 24, and so on. When a monster has a speed that isnât a multiple of 12, itâs rounded randomly: a monster with a speed of 9, for example, has a 75% chance on each turn boundary of receiving 12 movement points, and a 25% chance of receiving none.

In a typical playthrough, Baalzebub is generated peaceful and invisible, but appears before the player on his turn. While our agent was making her way to Baalzebub in his chamber, the fuzzer never let him get a turn â he rolled an unlucky 25% for seven turns in a row. Agent the Heroine sensed Baalzebubâs presence using the Amulet of Yendorâs clairvoyance, walked up to him, and punched into his square, which angered him without giving him a chance to undo his invisibility. He spent the whole fight invisible, which disabled his stunning gaze â a gaze attack can only harm a creature that can see it.

Later, our agent polymorphed into a master mind flayer, which sees invisible, and got stunned from Baalzebubâs gaze. Oh well. But after she ate his brains, he teleported away and was never seen again.

The rest of the climb was uneventful. Our agent declined to bribe Asmodeus, who harassed him or her ineffectually all the way to the Plane of Earth. Soon after our agent left the Castle, an energy vortex broke his unworn topaz ringâ¦ and his ring of polymorph, but luckily he had a backup. Our agent prayed for the first and only time on the Plane of Air, for a heal while engulfed by an air elemental, which prompted the fuzzer to wait on the Plane of Water for the prayer timeout to reset. Agent the Champion reached the Astral Plane, had an unpleasant encounter with a green slime near the door to the high temple of Tyr, and ascended three turns before she wouldâve died of sliming.

There were at least two gender changes from own-race polymorph on the climb.

Maybe I should open your skull and see if my instructions are inside? â The Master of Thieves

Because our agent is powered by a grey-box fuzzer that reads features from a patch of the game, we had the option to make use of any information available to the game. We had to decide what was in the spirit of the fuzzer and what wasnât.

We first decided that mechanical knowledge was fair game. An experienced player will have memorized most of the wiki, and may have done some âsource divingâ â reading NetHackâs source to learn its mechanics. We decided that our agent could know anything an experienced human could â the best armor for its gameplan, the ascension kit to wish for, and details like the invocation ritual.

We also gave the fuzzer some information about the underlying system. NetHack itself provides players with some of it, with limitations. Players can see the remaining hit points of an enemy with a stethoscope (a free action once per turn) or a wand of probing, for example, but our harness reads the remaining HP of every monster on the level, and our agents use it to choose targets and score boss fights.

Other information is inaccessible in a normal environment. In normal NetHack gameplay, for example, much of the early game revolves around identifying items: many items in the game start unidentified, with a randomized appearance, and the use of every magical item must be determined, either with scarce sources of magical identification or with tricks like price identification and engrave-testing. Many items are only useful in certain contexts and others have negative effects, so using items blindly is not a good idea in normal play. A human player running NetHack inside the Antithesis environment, however, could use an item to identify it, then rewind, branch from a moment before the item was used, and track its identity.

We decided that anything that a human could trivially access with branching was acceptable for our agent, so we gave it access to its raw item inventory â as if every item had been fully identified for it. We obtain almost all of our inventory from wishes, where items arrive with their identity known, and determining whether an unknown wand is a wand of wishing costs a single charge per unknown wand type and doesnât even waste a wish.

We read out some hidden numbers that we couldâve tracked. Consider the playerâs hidden luck stat: because every action that affects luck is either the playerâs own or indicated with a message, and luck times out on a predictable schedule, a conscientious human player â or a regular agent harness â could reliably track luck to within a reasonable bound. Rather than write the tracking code, we elected to read it from the game. We handled alignment record similarly: a human could estimate it, but we read it. Prayer timeout, which we read, canât be known exactly by a human, but can be given a conservative estimate. At the time of our first ascension, our tactics used the playerâs raw nutrition counter, but we later removed this and used only the player-visible hunger state.

Some of our tricks were more consequential. The fuzzer reads the full current level, including every trap, item, and monster, and every monsterâs inventory, directly from the harness; it doesnât have to discover as it goes. Our later runs also read the dungeonâs layout and knew which level held features like the quest portal, the entrance to Vladâs Tower, and the vibrating square. Certain applications of this are small optimizations: knowing which high altar is the correct one, for example, would be immensely useful for a human, but for a branching fuzzer is a mere 3x optimization on the final level of the game. Other optimizations are perhaps larger: the fuzzer can reward descent to a level containing a wand of wishing as soon as it lands on the level, and our first ascension rerolled the Castle until its wand had enough charges. And a few are trivial: because the agent can see the age of a corpse, for instance, it can fearlessly eat monsters it didnât see die, but players eating tainted meat are made immediately aware, so this instrumentation only saves us some rewinds.

And, finally, our agent knows that, in our harness, the fuzzer controls /dev/urandom, which derives its entropy from the input history up to each moment. NetHack only reads /dev/urandom at the start of the game and when the player changes dungeon level, but the agent is able to provide meaningless inputs before seeing a new level to draw new entropy when it descends.

At the time of writing, weâre actively working on removing this scaffolding. Weâve already found some success with tracking estimated bounds for values like luck and prayer timeout instead of reading them out, and replacing inventory instrumentation with menu information â prohibiting even the cross-branch identification trials that any human playing NetHack in our system would do. Using only whatâs on screen would make NetHack very unlike the real systems we test â most systems donât have screens! â but we think a black-box ascension is within reach. Who knows? Maybe weâll even have a zen ascension someday.

Our first run had another trick up its sleeve which subsequent ascensions didnât, but weâll talk about it later.

tbh I still have zero clue on how to play nethack after all this ð¤£ â Shuxian Wang, internal Zulip, October 2026

While Mikail was pushing the existing fuzzer config to its limits, a separate workstream was rethinking our whole approach to the game. My colleague Shuxian Wang was working on an experimental system for facilitating the development of workloads â drivers that sit between the fuzzer and the system under test and translate entropy into inputs â and used NetHack as a test bed.

Up to this point, weâd treated NetHack the same way we treat NES games. In a typical NES setup, the game receives fuzzer entropy directly. We can tune the distribution of bytes that the fuzzer produces, but theyâre still just bytes. This is fine for action games on a console where bytes map naturally to controller input, but NetHack requires much more high-level planning and has a much wider range of inputs. The invocation ritual, for example â lighting the Candelabrum of Invocation, ringing the Bell of Opening, and reading the Book of the Dead, all while standing on the vibrating square â was expressed as a complicated series of nested value functions, which spelled out in exacting detail the reward gradient of the menuing required.

Remember the 14-page history dialog? we eventually configured the fuzzer to never send NetHack a V.

Needless to say, this is not how we handle typical systems. When testing a SQL database, we donât wait for the fuzzerâs raw bytes to produce interesting SQL. Instead, we have a driver that translates those bytes into operations and assertions to be exercised under faults â a workload. Similarly, Player, the system Shuxian built for NetHack, translated bytes into sensible actions, like âwield this weaponâ, âdrink a potion of full healingâ, or âlight the Candelabrum with seven candlesâ.

With Player able to translate bytes into high-level actions, we were able to radically simplify our strategy, which had ballooned to thousands of lines of code, and produce new ascensions in minutes. NetHack wasnât quite a well-behaved system under test yet â it maintained its own PRNG instead of drawing its rolls from the fuzzer â but Player brought it in line with the customer workloads that it was complex enough to resemble. Right after its first ascension, the old strategy was superseded.

The new strategyâs game plan was different. Instead of waiting until the Castleâs wand to wish for an ascension kit, it farmed fountains and thrones for early-game wishes. It spent some of its increased wish budget on blessed potions of gain level to expedite the XL grind, and cursed potions of gain level to expedite the climb back from the Sanctum, and the rest to assemble a fuller ascension kit: a pick-axe and a wand of digging to break into the Fake Wizardâs Tower, a complete suit of armor and a cloak, and an amulet of magical breathing for the Plane of Water, among others.

Sitting on a throne has a 1 in 39 chance to grant a wish. Quaffing from a fountain or dipping an object into it has a 1 in 30 chance of summoning a water demon, which has a small chance of granting a wish.

A normal potion of gain level causes the player to gain an experience level. A cursed one causes the player to gain a dungeon level. âYou rise up, through the ceiling!â

This increased wish budget let us change our game plan in another way. The old strategy had already fixed its ability to retain items and armor, which had made it less reliant on polymorph for combat, but it still needed polymorph in a few places â to phase into the Fake Wizardâs Tower and the Castle for the wand, and to reroll nutrition to ward off hunger on the long climb up. With the Tower diggable and the Castle wand removed, polymorph became a hindrance. We replaced its last use case with a wish for a ring of slow digestion. Our first ascension run was our last run to abuse polymorphitis.

when AI takes all our jobs I hope I can be a quantum mechanic â Harrison Brown, internal Zulip, April 2025

With our first ascension under our belt, we asked ourselves: could we take this further? We hadnât been the first to get an autonomous ascent â BotHack had done this in 2015 â but could we really settle for fourth place when there was so much else that had yet to be done?

We considered a few directions. A detour through speed ascensions prompted us to refine how we hunted for wishes, and to briefly restructure our gameplan to do the Quest late. (Your Quest leader wonât admit you until 2000 turns have passed.) We also added a new RNG manipulation with an expected time of less than a turn. SWAGGINZZZâs zero-turn manips had been patched out, but we noticed that toggling twoweapon had a DEX/20 chance to not use a turn. But in time we decided to ascend every role.

Every role and every race. There are five playable races in NetHack: human, dwarf, elf, gnome, and orc. These each have their strengths and weaknesses, but the playerâs choice of race has fewer implications than the playerâs choice of role. In the end, we ascended a dwarven Valkyrie, an elven Wizard, a gnomish Archeologist, an orcish Rogue, and humans for everything else.

Like BotHack and Astra, weâd started as a Valkyrie. BotHack had later ascended a Knight and a Samurai, and SWAGGINZZZ had ascended a Tourist, an ordinarily difficult class whose wide range of starting inventory possibilities made it ideal for RNG prediction. But this left nine roles unascended. Some, like the Barbarian, were melee-focused roles, widely regarded as on the easier side, which we expected to beat without much difficulty. Others, like the Priest and the Wizard, had playstyles we hadnât yet had cause to support: the Valkyrie makes minimal use of magic. And then there was the Monk â bound by restrictive conducts backed by massive penalties, bearing the most feared Quest nemesis in the game, and relying heavily on spellcasting. We expected to have a hard time with the Monk.

We patched logic into our workload to parameterize our character build, generalized a few things in our strategy, and kicked off some more runs.

Our new runs quickly revealed problems in our workload that weâd lucked out of seeing before. In one of our first runs, our hero wasted hundreds of turns trying to dig through an undiggable square, only freeing herself when a randomly spawned quantum mechanic hit her with its teleportation attack, and then got stuck again trying to squeeze through a diagonal gap that she was carrying too much to fit through, only resuming progress when an umber hulk summoned by the Wizard of Yendor ate the offending wall. A Samurai wished for gray dragon scale mail and then stood at the throne for 1400 turns, not realizing it had to take off its starting splint mail to put its new armor on.

Because weâd started with Valkyrie, an all-female role, our workload defaulted to female characters. Gender has very little effect on gameplay, so we left it.

We fixed the problems as we found them. When a Barbarian died swarmed by trolls in its Quest, we had Barbarians wish for a tinning kit: trolls can return from the dead as long as their corpses arenât tinned. When a different hero (a Valkyrie, run for testing) stalled out at a shop door, barred from entry because of her open-carried pick-axe but fixated on the cursed scroll of teleportation sold therein, we added a CONTRARY term to give our agent a chance to do something other than what it believes to be best.

Most roles ascended uneventfully. With a table of artifact weapons and a generalized Quest, we won as a Knight, a Ranger, and a Samurai. Our first Caveman stalled at the Quest, as did our second; we patched our pathfinding code to handle boulders dropped by hill giants and ascended on our third attempt. Our next role, a Rogue, also stalled out at the Quest â the Stronghold of the Master Assassin is impenetrable by normal means, so pathfinding failed. Polymorph into a xorn could allow us to phase through walls and reach the Master Assassin in his lair, but a means of aggravating monsters could wake him and bring him to us. We added 2 cursed potions of invisibility to the Rogueâs wish list and ascended on our next attempt. Archeologist, with its starting pick-axe and stealth, proved to be one of the easiest roles for our fuzzer â maybe even easier than the Valkyrie. When the Barbarianâs new tinning kit gave us a winning run, the only roles remaining were the spellcasters and the Monk.

Our gameplan thus far had been designed around melee. We gathered strong weapons to bash monsters with, the Gauntlets of Power to boost our strength further, and iron armor to protect our heroes at the cost of spellcasting penalties. We ignored spellbooks completely. Could we pivot into a very different build? Because runs were cheap, we tried running a Wizard before we made any changes, just to see what would happen â and it ascended! Priest and Healer followed. Only the Monk remained.

Monks are much different in design from the other roles of NetHack. â NetHack Wiki

Maybe we couldâve ascended a Monk with our existing strategy, but I wanted to see if we could ascend while playing into the role â perhaps the most unusual role in the game. In NetHackâs combat skill system, the Monk canât advance beyond Basic in any weapon class, and most weapon classes are locked to unskilled, but the highest skill of all is reserved for the Monkâs martial arts, the replacement for other rolesâ bare-handed combat. Monks suffer punishing to-hit penalties from wearing armor, but to make up for it, they gain more intrinsics by leveling up than any other role. Monks are particularly well-suited to conduct ascensions, in which the player adheres to additional limitations beyond the rules of the game: never using a weapon, for instance, or never eating meat. (Monks incur an alignment penalty from eating meat.) We wouldnât just ascend a Monk; we would ascend a weaponless vegan Monk.

We started by customizing our strategy. To maintain weaponless conduct, the Monkâs artifact wish wouldnât go to a weapon; to avoid penalties to martial arts, the Monk would wear no body armor. In place of the artifact weapon, the Monk would wish for a co-aligned quest artifact with defensive utility, like the Master Key of Thievery (chaotic; halves physical damage) or the Orb of Fate (neutral; halves physical and spell damage). The Monk would wear its own quest artifact, the Eyes of the Overworld, for magic resistance, but wish for a cloak of magic resistance (not considered armor) besides, because the Wizard of Yendor can steal artifacts. The Monk would eat only vegan food, make use of its intrinsic teleport control, and obtain a wand of death, by a wish if necessary, to dispatch Master Kaen.

Our first few attempts failed. Our next few attempts also failed. The few extra wishes weâd added strained our ability to control our luck, which was already limited by the Monkâs inability to two-weapon. Without a new way to manipulate RNG â ideally in zero turns, the way SWAGGINZZZ had â weâd need to trim our wish list, imperiling our ability to survive in the endgame.

We werenât sure if any zero-turn RNG manipulations still existed. After SWAGGINZZZ, the NetHack developers had split random numbers used for display â like hallucination, which was faster and easier than walking into walls â into a separate RNG stream, and patched out the walk-into-walls exploit. But a close inspection of the code found one that weâd overlooked: artifact naming.

In NetHack, no object of a certain type can be given the name of an artifact of that type. The Eyes of the Overworld are an artifact pair of lenses, so no pair of lenses can be given the name The Eyes of the Overworld. A player who attempted to name an ordinary pair of lenses The Eyes of the Overworld â which, in the world of NetHack, meant engraving the name on the object â would find their hand to slip, and their lenses to emerge with a name like The Lyes of the Overworld instead, mutating exactly one letter in the name. And this mutation called the gameâs main RNG!

We patched Player to find an orcish dagger (a common early-game item) to repeatedly fail to name after the mediocre artifact Grimtooth and kicked off a few dozen jobs to run overnight.

We updated our strategy to reject runs that had broken their conducts, kicked off a new batch, and had our first ascension twelve minutes later: a weaponless vegan atheist Monk. Weâd gotten a third conduct for free! Our fuzzer doesnât use altars and only prays in certain emergencies, so this came down to luck: this run had never encountered a situation that called for prayer. Of the two other ascensions that this batch produced, one more also kept atheist conduct.

Then we got more ambitious and added another conduct to the wishlist. This called for some changes to our fuzzer config. Weâd replaced polymorph with weapons and armor, but a weaponless nudist has neither. Instead of wishing for gray dragon scale mail, this monk would get a ring of polymorph. We thought about adding code to drive the protection racket, but in the end, we didnât need two: two hours after weâd started on the fourth conduct, we had its first win.

Here is the ascension of Agent the weaponless vegan atheist nudist Monk, with our multiverse map plotted below:

with the RNG workload twiddle we can ascend in 20 seconds sometimes. as a neutral monk â Paul, internal Zulip, Nov 2026

One question still remained. Weâd introduced Player to bring NetHack in line with our real-world engagements. But NetHack violates an important best practice of real-world Antithesis use â it maintains its own PRNG. NetHack versions released after 3.6.1 (the version SWAGGINZZZ played) maintain two ISAAC64 PRNGs, one for game logic and one for display, seeded at the start of the game and only reseeded when the fuzzer changes dungeon level. Our environment controls /dev/urandom, the external entropy source that NetHack reseeds from, which allows the fuzzer to steer the generation of new levels. But within a level, the fuzzer can only control the player, not the game.

This is a desirable property for an ascension generator: every run is something that couldâve happened in stock NetHack. But it comes with a cost. When the fuzzer has indirect or otherwise limited control over the system itâs exercising, itâll take longer to find interesting states. As an experiment, we patched our NetHack harness to reseed its RNG with a fuzzer-controlled value after every keypress, and found that time to ascension became up to three times faster.

Really, we removed a patch. Our first ascension was generated with NetHack wired in as a well-behaved system under test. This was the trick up its sleeve that we hinted at above: the fuzzer could force-reseed NetHackâs RNG. After weâd generated our first few ascensions, we decided to see what we could do with stock RNG â and we found we could still get ascensions. Lots of ascensions.

In 100 trials out of 120, the fuzzer, configured to play as a dwarven Valkyrie and running on the workstation at my desk (not a super-fast cluster â but I wish I had a super-fast cluster at my desk!), found an ascension in NetHack within five minutes â using stock RNG. The median time to ascension was 49 seconds, the p90 ascension time was 78 seconds, and the fastest ascension in these 120 trials took only 28 seconds to find. With the well-behaved system patch, it ascended within five minutes in 113 of 120 trials, with a p90 of 64.8 seconds and a fastest of only 7.5 seconds.

As a Tourist, traditionally considered one of the hardest roles in NetHack, the fuzzer ascended within five minutes in 95 trials out of 120 using stock RNG, with a median time of 74 seconds. With the patch, it ascended 111 of 120 within five minutes, with a median of 28 seconds.

We also ran Monks (the hardest role for our fuzzer, and the one with the most special handling) and Wizards. A full data table is under the expander.

Below, you can watch the fuzzer ascend as every role. (Note: these runs use stock RNG, not our well-tempered workload patch.)

You hear a faint typing noise. â NetHack, when the player uses a stethoscope on the edge of a map

At the start of this post, we said Antithesis is something like a probabilistic programming language: a way to partially describe a task and let search and optimization fill in the rest. Hereâs what we meant. Playerâs plan for the early game fits in a sentence: sit on thrones and drink from fountains until you have all the wishes you need. It doesnât say how to get the wishes. Nothing could â a sit on a throne only grants a wish one time in 39, and if it doesnât, it can curse you, surround you with enemies, or vanish. But we can throw those other 38 timelines out. We tell the fuzzer how to sit on a throne, we tell it that a moment with one more wish beats the one before, and we tell it how to shake the dice. The fuzzer does the rest.

Sometimes it surprises even us. When we threw it into a battle weâd given it no way to score, it didnât give up or get stuck. In the middle of a long and losing fight with Vlad the Impaler, with no reward until it could get the Candelabrum in its hands, it turned into a purple worm and ate him. When we rewarded it for code coverage and gave it the tools to construct situations, it started finding bugs. And when we told it what pointed toward victory and how to play the game, it ascended.

This partial specification paradigm has three advantages.

First, it lets you do less work. Any bot needs three kinds of knowledge. The first is how to act: how to turn âput seven candles on the Candelabrumâ into keystrokes. These are the tactics. The second is a vision of the good: high health, great strength, alignment with your god, and a magic silver saber. This is the strategy. The third is foresight: knowledge of the paths from here to there, and of how to recover from a misstep. This is what search replaces. BotHack needed 16,000 lines of Clojure and Astra needed a trillion or so dollars of CapEx; our fuzzer ascended with a short config file, and I hear Antithesis has received a tiny bit less funding than OpenAI.

Second, itâs more robust to evolution of the system under test. If you move a block in Super Mario Bros., your scripted run might fail, but partial specification doesnât care. If you change the CSS of your website, your scripted tests wonât know where to click, but Bombadil will. And if your partial specification can ascend a Valkyrie, it can probably ascend a Wizard.

And finally, it can find unknown unknowns. The usual way to gain confidence in a program is to understand it: to read the code really hard, reason through the logic, and try to consider each case. Few programs have been read harder than NetHack. Its players have been source-diving for decades, and thereâs extensive documentation for nearly every mechanic. We read it too. Reading is how we found the 1-in-39 wish chance and the Grimtooth naming trick. But years of reading never turned up the del_light_source bug. The fuzzer found it by wandering into it. So did its eventual reporter.

Every piece of that bug was known. A quest artifact blasts a hero whose alignment is negative, even its rightful owner. A playerâs polymorph is an opportunity for artifacts to blast. A polymorphed hero who runs out of hit points returns to normal form. A yellow light gives off light. What nobody had read about was the moment where all four combine: a Valkyrie at -70 alignment turning into a yellow light, blasted by her own Orb for all the lightâs HP before her new body had started to glow. Once the reporter had stumbled into it, AI-assisted testing found related bugs in the same code. Reasoning, whether human or machine, is great at checking a bugâs vicinity. Itâs much worse at telling you where to look.

We never told the fuzzer where to look. We wrote down the pieces â what a player can do, what counts as getting better, and that new code is worth visiting â and let search find the combinations.

A good Antithesis test works the same way. You donât write down the precise sequence of events that breaks your system. (You probably havenât thought of it yet.) Instead, you tell the system what should never happen and what a client can do, and our exploration agent â Daveâs âfuzzer so smart it can beat NetHackâ â uses the actions youâve provided to discover paths to the impossible.

#9839. Philippine Migrant Worker Data Likely Leaked in 69GB Government Breach

Breaking cybersecurity news, news analysis, commentary, and other content from around the world, with an initial focus on the Middle East & Africa, the Asia Pacific, Europe, and Latin America.

An unknown operator appears to have exfiltrated SQL Server backups from the Philippine Overseas Employment Administration in under a half hour.

An unknown threat actor managed to gain access to sensitive databases belonging to the Philippine Overseas Employment Administration, exfiltrating nearly 69GB of information on workers, contracts, and financial records, according to an analysis of a staging server used in the breach.

Over 24 minutes, the attacker copied 27 backup databases with information on overseas-employment case management, including accreditation, contracts, and cashier and LandBank records, according to threat intelligence firm Hunt.io's Oct. 28 analysis of the logs found on a Singaporean staging server used by the attacker. The cyberattackers used privileged escalation tools, namely GodPotato and SeImpersonate, and the Impacket network library for Python to move the data, but the trail stopped at the staging server, says Esteban Borges, head of research for Hunt.io.

The server had been accessed later, but by whom is not clear, Borges says. While Hunt.io has not yet discovered the data as advertised for sale, the information may have been detected and removed, but that seems unlikely, he says.

Related:State Bank of India Suffers a Customer PII Data Leak

"I won't claim the backups stopped on the staging server," he says, so it's "still a breach, since the data was copied out of the agency’s control and the log shows the transfer completing."

This is not the first time that cybersecurity firms have found evidence that Philippine government data had been stolen. In August, Hunt.io discovered another threat actor's workspace hosting a number of tools and, in that case, 1.2GB of data stolen from a Philippine nuclear regulatory agency and a maritime shipbuilding contractor. A year ago, Philippine police arrested the mayor of a small town after discovering she was a Chinese national posing as a Filipina citizen and operating a cyber-scam center.

Whether the current incident involved China or cybercriminal groups is not clear. While Hunt.io did find some Chinese language fragments in the parts of the code, that code belonged to a third-party software library; thus, Hunt.io did not attribute the hack. The company did say, however, that both cybercriminals and nation-state adversaries would find value in the personally identifiable information (PII).

"That kind of migrant-worker PII, plus contract and payment data, is useful for fraud and identity theft, so it has commercial value," Borges says. "It's also a detailed map of a diaspora population, which can interest a state actor."

The latest insight into attacks on the Philippine government came after Hunt.io researchers discovered an open directory on a server hosted on the Singaporean address space of a Helsinki-based firm, UpCloud Ltd., the analysis stated. The open directory contained tools and log files for the attack, including a rebranded version of the GodPotato privilege escalation library, a PowerShell stager to unpack tools in memory, and the full Impacket Python environment.

Related:Russian Influence Operation Widely Targets Latin America

While Hunt.io considered the incident a confirmed compromise, the lack of runtime telemetry meant that Borges could not answer where the attacker moved the data.

"[W]e still can’t answer ... how they got in, whether the payload ran, and where the data went," he says.

However, the tools and the attacker's process indicated an operator with some strong ability, but who also made some simple mistakes, Borges says.

"The payload engineering is competent, [but] the operational security is poor — they left the staging server and its logs wide open," he says. "[It was] someone who can build the tool properly but was careless about keeping their own server quiet. I wouldn't call that top-tier or amateur."

The impact of the breach may boil down to the identity of the attacker and what they do with the stolen data. While Hunt.io notified the CERT Philippines (CERT-PH) and the Department of Migrant Workers (DMW), the company declined to provide any more details of the national responses to the leak.

Related:Venezuelan Cartel's Malware Honcho Nabbed for ATM Jackpotting

However, Borges did say that, so far, the information has not appeared for sale on the Dark Web.

"We haven't seen the backups surface for sale or in a leak," he says. "We never opened the backups themselves."

Governments in the region need to scan their own networks and lock down their attack surface area, he says. Workers with too many privileges allow attackers with tools such as SeImpersonate to gain more access to assets on the network. Hunt.io also found that the migrant-worker portal exposed a number of risky ports, including SMB on 445 and WinRM on 5985 and 47001.

Rob is an award-winning, veteran technology journalist of more than 30 years, reporting on global cybersecurity issues, the latest offensive and defensive technologies, malware incidents, cyber conflict, and AI's impact on software and cybersecurity.

A former research engineer, Rob has written for more than two dozen publications, including CNET News.com, Dark Reading, MIT's Technology Review, Popular Science, and Wired News. He has received five awards for journalism, including Best Deadline Journalism (Online) in 2003 for his coverage of the Blaster worm. Rob also analyzes data on various trends using Python and R for both his reporting and his clients. Recent reports include analyses of the shortage in cybersecurity workers, annual vulnerability trends, and annual threat reports.

Rob holds degrees from Cornell University in Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (double major).
