#9783. Black Hat India 2026 Makes a Landmark Debut in Bengaluru, Bringing the Global Cybersecurity Community to India

Inaugural edition by Informa Markets in India brings together leading researchers, security practitioners and industry decision makers for four days of cutting-edge research, technical exchange and strategic dialogue.

13 Trainings delivered by 19 trainers, 70+ Summit speakers, 200+ CXOs, CISOs and VIP buyers, and 2,000+ Business Hall delegates across four days.

Black Hat Arsenal featured 44 open-source security tool demonstrations across 32 workstations and four hands-on labs.

Keynotes by leading cybersecurity experts Dr. Sanjay Bahl, Director General, Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) and Controller of Certifying Authorities (CCA), and Nathan Hamiel (Kudelski Security), alongside a special address by Shri Rajesh Kumar, IPS, Chief Executive Officer, Indian Cybercrime Co-ordination Centre (I4C), Ministry of Home Affairs, Government of India.

Key themes included AI security, digital payment fraud, emerging cyber threats and post-quantum readiness.

Bengaluru, November 5, 2026 — Black Hat India 2026, organised by Informa Markets in India, concluded its inaugural edition at the Sheraton Grand, Brigade Gateway, Bengaluru, following four days of high-impact training, leadership discussions, original technical research and industry engagement from October 27 to 30, 2026.

Related:Attackers in Binance Breach Targeted Known Weakness, Missing Controls

Founded in 1997, Black Hat is one of the world's most respected cybersecurity conference series, renowned for its independent, vendor-neutral research and technical depth. Its debut in India marks a significant milestone for the country's cybersecurity ecosystem, bringing a globally recognised platform and its international community of researchers and practitioners to one of the world's fastest-growing digital economies.

The inaugural edition brought together a diverse mix of technical training, strategic discussions, cutting-edge research and hands-on engagement, with each day offering a distinct experience for the cybersecurity community.

Day 1 opened with specialised Trainings, featuring 13 hands-on courses delivered by 19 trainers and covering subjects ranging from offensive security fundamentals to securing emerging AI systems.

Day 2 was dedicated to Summit Day, bringing together 70+ speakers and 200+ CXOs, CISOs and VIP buyers across two tracks, Frontier AI Security and CISO Strategy. Discussions examined the changing cybersecurity landscape, enterprise risk and the growing strategic responsibilities of security leaders.

Days 3 and 4 featured the Briefings and Business Hall, with 35 researchers and practitioners presenting original work on emerging threats, software and cloud security, AI and digital identity, while welcoming more than 2,000 Business Hall delegates. A major attraction was Black Hat Arsenal, where 44 presenters demonstrated open-source security tools across 32 workstations and four hands-on labs, enabling attendees to engage directly with developers and explore practical security applications.

Related:Getting Past the Post-Quantum Cryptography Discovery Phase

The event brought together prominent government representatives, industry leaders and international cybersecurity experts. Summit Day was inaugurated in the presence of Lt. Gen. Rajesh Pant and Lt. Gen. M.U. Nair, both former National Cyber Security Coordinators of India; Dr. Sanjay Bahl, Director General, Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) and Controller of Certifying Authorities (CCA); and Brijesh Singh, IPS, Principal Secretary, Government of Maharashtra.

Dr. Bahl's keynote examined the implications of emerging AI technologies for India's digital ecosystem and the importance of strengthening cyber resilience. Nathan Hamiel, Senior Director of Research at Kudelski Security, delivered the Briefings keynote, exploring how AI is transforming cybersecurity and why human expertise remains indispensable. Shri Rajesh Kumar, IPS, Chief Executive Officer, Indian Cybercrime Co-ordination Centre (I4C), Ministry of Home Affairs, Government of India, delivered a special address on transnational cybercrime.

Related:Cyber Experts Weigh In: How to Fight Artex & AntiFox

Senior representatives from NPCI, the Reserve Bank of India, NCIIPC, PhonePe, CRED, Razorpay, Groww, Reliance, Adani Enterprises, HCLTech, EY, Deloitte, KPMG, Microsoft, Mandiant, Akamai, Zscaler and Zoho participated alongside independent and academic researchers.

Across the programme, discussions consistently highlighted the growing importance of securing and governing AI, the increasing sophistication of cyberattacks, software supply-chain vulnerabilities, digital payment fraud and deepfakes. Protecting India's Digital Public Infrastructure, preparing for post-quantum technologies and translating technical risks into business priorities also emerged as important themes.

India's rapid digital expansion is creating unprecedented opportunities, alongside an increasingly complex cybersecurity landscape. The average organisational cost of a data breach in India reached ₹25.5 crore in 2026, nearly 16% higher year on year, underlining the growing economic implications of cyber risk.

The successful debut of Black Hat India is a significant achievement for us and an important addition to India’s cybersecurity ecosystem. The scale of participation and quality of discussions reflect the strong appetite for a platform of this calibre. As AI reshapes the threat landscape, staying ahead of emerging risks becomes even more critical. We are proud to have brought this globally recognised platform to India and look forward to building on this strong beginning,” he added.

The inaugural edition was supported by Diamond Partners TrendAI, Upwind and EY, alongside other sponsors and exhibitors, and shaped by the Black Hat India Review Board.

Black Hat India's debut comes in a milestone year for Informa Markets in India, marking 20 years of its presence in the country. Spanning 100 days, the campaign celebrates the optimism, energy and entrepreneurial spirit driving India's growth, bringing together the country's vibrant festive season and its high season of business events.

The successful inaugural edition establishes a significant new platform for India's cybersecurity community, bringing global expertise, original research and industry leadership together at a time when securing the digital future has never been more important.

Black Hat India extends the globally recognised Black Hat platform to India's rapidly evolving cybersecurity landscape in Bengaluru, connecting the country's growing community of information security professionals with global research, expertise and industry developments. #9782. Microsoft Fixes RCE Bug in Windows Paint After Weeks of Confusion

Last month, Microsoft disclosed a vulnerability in Microsoft Paint, but messaging regarding a patch was unclear.

Microsoft recently patched a remote code execution (RCE) vulnerability in Windows Paint, though details regarding how to fix the flaw seemingly remained unsettled for nearly a month.

According to an advisory, the flaw, CVE-2026-83844, is an "out-of-bounds read in Windows Paint [that] allows an unauthorized attacker to execute code locally." It carries a high severity CVSS 3.1 score of 7.0.

The advisory offers few technical details for defenders. Microsoft said acquiring RCE requires local access, meaning hands-on-keyboard or a direct remote connection to the attacker's machine. Some user interaction is also required; altogether, this may explain why the attack is "only" high severity rather than a 9 or 10 CVSS, as is so often associated with RCE flaws. Microsoft has observed no exploitation reports to date, further marking exploitation as "less likely."

A Windows Paint patch is available now. The fixed version is 11.2609.401.0, and customers can see it under Paint > Settings > About.

Related:F-Secure Identifies 26 Ways AI Can Harm Consumers, and Where to Stop Them

A Microsoft spokesperson tells Dark Reading, "A security update for Paint is available through the Microsoft Store, and customers with automatic Store updates enabled are already protected. We recommend customers check they are on the latest version and install the available updates to remain protected." Customers can also manually apply the update via Microsoft Store App > Downloads > Check for updates.

CVE-2026-83844 is an unusual vulnerability for multiple reasons, beyond it being a high-severity Paint vulnerability capable of RCE.

As Brian Vitko, founder of device management software provider RFF, wrote in a blog post, Microsoft first disclosed the bug on Oct. 13, but there seemed to be no indication the reported fix (11.2605.91.0) was live, even as of Oct. 30. By Nov. 4, Vitko, the correct fixed version was listed in the security advisory (11.2609.401.0) but 11.2605.81.0 was the latest update available in the store. The correct version was added to the store on Nov. 6.

The original version of the advisory FAQ, according to Vitko's post, said the attack could possibly be exploited, "by sending a specially crafted packet to an affected service over the network."

But the latest version of the FAQ reads, "For example, when the score indicates that the Attack Vector is Local and User Interaction is Required, this could describe an exploit in which an attacker, through social engineering, convinces a victim to download and open a specially crafted file from a website which leads to a local attack on their computer."

Related:AI Makes Reverse Engineering Mainstream Software & Malware Far Easier

Vitko tells Dark Reading that this latter explanation aligns more with his expectations for a vulnerability targeting Windows Paint, and that the wording may just be the result of standardized Microsoft FAQ language than speaking directly to the vulnerability.

"Paint isn't something that listens on the network. When it was published, it was CVSS 8.1 with a network attack vector, and the FAQ talked about 'a specially crafted packet to an affected service over the network.' Microsoft changed that on Nov. 7: it's now 7.0, local, user interaction required, and the FAQ says an attacker 'convinces a victim to download and open a specially crafted file from a website,'" he says. "That makes a lot more sense for an image editor. Microsoft hasn't said anything more about the actual trigger."

Dark Reading asked Microsoft for additional information regarding the update timeline.

Alex is an award-winning writer, journalist, and podcast host based in Boston. He has previously been published on VentureFizz, Search Security, Nintendo World Report, and elsewhere.

At Dark Reading, he covers a variety of cybersecurity topics, including the cybercrime ecosystem, open source security, and the intersection between AI and threat actors. In his spare time, Alex hosts the weekly Nintendo podcast, "Talk Nintendo Podcast," and works on personal writing projects, including two previously self-published science fiction novels.

He has received numerous awards, including TechTarget's Writer of the Year in 2022 as well as more than 10 Azbee awards for his reporting between 2022 and today.

#9781. AnyLanguageModel 1.0: One Year of Local Models on Apple Platforms

Last November, we introduced AnyLanguageModel on this blog: a drop-in replacement for Apple's Foundation Models framework that lets you choose the model and provider your app uses. We heard from app developers who were curious about local models but weren't always sure how to get started. They also wanted to avoid the added complexity of supporting multiple inference providers. AnyLanguageModel grew out of that feedback.

Local and hosted inference each have their strengths, and both have a role in building this new generation of intelligent apps. A shared API makes it easier to choose the right model for each task.

A year and dozens of releases later, AnyLanguageModel 1.0 is out, along with swift-huggingface 1.0 and swift-xet 1.0.

The core idea of AnyLanguageModel remains the same: use the Foundation Models API with the model that fits your app. To get started, change your import statement:

The same session code then works with the system model, with open-weight models through llama.cpp, MLX, and Core ML, and with the hosted providers below.

Over the past year, we've added several major features:

On OS 27, AnyLanguageModel also works with any model that conforms to Foundation Models' LanguageModel protocol, including Core AI models.

Alongside AnyLanguageModel, we've built out swift-huggingface and swift-xet to bring accelerated model downloads from the Hub to Swift apps.

Support for hosted models expanded this year, too. AnyLanguageModel now supports:

With Inference Providers, you can use open-weight models that are too big to run on the device with the same session code:

Hosted providers get the same features as local models: guided generation, tool calling with streaming, and token usage on responses.

Reasoning is now part of the transcript too. When you switch providers, reasoning blocks are automatically omitted from requests if the new provider can't replay them.

API keys come from a closure instead of a string, so your app can fetch short-lived tokens from your own server. The README explains when to let people bring their own keys and when to route requests through a proxy.

AnyLanguageModel also runs on Linux, so the same code can work on a server.

While we've made local models easier to use, the models themselves have become more capable, making the small ones a good place to start. Here are some of the most downloaded models on the Hub right now:

The first two fit on an iPhone, and Qwen3.8 27B runs on a Mac with 32 GB of memory or more. Selecting the MLX model takes one line:

And if you have four maxed-out Mac Studios handy, GLM-5.3 from Z.ai takes about 1.5 TB in BF16. For the rest of us, it's available through Inference Providers.

If you're upgrading an existing app, see the migration guidance in the AnyLanguageModel, swift-huggingface, and swift-xet release notes for help updating your code.

Community feedback and contributions have shaped several of our major features. Thank you to everyone who contributed for helping make AnyLanguageModel more useful to app developers.

Language models have proven to be a powerful tool for building intelligence into products. They're also one of many kinds of models developers can put to work. We're excited to bring the same approach to more capabilities: familiar Swift APIs with a choice of models running on the device. Coming soon: models that decide, and models that listen.

#9780. Hugging Face ❤️ TorchTPU: TPUs, Natively

If you ever tried to run PyTorch on a TPU, you probably ported your code to torch_xla, or you ended up having to learn JAX. With TorchTPU, a native PyTorch backend, TPU is now just another device. It opens up native support of TPU in the Hugging Face ecosystem. Transformers, Diffusers and Kernels run natively on TPU. Pick a model from the Hub, send it to "tpu", and you're done.

TPU stands for Tensor Processing Unit. TPUs are Google's own AI accelerators. They are chips built for one job: the matrix math that neural networks spend most of their time on. Google has been designing them for about ten years, and uses them to train and serve its own models, including Gemini.

TPUs are available on Google Cloud, from a single chip up to pods of thousands of chips. They shine when you need a lot of compute, for training or for serving at scale.

The catch has always been software. The TPU stack grew up around TensorFlow and JAX, and PyTorch users had to work harder to get in.

Until now, running PyTorch on TPUs meant going through PyTorch/XLA (torch_xla). It worked, but it had its quirks. Tensors were lazy (the tensors, not you), so your code didn't always run when you thought it did. Small changes could trigger graph recompilations, and debugging was hard to reason about.

To make life easier, we built Optimum TPU. It gave Hugging Face models inference and training support on TPUs. Now that TorchTPU brings native support, Optimum TPU is not required anymore to run Hugging Face models with Transformers and Diffusers.

TorchTPU adds TPU as a new backend to PyTorch. You write regular PyTorch code. It comes with Pallas kernels tuned for TPUs, support for distributed training, and a torch.compile integration for when you want more speed. Installing it on a TPU VM takes one command:

The extra index gives you the CPU build of torch. Without it, pip pulls the much bigger CUDA build, which you don't need on a TPU.

Transformers v5 was built around one idea: be the source of truth for model definitions, so they can run anywhere. "Anywhere" now includes TPUs. To load a model on a TPU, pass device_map="tpu". That's it.

The model runs in eager mode by default. You can also use torch.compile for better performance, or run it in a distributed setup.

TPU is now a first-class device in Diffusers. For prototyping or debugging, eager mode only needs pipe.to("tpu"). For deployment, compiled mode adds one compile call. Your pipelines and code stay the same, and there's no TPU fork to maintain.

The first call compiles, and every call after that with the same image size reuses the graph.

Models too big for one chip? Pass a TensorParallelConfig to from_pretrained and the transformer is sharded across chips as it loads, so the full model never has to fit in one place. Many popular pipelines support it out of the box, and the ones that don't are just a tp_plan away. The Diffusers TPU guide has the full recipe.

Here are some examples run on a Cloud TPU v6e-4:

TP=4 (each model split across four chips) · bf16 · batch 1

The Kernels Hub has ready-to-use TPU kernels. Load one with the Kernels library and give your model a speed boost.

TPU kernels are written in Pallas, which gives you low-level control over the hardware. You can also bring in kernels from the Tokamax library. Here is a ragged-dot kernel from Tokamax plugged into a Mixture-of-Experts model:

The bigger the batch, the bigger the win. At batch size 64, decoding is 21.5× faster on Qwen3-30B-A3B and 12.8× faster on Gemma 4 26B-A4B.

Decode throughput on a TPU v6e-8, Hub kernel vs. the default implementation.

We're continuously improving TPU support in transformers by running the library test suite. We are working to add a nightly CI on TPU and make the results available in the (transformers dashboard)[https://huggingface.co/spaces/transformers-community/transformers-ci-dashboard].

The Transformers CI dashboard, with TPU results next to other accelerators. Work in progress!

It's not all green yet, and we're fine with that. Of the tests that run on TPU, 96.5% pass. Every failure we find becomes a small repro script and an issue on the TorchTPU repo. So far we have reported 34 issues, and 19 are already fixed. Running on TPU also caught a few bugs in Transformers itself, like in StaticCache and the Qwen3 tensor-parallel plans. We fixed those upstream.

If something breaks on TPU, we want to find out before you do.

TPUs are no longer a side quest for PyTorch users. Install TorchTPU, grab a model from the Hub, and send it to "tpu".

We can't wait to see what you build 🤗. If you hit a problem, open an issue and tell us about it.

#9779. CISA Announces Enhanced Reporting Form for Cyber Incidents

New questionnaire captures critical data and information that improves the agency’s ability to assess incidents, identify trends and prioritize response actions.

WASHINGTON — Today, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) unveiled the updated cyber incident reporting form, an enhanced web-enabled questionnaire available on CISA’s Incident Reporting Portal for reporting cyber incidents. By improving data quality, the more robust form strengthens the effectiveness and efficiency of national cyber defense. For instance, the new form will help CISA correlate related cyber threat activity to identify a larger trend from what otherwise would appear as independent incidents.

The new cyber incident reporting form is guided by community feedback CISA has received over the years and the agency’s efforts to improve data quality that enables rapid yet thorough threat analysis. For example, questions about the type of incident are more comprehensive and seek more granular information, including whether the incident involved malware, social engineering, hacking techniques or an insider threat. Also, questions about observed activity now incorporate the MITRE ATT&CK® Framework, language about adversary behavior that is familiar to the cyber community.

Related:Inside an AI Attack Against a US Retailer

“In the team sport of cybersecurity, one organization’s detection is another’s protection,” said Acting Executive Assistant Director for Cybersecurity Chris Butera. “As the national coordinator for critical infrastructure cybersecurity and resilience, CISA is able to leverage such incident reporting to identify emerging cyber campaigns, warn potential targets, and strengthen the Nation’s collective defense.”

While only federal civilian agencies are required to report, CISA encourages any organization that experiences a cyber incident to voluntarily report.

For more information, please visit the Frequently Asked Questionsweb page.

As the nation’s cyber defense agency and national coordinator for critical infrastructure security, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency leads the national effort to manage, uncover, and reduce risk to our digital and physical infrastructure Americans rely on every hour of every day.

#9778. The Psychology of Luxury Marketing: Why We Pay More for Less

Hi, I'm Yukti Sachan, a writer and content creator from India with an interest in storytelling, books, marketing, and formula 1

Hi, I'm Yukti Sachan, a writer and content creator from India with an interest in storytelling, books, marketing, and formula 1

Hi, I'm Yukti Sachan, a writer and content creator from India with an interest in storytelling, books, marketing, and formula 1

Have you ever looked at a piece of bent metal and thought, “Why does this cost as much as a decent used car?”

Recently, I stumbled across a Ferrari metal collar online. It cost $2,500. It looked like someone picked up a sheet of basic aluminum, bent it aggressively, painted it Rosso Corsa red, and said, “Yep, that’ll be two grand and a half, please.”

It made me genuinely sit down and ask: Why the fuck would anyone pay that?

Well, welcome to a niche little world called luxury marketing, which apparently means we add a ridiculous price tag to ordinary items and watch everyone scramble to buy them.

Luxury marketing has three main pillars that conveniently work together to gaslight you into thinking that a tiny bottle of perfume = a down payment for a prime city apartment is a completely reasonable thing to pay for.

The three main pillars of luxury marketing are: I know those sound like really scary terms, but trust me, I’m going to hold your hand and explain how they collectively gaslight you.

(Disclaimer: I’m not a marketing person. All of this has come from research papers and articles I’ve read, plus whatever marginal bits I actually understood from them. 😭)

When you think something you want is about to sell out, you’re more likely to impulsively buy it, even if you haven’t stopped to think about the pros and cons yet. You see something you like, notice that there is very little stock left, and suddenly you’re buying it without thinking about whether you actually need it or not.

That’s essentially what the illusion of scarcity is: less availability, more wanting, quicker decisions, more impulsive buying, more urgency, and ultimately, more sales.

The illusion of scarcity refers to the tactic of creating a perception that a product or service is in limited supply when, in reality, it might not be.

It plays on the psychological principle that people are more likely to desire something they believe is running out or hard to obtain.

It compels people to take action when they believe they might miss out on something valuable or desirable.

The illusion of scarcity uses this fear to make customers more likely to buy to avoid the regret of missing out.

People are more motivated by the prospect of avoiding loss rather than gaining something.

The illusion of scarcity creates a sense of potential loss. Consumers fear losing the opportunity to purchase the product or service. This fear of loss motivates consumers more than the desire to gain, pushing them to act quickly.

When a consumer sees that a product is in limited stock or others are purchasing it quickly, they are more likely to believe the product is valuable and worth buying. The perception is reinforced by the idea that if others are scrambling to buy it, it must be worth having.

(Shameless advertisement: I talk more about this in my July edition, where I talked about how Red Bull used this tactic in the trash can myth. For more info, click here — July Edition.)

In luxury marketing, people aren’t just buying the product; they are buying the perceived social status that the said product provides them with.

In emerging markets (such as the BRIC nations, i.e., Brazil, Russia, India, and China), it was observed that logo-flashy or more easily recognised luxury goods are more widely sought after by people, as they felt the need to separate themselves from the masses and perceive a higher social status, like Look at me, I am richer as compared to you, which is why I am higher on the social ladder as compared to you and make themselves stand out.

Meanwhile, mature markets (such as the United States, Italy, and France) were observed to be moving towards more subtle, less flashy luxury items which aren’t very easily recognisable by someone who doesn’t know about it because they tend to do it for (so-called) internalised-luxury consumption. The term refers to the perception of purchasing luxury goods for themselves or to express themselves better and to integrate themselves into a certain social group.

Mature market, in the above context, refers to markets that have reached a certain equilibrium and are characterised by modest growth.

An emerging market, in the above context, refers to markets that have a chronic shortage of resources and are characterised by inadequate infrastructure but also yield impressive economic growth.

So, in mature markets, people are moving towards a more subtle display of luxury, such as minimalistic or no logos, or a higher emphasis on the craftsmanship of the product. While emerging markets move more towards flashy, easily recognisable logos or/and patterns.

Yet in general, both aren’t buying the product for the utilitarian purpose of the product, but rather are purchasing the product or service to display a certain social status and separate themselves from the masses, such as: I am different from you; I have a higher perceived social status than you; and I’m richer than you, and I have a certain expensiveness that you lack and am living a certain level of luxurious lifestyle that you cannot attain.

Luxury marketing emphasizes the item's perceived social status. And consumers invest in it as they associate a certain sense of self-importance and a separation from the masses and their supposed (*air quotes*) superior social status with the ownership of the product, and therefore are willing to invest more in products that are marketed as a luxury, with the illusion of scarcity, than what might be the actual justified cost of the product solely based on utility if it wasn’t marketed as a luxury good or service.

Heritage is a crucial part of a luxury brand, as it needs to have a modern aspect for the current society yet, at the same time, have a certain historical aspect to it.

It adds an association of depth, authenticity, and credibility to the brand's perceived value and can result in increased brand loyalty and a willingness to accept higher prices.

It marks within itself the strategic cultivation of the brand’s origins, traditions, and values over time. As Heritage builds on permanence, prestige, and authenticity, it gives luxury consumers a narrative and a mythology to associate themselves with, linking back to how they view their perceived social status increasing with consumption of luxury brands’ goods and/or services.

The $50 Million Gamble That Made Red Bull Marketing History

#9777. Profiling TorchNeuron (Part 1): System-level profiling on AWS Trainium.

Many ML practitioners have some intuition about how to make models run fast, but fewer know how to analyze why a model is slow. In Part 1 of this series, you will learn how to systematically analyze inference performance and identify where the time is spent.

This post starts from scratch and assumes no prior profiling experience. The walkthrough uses AWS Trainium, a purpose-built AI chip for deep learning training and inference workloads, and TorchNeuron, its open source native PyTorch backend. TorchNeuron supports standard PyTorch workflows on Trainium, including eager execution, torch.compile, and standard PyTorch APIs, with minimal code changes. Additionally, TorchNeuron integrates with Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI) to enable custom operators and performance optimization for Trainium hardware. By the end, you should know:

Before you profile a workload, it helps to understand how Neuron integrates with PyTorch.

The Neuron backend uses PyTorch's PrivateUse1 extension point. This mechanism lets an accelerator integrate with the framework without adding a dedicated dispatch key such as cuda. The torch_neuronx package works with upstream PyTorch to register Neuron as a native backend for PyTorch code. For details about this extension mechanism, see Facilitating New Backend Integration by PrivateUse1.

You use two objects to profile a Neuron workload:

The modes parameter selects the data streams to capture, such as device instructions and runtime traces. The capture_enabled_for_nc parameter selects the NeuronCores to trace. Setting correlate_device_time=True propagates device time from the trace into the key_averages() table, where you can compare CPU and Neuron device time. For the complete parameter reference and available ProfileMode values, see the NeuronConfig Profile Modes documentation.

Neuron Explorer is a browser-based viewer for the system trace, device timeline, and per-engine breakdown. You can access it through an SSH tunnel or the Visual Studio Code extension. In this post, you use Explorer to confirm what key_averages() reports numerically and inspect what happens between dispatches.

After profiling, the output directory contains the system trace and, when you capture device data, matched .neff and .ntff files. The Neuron Executable File Format (NEFF) contains the compiled Neuron executable, while the matching NTFF contains its hardware instruction trace. The files share a numeric hash that identifies them as a pair. To open the profile in Neuron Explorer, upload the complete output directory for a system or combined profile. For a device-only profile, upload the matching .neff and .ntff files individually. See Step 5: Upload your profile for the UI and command-line instructions.

For this first analysis, you profile RMSNorm, a small operation with a clear sequence of arithmetic and reduction operations.

You profile three implementations of the same operation:

The scripts use the same inputs, profiler configuration, and schedule so the results are directly comparable.

All scripts to reproduce this work are available in the torch-neuronx examples directory.

Start by writing RMSNorm with individual PyTorch operations. Each line maps to one or more ATen operations and can create intermediate tensors.

Call the profiler with two arguments required for the Neuron backend:

The schedule uses wait=2, warmup=1, and active=1 across four prof.step() calls. This records one warm iteration without including initial setup overhead.

Call torch.neuron.synchronize() inside the profiler loop. Without this synchronization, the profiler can export before the device finishes and leave the Neuron time column empty.

After profiling finishes, inspect the key_averages() table. Sort by self_privateuse1_time_total to place the operations with the highest device cost first. The table shown here is filtered to the RMSNorm operations that report Neuron device time. The full key_averages() output also includes CPU-side events such as allocations and host-to-device transfers.

The key averages table shows that three aten::mul calls account for the largest share of Neuron device time.

The table shows which ATen operations ran, how often they ran, and how much time they spent on the CPU and Neuron device. aten::mul has the highest total device time because the function performs three multiplications.

Each row maps directly to the function. aten::mul runs for x * x, x * rms, and the final multiplication by weight. aten::mean reduces the last dimension. aten::add adds the epsilon value and triggers a host-to-device copy because the scalar starts on the CPU. aten::rsqrt computes the reciprocal square root.

Neuron Explorer follows an aten::mul operation from framework dispatch through runtime scheduling to execution on the Neuron hardware lanes.

In Explorer, time flows from left to right and the event lifecycle flows from top to bottom. Each ATen operation follows the same pattern: creation in the framework lane, scheduling in the runtime lane as nrta_execute_schedule, and device execution in the hardware lane as nc_exec_running.

The system trace view organizes events into lanes. In the Default grouping mode, labels follow the pattern instance/PID/subsystem/identifier:

In eager mode, each operation runs independently. Use the dependency chain viewer to follow aten::mul.Tensor from the framework layer through runtime scheduling to device execution.

The dependency chain viewer highlights the lifecycle of one operation across the framework, runtime, and hardware lanes.

Replace the individual operations with PyTorch's built-in rms_norm function. Neuron lowers the operation to one fused kernel:

The fused RMSNorm appears as one device operation in the key averages table.

The fused RMSNorm follows one framework-to-hardware path instead of dispatching each arithmetic operation separately.

In the naive implementation, each operation crosses the dispatch boundary independently and follows its own framework-to-runtime-to-hardware path. In the fused implementation, one Python call covers the complete computation. The trace contains one dispatch and one hardware event, with no gaps between component operations.

For the final example, compile the original naive RMSNorm function with torch.compile.

With @torch.compile(backend="neuron"), TorchDynamo captures the Python bytecode as an FX graph and AOTAutograd lowers it to ATen operations. The Neuron backend receives the complete graph instead of dispatching each operation separately. It fuses the operations, optimizes memory access, and compiles the graph into a single NEFF artifact. The artifact runs as one hardware dispatch.

The compiled function appears as one Torch-Compiled Region in the key averages table.

The compiled graph follows one path through runtime scheduling and hardware execution.

The table shows one device execution, as in Profile 2, but the code takes a different path. Instead of calling a purpose-built fused operation, the compiler discovers the fusion from the original Python function. In this run, the Neuron time is comparable to torch.rms_norm, at 375 μs compared with 403 μs.

Both torch.rms_norm and torch.compile fuse RMSNorm into one kernel dispatch. In these runs, either approach takes about one-sixth of the naive implementation's device time. Fusion removes the gaps between hardware executions and avoids materializing intermediate values such as x_sq and mean_sq between separately dispatched operations.

key_averages() shows which operations consume device time, while its full output also reveals CPU-side setup and transfers. Explorer provides the corresponding visual trace. You can follow one operation from framework dispatch through runtime scheduling to hardware execution and see the gaps that fusion removes.

You can use the same workflow on larger models: find a hotspot in the table, verify it in the trace, and then determine whether a fused operation or torch.compile can reduce its cost.

In Part 2, we will move into the device-level profile. You open the NEFF, inspect the TensorEngine, VectorEngine, and direct memory access (DMA) breakdown, and place the kernel on the roofline to determine whether it is compute-bound or memory-bound.

Special thanks to Aritra Roy Gosthipaty for the inspiration to begin this series, and to my peers Pinak Panigrahi, Samir Araujo, Akhil Azhikodan, Esha Lakhotia and the rest for reviewing!

#9776. People Are Getting Weird About AI

Dark Reading Confidential Episode 22: You can love AI without being blind to cybersecurity being sacrificed for utility. The tendency for humans to anthropomorphize the conversations and interactions we're having with AI is growing into potential delusion.

Dark Reading's Becky Bracken: Hello everyone, and welcome back to Dark Reading Confidential. It's a podcast from the editors of Dark Reading, bringing you real-world stories straight from the cyber trenches. I am so excited to introduce our guest, Jaya Baloo, who is currently CISO and COO of Aisle. Welcome. Thank you so much for joining us, Jaya.

Jaya Baloo: Thank you so much for inviting me, Becky. Thank you.

DR's Becky Bracken: We are thrilled you're here. I want to explain to our audience a little bit about why I am so particularly excited to have you here. Recently, I was in the audience at ISC2 Security Congress in Denver, and Jaya gave what I just thought was a blockbuster talk about sort of merging AI and quantum, and it was fascinating. There's a specific chunk of her talk that I invited her to talk about today. And it's something I'm just calling: Why is everyone so weird about AI?

Related:AI Raises the Stakes for Cyber Resilience

And so, it stuck with me for days afterward. I kept having the conversation with people because, as I was just explaining to Jaya, we hear people talk about this on the edges, but I hadn't heard a technologist and an expert explain it so plainly, which I think Jaya is also sort of your superpower. But just in the past couple of days, we have Sam Altman who came out saying no one needs their own RAM. They're calling him "RAM Altman." I mean, it's just that people are weird. So, can you explain to me why you dropped that section in, and do you know why it stuck with me for so long? Why is it hitting so close?

Jaya Baloo: I think it's because for ages, when we looked at AI, we had this notion of the uncanny valley, you know? Like, at what point is it so convincing to me that I think I'm speaking to a human? And I think it's clear to say we've passed this uncanny valley. We're fully, you know, believing the conversations that we're having with AI. They could be coming from another human. So, the tendency for us to anthropomorphize the conversations, the interactions that we're having with AI is growing and growing.

And you see people who are not just having a sort of delusional psychosis sometimes of aggrandizement of their own intellect when talking to AI and convinced because of some of the sick fancy that's built into AI that they're super intelligent or their ideas are incredibly unique and creative, or that they're actually the ones to save humanity. You know, I think that the problems that we see with people who are potentially susceptible to that are just made much worse by the current evolution and this current state of AI that we have today. It's just so real. It's so convincing. And we then tend to make it more human.

Related:AI Coding Agents Leak Thousands of Secrets to GitHub

DR's Becky Bracken: So, let's go through some of the examples that you gave in your talk. One of them that made me cackle out loud was when you were playing video of a robot doing kung fu with a caption: Why can't we teach it to do laundry? Explain that example for us.

Jaya Baloo: Yeah, so really what I'm talking about is that, you know, we already have a whole bunch of threats right now when we're dealing with AI. And that's really about AI's capability to both uncover vulnerabilities as well as having vulnerabilities in and of itself. So, AI as a potential for insider threat. As we already have these problems, both in our legacy tech debt and in the new technology that we're building with AI, we have more problems.

Now, I have no idea who thought this was a great idea to take these things that are entrenched with these problems, and put it into something that can actually cause physical harm and teach a robot, which by the way, I should be clear, this was the Unitree humanoid robot. It was announced a little bit over a week ago. But let's say that it was announced at the end of October. And this robot was demonstrated on YouTube to do all this cool kung fu stuff.

Related:AI Gave Your Incident Archive a Second Job

And the issue with this that I have is that this can cause actual physical harm. What is it actually bringing humans in terms of value? And honestly, I would be much happier with a humanoid robot that can do the wash, fold the laundry, and sort it out in the kid's hamper. That would be helpful. It wouldn't be something where I'd be terrified to have this thing anywhere near us. And I think that this is something that I feel is genuinely problematic. Just because you can doesn't mean you should when it comes to some of these implementations. And if you cannot get the security right, don't exacerbate and increase the potential for doing damage and harm to humans.

I feel like we forgot that as we're building. You know, we need to solve tech debt, we need to make sure that we have secure-by-default systems, and then you can implement it in something that coexists with us in the physical realm. So that was my point about that. But I really want to say the real issue here is that Unitree had not one, but two, remote backdoors in its quadruped robots. There are multiple security issues with its humanoid robots. And I think knowing that you can remotely take over these robots, and again, like they're capable of physical harm, I think that we really need to rethink and really considerately position these types of devices in light of things like the Cyber Resilience Act.

You know, should we allow hardware and software manufacturers to bring out this kind of technology with the potential risk that it poses? And not just from a cyber perspective, but from a physical one as well.

DR's Becky Bracken: What were some of your other top examples of what's another one that you'd like to highlight here of people being kind of weird about AI?

Jaya Baloo: Well, so I think a slide that you may have initially seen is, and I kind of didn't want to reference it right away in my first answer, was about the fact that we're getting strained in terms of the religiousness around AI. That we both have this tendency to first say, actually, you know, maybe they're sentient, which Anthropic has been talking about in the Vatican with different religious leaders trying to talk about the potential consciousness of AI.

And although I love science fiction, I love it, I just feel, are we really there yet? Are we there, or is this a marketing ploy? What is this? And I'm genuinely trying to understand because it polemicizes what should be a very rational debate into two camps. Those who believe, like already now, we're at the point of talking about consciousness and sentience of these AI systems.

And then the other camp, which actually rebukes AI in the name of Jesus. And I think that was the slide that people also laughed at the conference about. But this is real. And I find it bizarre that we have these phenomena happening and that we don't fully understand the societal consequences either of introducing these systems, which again, let's talk about what they are. They're a bunch of graphics cards in a data center running software.

I am a full Kool-Aid drinker of the notion of complexity and emergence and understanding that even though with a relative set of simple ingredients you have potentially complex outcomes. Drank that Kool-Aid long ago. I believe in this stuff, but I just don't think we're there yet.

So, I feel this has a sort of reductionism effect for the debate that we should be having over how do we do responsible AI by pulling it into these two polemic camps.

DR's Becky Bracken: You also tied it to a lot of end-of-times cult-like thinking, but it does raise the question, which you sort of alluded to a moment ago, how much of this is being driven by marketing of these frontier models, of the [Sam] Altmans of the world, of the Peter Thiels of the world who are out talking. How much of a receptive audience are they finding in the cybersecurity sector, do you think? I mean, is that the primary dynamic at play?

Jaya Baloo: Well, look, I think that we need to separate what is actually happening, which is we do have a bunch of vulnerability discoveries that are happening because of AI. We do have automation for real. It is genuinely happening. We do have automation of these hacking frameworks from Strix, RTec-Ai, Cairn. We are seeing hacking frameworks that are actually in RTec specifically, that are actually being used in real-world hacks. So I'm not trying to discount the facts.

However, what I'm urging to do is the call that, for example, Ciaran Martin, the former head of GCHQ (Government Communications Headquarters), always makes, which is, "Calm the FUD down."

And the fear, uncertainty, doubt that we're introducing here is not helpful. And the reason that I find it really unhelpful is because we know to a large extent how we should perform some sort of containment in terms of egress filtering and sandboxing of these systems.

They may not be perfect, but we've always worked with this notion of defense in depth: assume that one measure fails and that you have additional countermeasures to prevent an actual collapse of the security of the system. I think that that is something that we are actually forgetting right now. And I think it's really important to say, OK, what are the things we genuinely need that would be considered helpful innovation for this? And I think that what we're missing is a lot of the observability here around these AI systems.

So, for example, if we're trying to understand how these systems have potentially been poisoned or Trojanized inherently, then the ability to actually understand how that training data has been populated, even when you only have open-weight models, that would be helpful.

Another thing is additional understanding around this notion of J-space (Jacobian space). So, agent intent. If you know that you have a human operator that brings their own intent to the mix, you know and understand that an AI system might have capabilities and intent that diverge from that human operator, you need to understand when and where that first point of evidence for collecting that divergence could be. We're not there yet either.

So, I would like us to focus on those things rather than the FUD, like Ciaran Martin and a bunch of other renowned cybersecurity people have been saying for a while, like we really need to focus on the things that are breaking.

And really need to focus on the things that we need to be building rather than everyone up in arms about this "Vulnpocalypse," "Breachpocalypse," etc. Apocalypses that are predicted.

DR's Becky Bracken: What is the best way to push back against this sort of rampant anthropomorphization of these agents? You know, I mean, even when researchers are using words like they will "cheat," which assumes that there is a moral compass there to begin with. But at the same time, the goal is for them to be as human as possible? How do we thread that needle?

Jaya Baloo: "They will cheat" is the reward hacking notion that this is a utility that is trying to find the shortest path to success. That means that things that a human would consider part of that moral compass, not to cheat, not to lie, not to evade, etc., that we are projecting this somehow on these AI systems and assuming that the guardrails that we've put in place will cover it.

But I don't think that you can make that assumption clearly, because I don't think we're always in the position to inspect all of the guardrails and know when they've been appropriately applied. And so, I think that there's also this issue of finiteness. Can you have a finite set of guardrails that are actually encompassing the kinds of things that you want to do? And I think the answer to that is probably not.

You know, you’re probably still going to have a few things that escape your potential for, like having this perfectly constructed set of guardrails. Those are like mathematical limitations.

What I would love to encourage us to do is genuinely try to understand better the types of technology that we put into our networks, give access to our data, give a single API token and say "YOLO" to our enterprises, because I don't think we have this under control. And I think that's the real worry that I have.

If we don't understand fully and we're not aware of all of the potential risks, for example, cheating or lying, misrepresentation, etc., if we don't understand that, then we certainly can't have all of these elevated privileges and permissions that we're doing. I think this was the point I was trying to make about when you have capability, you need to kind of always have this subset of this accountability and authorization that you're giving something. And right now, we forgot that lesson. You know, we said, here's all the stuff that you've got access to. You go. And I really feel like we need to rewind a little bit just this part. And that requires better understanding of what they're capable of in terms of the risks.

DR's Becky Bracken: So, what is the next step forward? If you had your team and you were seeing some of this sort of extreme thinking, you know, seeping into your defense planning, what would you say to them? What is the correct reset function here?

Jaya Baloo: I'm really worried about the fact that we are genuinely at risk of losing some of the critical thinking when we're applying AI systems. And you see that already with our coding practices; we are allowing more and more of that initial thinking. So, planning our projects, actually executing the code, reviewing that code, proving it, etc.

DR's Becky Bracken: Which is shocking in such an evidence-based field. You know, it is shocking that it's gone so fast. Am I right?

Jaya Baloo: I feel like we kind of learned this lesson in security in the past too. So it's kind of like, Back to the Future, as well. Every time we tell people about "you should do this because it's secure," if it's not an easy or fun thing to do, you know people won't do it, right? The utility surpasses the convenience. All of the brain elements that would constitute your frontal lobe warning you for this risk. Like, we just lose it. We become teenagers again. Our risk level and tolerance are high. We are happy to take these risks if it makes our life a little bit easier. And I think we shouldn't forget that.

So, AI as an assistant is an incredibly powerful, incredibly useful tool. And especially when we're trying to drive efficiencies with all this technology and all this cost. And you're talking about, you know, "RAM Altman." I think the accessibility of AI and the sovereignty of it is not something we should be taking for granted. And it absolutely is a problem.

So, knowing all of this, you know, the drive to get this convenience, to get this utility, to get this thing available, that is so overcoming any type of hesitation we would have, like, "Is this safe? Should I really use this?" "Will I get dumber if I keep doing this all the time and outsource my thinking?" And I think that's where we actually still need to keep in mind this notion of: What are we giving up to get this utility?

DR's Becky Bracken: Maybe that's why what you were saying hit so hard because I haven't heard a lot of technologists take that position. You know much better than I do, but they are all gas, no breaks, whatever it takes, let's just not lose the wave. And this return to critical thinking, it seems new. Among your peers and colleagues, do you hear the same kind of concern about losing critical thinking?

Jaya Baloo: I think this is the problem with the Kool-Aid. I think at Aisle we certainly have that. I think there's a strong tendency amongst security professionals, but also AI professionals. So, my co-founder, Stanislav Fort, who is amazing, has always kind of thought about AI safety and interpretability. And he has been the person to say, for example, we initially set up Aisle to do vulnerability remediation. And you can imagine that as a CISO, I was like, all right, if we can do this and we can do this well, let's just remediate all the things. Let's just give it access. And he has always urged caution, always urged caution to say, "You know what? We're not there yet"

Unless we can fully confidently trust the AI to make those changes, I always want a human approving the PRs to any code request. I just don't think that what we have in our co-founder is a universal quality in all AI companies. So, I think that like my other co-founder, Ondřej Vlček, who is CISO for multiple companies, including Avast. We have this tendency because we've been burned. So we are, you know, a once-burned, twice-shy kind of notion.

We really think about this from a security-oriented risk-mitigation perspective while actually wanting. I have to be very honest with you, I love AI. But that love shouldn't be blind. It should take the appropriate measure of what is it that I love? And why do I love it? And, you know, what is the benefit to humanity? And Becky, there's a story that I didn't tell on stage.

There are so many good things we can do with AI, but the one thing that I'm the most encouraged of is ... have you heard about the story with the guy and the dog in Australia?

DR's Becky Bracken: No, I don't think I have.

Jaya Baloo: So, this was a machine learning engineer whose dog developed cancer, inoperable, and the dog had to be put down, was the diagnosis. And what he then did is sequence the dog's DNA. You know, this is a guy with no biology background, sequenced the dog's DNA, and figured out what was wrong in the DNA that caused the cancer, developed an mRNA vaccine with AlphaFold.

The most expensive part of the experiment apparently was to actually synthesize the vaccine. And then he administered it to his dog; he had to get permission for that. And Rosie's tumors shrank, and she's is still here and is still hanging out and playing ball with this machine learning engineer.

So I love this story, and this is why I love AI. Because I think if it can unlock the potential benefits, that is amazing. I want those benefits. I just want to make sure that we minimize the downside risks that are inevitable with this kind of technology. And we just need to figure out how we do that. So, we shouldn't go screaming into the abyss, like, yay! You know, I don't want us to be a bunch of lemmings following AI down the abyss.

I just want us to manage that risk and take the benefits while eyes wide open, understanding that right now we need to make sure that we do have enough RAM, you know, and that we do have sovereign compute, that we do not sacrifice all our clean water

DR's Becky Bracken: No one has to give up their computer for OpenAI?

Jaya Baloo: Yeah. I think the future of AI is probably more decentralized than the frontier labs have us think right now.

DR’s Becky Bracken: How much of this is being driven by investment dollars and hyping up stock price? Because we talked around in our editorial meeting about well, is this just a collective psychosis issue? And it's like, well, first, let's be careful about saying "psychosis," but also are we being marketed into a psychosis?

Jaya Baloo: I would love to have a balanced approach. I'm not saying that there's no marketing being done. I think that is certainly being done. I don't think we should eliminate that. I think it would be naive to assume otherwise. At the same time, going full tilt that it's all just marketing is the wrong approach. I think two things can be true at the same time. And I want us to consider this more nuanced thing. And I really want our brains to hold the capacity that both things are true.

There is absolutely a marketing effort. OK, when you have these kinds of companies going to IPO and it's not just OpenAI, it's also Anthropic, and it's also probably a whole bunch of other, you know, parts of this wheel that are actually driving this rage. But there are genuinely risks that we must counter. So, I really do worry about that. And I don't think that that is psychosis.

You must have seen the filing of Anthropic for the IPO. And one of those things that is in that document is there's a very real existential threat that AI could kill us all. I think that's maybe the first time that was ever put into a filing of a company potentially going to IPO. And even there, I think, surely that is not marketing. Surely there are intelligent, thoughtful humans that want to warn of a potential risk that they genuinely see for themselves. I think we need to evaluate the difference between that and how much space there is between the marketing and the genuine risk. But I do think there is a genuine risk. There is. And we shouldn't downplay it as psychosis, while at the same time recognize that there's marketing.

DR's Becky Bracken: I want to thank you so much for coming. You've given me a whole other set of things to think about. Thank you for sharing your deep expertise and your thoughts with us today. We really appreciate it.

Jaya Baloo: No worries, thank you for having me.

DR's Becky Bracken: This has been Dark Reading Confidential. It's a podcast from the editors of Dark Reading, bringing you real-world stories straight from the cyber trenches. I'm Becky Bracken. Thank you so much for joining us. We'll see you next time.

The Dark Reading Editorial Team consists of Kelly Jackson Higgins, Fahmida Y Rashid, Tara Seals, Rob Wright, Becky Bracken, Alex Culafi, Arielle Waldman, and Kristina Beek. #9775. ShinyHunters Extorted Boeing Spin-off Prior to Arrests

A teenager from Amman, Jordan suspected of leading the prolific data theft and extortion group ShinyHunters has been detained and is reportedly cooperating with the FBI to identify other members of the hacking gang. KrebsOnSecurity has learned that the suspect, who uses the hacker handle “Rey,” was detained as ShinyHunters was in the process of extorting a business unit recently divested by the global aerospace company Boeing, which manufactures the fleet of planes used by the employer of Rey’s father — Royal Jordanian Airlines.

The logo for Jeppesen ForeFlight, a business unit divested last year by the aerospace firm Boeing.

On October 3, Reuters cited three unnamed sources saying a suspected ShinyHunters member in Amman named Saif Al-din Khader was detained by Jordanian authorities and was cooperating with the FBI. KrebsOnSecurity identified Rey as Khader in a November 2025 profile, in which the young man admitted working with multiple ransomware groups.

Rey was featured again in a September 28 exclusive about the Dutch police arresting 24-year-old convicted cybercriminal Pepijn van der Stap on suspicion of aiding in data thefts and extortions by ShinyHunters. The story noted that immediately following the Dutchman’s arrest on the evening of September 15, Rey assumed control over the ShinyHunters brand and boasted publicly about stealing highly sensitive data from the FBI and extorting the ransomware group Cl0p.

Rey taunted both the FBI and Cl0p with memes posted to his longtime account on Twitter/X, while simultaneously including images of the avatar used by Van Der Stap’s former hacker alias “Umbreon” in an apparent attempt to frame the Dutchman for both hacks.

A taunting meme uploaded to Twitter/X by Rey on Sept. 22. A giant sized version of the Pokemon character Umbreon can be seen in the bottom left.

As noted in our September 28 report, ShinyHunters gained access to the FBI site and other victims by exploiting a vulnerability (CVE-2026-35273) in PeopleSoft, a software-as-a-service platform from the tech giant Oracle that is broadly used by companies to manage hiring and human resources, benefits and payroll. Oracle quickly issued a fix for CVE-2026-35273, which ShinyHunters first began exploiting as a zero-day in June, and at the time Mandiant released web application firewall rules intended for organizations that couldn’t apply the security update quickly enough.

ShinyHunters told BleepingComputer in June that the original goal behind exploiting the PeopleSoft vulnerability was to breach the FBI’s own PeopleSoft database, but the hackers said those attacks were unsuccessful for some reason. In recent weeks, however, ShinyHunters turned to a well-known URL-encoding trick to bypass Mandiant’s suggested web application firewall rules.

In a report released Sept. 25, security experts at Mandiant and the Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) confirmed that ShinyHunters had mass-exploited the PeopleSoft vulnerability to steal data from dozens of systems across a range of industries, including higher education, technology, healthcare, agriculture, transportation and government.

Reuters reported October 5 that the FBI has removed a contractor at Accenture over their failure to patch the FBI recruitment website hacked by ShinyHunters, which exposed sensitive data on more than 5,000 FBI personnel, including each’s person’s unit and specialization, as well as medical and psychiatric records.

According to two sources familiar with the ShinyHunters investigation, a navigation and digital aviation unit recently divested by the global aerospace company Boeing was among the victims that ShinyHunters was in the process of extorting when Rey was apprehended by Jordanian authorities.

Those sources said the FBI’s investigation into ShinyHunters gained renewed urgency with the group’s attempted extortion of the former Boeing unit, which allegedly included the theft of sensitive information that sources said could pose operational safety and security risks.

In a brief statement shared with KrebsOnSecurity, Boeing acknowledged the extortion attempts by ShinyHunters, and said the incident concerned data stolen from Jeppesen ForeFlight, a subsidiary that Boeing sold in November 2025 to the private equity firm Thoma Bravo for $10.55 billion.

“We are aware of claims by a threat actor regarding data allegedly associated with Boeing and our former subsidiary Jeppesen ForeFlight,” a Boeing spokesperson shared. “We are actively reviewing the matter with the Jeppesen ForeFlight team.”

A spokesperson for Jeppesen ForeFlight shared a written statement in response to questions, saying the company has seen no impact on their end. “Based on our investigation to date into this claim and proactive security posture, there was no impact to our operations or products.”

Rey’s alleged involvement in attempting to extort the former Boeing unit is noteworthy because there is strong evidence that his father works for Royal Jordanian Airlines, which is mostly controlled by the Jordanian government and operates its long-haul fleet on passenger planes built by Boeing. Rey claimed on Telegram in early 2025 that his father was an airline pilot, although that could not be independently confirmed.

However, as noted in our November 2025 profile of Rey, his family’s shared computer was at one point compromised by password-stealing malware, and the data collected by that malware clearly shows Rey’s father used the same credentials to log in at multiple online portals for Royal Jordanian Airlines employees.

Royal Jordanian Airlines has not yet responded to a request for comment. In advance of our September 28 story, KrebsOnSecurity once again emailed Rey’s father to seek comment and update him on his son’s alleged activities. Neither of the Khaders have responded. But just hours after that request was sent, Rey began deleting his various social media accounts, including the Twitter/X account he previously used to taunt the FBI, Cl0p, and other ShinyHunters victims.

Rey may have nixed many of his social media profiles, but his cybersecurity blog on GitHub somehow escaped the purge, and it shows that Rey was fixated on the leaders of the Cl0p ransomware group. In March 2026, Rey’s blog featured a lengthy post that identified two Russian men as the core developers and hackers behind Cl0p.

Rey’s blog on GitHub. This post doxes two Russian men as the core operators behind Cl0p, one of the oldest and most established ransomware groups still in operation today.

Meanwhile, news outlets in the Netherlands reported explosive new allegations leveled at Van der Stap, whose supposed personal transformation from convicted to reformed hacker has been widely covered in the tech news media. The Dutch daily RTL reported on Sept. 29 that investigators suspect Van der Stap tried to orchestrate at least two murders. According to RTL, the murders were allegedly to be committed abroad, and there are indications Van der Stap gave the order for these attacks.

Van der Stap was released from prison after serving the better part of a four year sentence for data theft and extortion activity that prosecutors said netted between €1.5 million and €2.7 million. In an interview with KrebsOnSecurity on September 9, Van der Stap described his new role as “offensive security lead” at the Dutch cybersecurity company Neo Security, saying the job involved probing client networks for security vulnerabilities.

Neo Security’s owner Benjamin Korper told Reuters he has hired an outside firm to investigate whether Van der Stap had hacked Neo Security or its customers, but that so far investigators have found no evidence he acted against his employer or clients. Korper said Dutch forensic investigators visited his office on September 15, the night Van der ⁠Stap was arrested in a dramatic police raid that reportedly involved flash bang grenades.

A screenshot of a Sept 16 story by the Dutch news outlet at5.nl, describing a police raid on Van Der Stap’s residence that reportedly used flash-bang grenades.

Prior to his first arrest in 2023, Van der Stap was working as a software engineer at the Amsterdam-based cybersecurity startup Hadrian, while volunteering at the Dutch Institute for Vulnerability Disclosure (DIVD) — even as he was hacking into and extorting a number of large organizations.

When asked in a recent interview why anyone should believe the word of a self-described “reformed” cybercriminal who had so casually deceived countless friends, co-workers and journalists for years, Van der Stap replied that his work spoke for itself and there was nothing he could say that would convince his worst critics.

“You can throw a bunch of nice words at someone, but you can’t convince them if they don’t want to be convinced,” Van der Stap told KrebsOnSecurity on Sept. 9. “I’m doing what I can to repay victims, and that’s all I can do. If someone doesn’t want to believe me, then that’s on them.”

Cybercriminals aligned with ShinyHunters have been responsible for dozens of data breaches involving billions of stolen records, and breaches claimed by the group stretch back to at least 2019. But experts say the people recently operating behind the ShinyHunters name are not the same core members that populated the group in its early days, most of whom are French citizens who have been arrested (if not also imprisoned) on at least one prior occasion for alleged cybercrime activity.

More to the point, ShinyHunters has become something of a franchise. Think the Dread Pirate Roberts character in the 1980s cult movie classic “The Princess Bride,” only succession by death is replaced with succession by arrest, and there can be multiple simultaneous Dread Pirate Robertses. Sources close to the investigation say the FBI is focusing on a remaining handful of cybercriminal freelancers or affiliates who have been feeding the group stolen credentials to various software-as-a-service (SaaS) platforms used by major companies in exchange for a cut of any data ransoms later paid by victims.

In the days after the news broke of Van der Stap’s arrest, a cybercrime-focused chat server on Telegram that was allegedly operated by Rey erupted with hot takes, with most participants heaping ridicule on the teenage hacker after he publicly backed down from threats against the FBI and Cl0p, and again when the ShinyHunters’s darknet website suddenly went offline. Several commentators accused Rey of resurrecting the ShinyHunters brand after its core members were rounded up in France, and making a mockery of the group’s name and reputation ever since.

“He bought the old forum PGP key and used it to make new Breachforum websites and Telegram channels larping as ShinyHunters to ransom companies and then sell the used data or resell his forum when he goes broke,” one member recounted.

A relatively new Telegram channel called “The Battle” has been doxing and needling Rey and other alleged ShinyHunters members for several weeks, and it has gained a considerable readership among the cybercrime communities operating on Telegram. One of the coordinators of that harassment campaign repeatedly portrayed Rey as clueless greenhorn who sought to ride the coattails of a cybercriminal brand that has long enjoyed a reputation for ruthlessly selling or publishing data stolen from victim companies who refuse to give in to extortion demands.

“Rey (Saif Al-Din Khader) made a serious mistake when he started pretending to be a member of ShinyHunters,” wrote the administrators of The Battle server on Telegram. “That group had already been dismantled, with many of its members either arrested or imprisoned, yet Rey still chose to use its name while carrying out his crimes. We’re aware of claims that [Rey] caused over $200 million in damages and helped around 5–6 friend groups in the community make money by using Shiny Hunters group aliases to negotiate deals for a 25–30% cut over the past few months.”

In an interview with The Register, ShinyHunters claimed they hacked the FBI to counter the agency’s narrative in a May 2026 alert that advised victims against paying a ransom to the group, which came off looking unprofessional and capricious in the FBI’s advisory.

A flash notice on ShinyHunters released by the FBI on May 15, 2026.

The public notice warned the group has been known to pursue a number of different victim harassment strategies, from sending threatening text messages and phone calls to victims and their family members to in some cases swatting victims. The FBI warned ShinyHunters members “may also falsely claim to have sensitive or compromising information, including embarrassing photographs or videos of victims, which frequently do not exist.”

The hackers told The Register their attack on the FBI “demonstrated our technical capabilities and directly refuted the misinformation disseminated by the FBI, journalists, and industry researchers.” At the same time, the group’s leaders seemed to acknowledge that the FBI’s warning materially harmed their prospects for convincing victims to pay, saying “this was fundamentally a public relations and marketing initiative for our business.”
