#9765. How to Assess OT Incident Response Preparedness

Cloud Range's free 28-question OT Cyber Readiness Assessment helps organizations identify gaps in operational technology (OT) incident response.

Cloud Range introduces a 28-question OT Cyber Readiness Assessment to help organizations identify gaps in preparedness for cyberattacks affecting operational technology.

The assessment covers seven critical areas, from OT asset visibility and IT/OT coordination to incident detection, response, recovery, and readiness validation.

Recent OT cybersecurity research reinforces the importance of preparing IT, security, OT, and engineering teams to investigate and respond to attacks that can disrupt physical operations.

NASHVILLE, Tenn., Nov. 10, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) — Cyberattacks affecting operational technology (OT) can disrupt production, equipment, and essential services, resulting in consequences that extend beyond disruptions to traditional IT systems. To help organizations evaluate their preparedness, Cloud Range today introduced the Cloud Range OT Cyber Readiness Assessment, a free, 28-question resource designed to identify potential gaps in OT incident response preparedness.

Related:Why Europe's Freezer Hacks Spread So Far, So Fast

The assessment provides a practical starting point for IT, security, OT, and engineering teams to evaluate how well they understand their environments, coordinate responsibilities, and prepare to detect, investigate, respond to, and recover from cyber incidents affecting industrial operations.

“Organizations can have incident response plans, security tools, and experienced teams in place without knowing how effectively those capabilities will work together when an attack affects operations,” said Debbie Gordon, CEO of Cloud Range. “The first step is understanding where teams are prepared, where they may be relying on assumptions, and where further validation is needed. The stakes are different in OT because decisions made during a cyber incident can have direct operational consequences.”

Recent research illustrates the scale of cyber threats facing industrial organizations. The Dragos 2026 OT Cybersecurity Year in Review reports that approximately 3,300 industrial organizations were affected by ransomware in 2025.

Palo Alto Networks’ 2026 State of Critical Infrastructure Cybersecurity Report found that 59% of surveyed critical infrastructure organizations experienced a significant security breach in the past year. The research also found that 74% had not fully integrated IT and OT security operations, highlighting the importance of coordinated incident response.

The report also identifies operational consequences of cybersecurity incidents, including safety concerns, unplanned downtime, production disruptions, and financial losses.

Related:Fresh European Fridge Attacks Put Cold-Chain Security in Focus

Together, these findings underscore a central challenge for organizations operating OT and industrial control systems (ICS): preventing attacks is important, but so is understanding whether teams can recognize, investigate, and respond quickly and effectively when incidents occur.

An attack does not have to originate within an OT network to affect industrial operations. Compromises involving enterprise IT systems, third-party access, supply chains, or interconnected infrastructure can create consequences for production environments and critical services.

The Cloud Range OT Cyber Readiness Assessment examines seven areas that influence an organization's ability to prepare for and respond to cyberattacks affecting OT environments:

Know Your Environment: Understand critical OT assets, systems, dependencies, and connections between IT and OT environments.

Know Your Threats and Stakes: Recognize relevant cyber threats and their potential impact on operations, equipment, and safety.

Bridge IT and OT: Establish shared responsibilities, communication, and decision-making across IT, security, OT, and engineering teams.

Detect and Investigate: Identify suspicious activity, investigate threats, and determine their potential operational consequences.

Respond Without Making It Worse: Make coordinated incident response decisions that account for production continuity, equipment, and safety.

Recover and Maintain Resilience: Understand recovery priorities, system dependencies, and procedures for restoring critical operations.

Prove Readiness Before It Matters: Validate response capabilities through realistic cyberattack simulations and measurable performance.

Related:Les supermarchés de l'UE paient d'un firmware de réfrigérateur non mis à jour

Each area includes three questions, with responses of Ready, Developing, or Unsure.

Rather than assigning a numerical score, the assessment helps organizations identify gaps, uncertainties, and areas requiring further attention. IT, security, OT, and engineering teams can complete it independently and compare their responses to uncover differences in understanding, unclear responsibilities, or differing assumptions about preparedness.

Why OT Incident Response Preparedness Requires Cross-Functional Coordination

OT environments present distinct incident response challenges because cyber decisions can affect physical equipment, industrial processes, production availability, and potentially safety.

Actions that may be appropriate in an enterprise IT environment, such as isolating a system or shutting down a device, can require additional operational evaluation when industrial systems are involved.

Effective OT incident response therefore depends on coordination among teams with different responsibilities and expertise.

IT and security personnel may focus on identifying malicious activity, containing threats, and investigating compromised systems. OT and engineering personnel understand process dependencies, equipment limitations, and the operational consequences of response decisions.

Both perspectives are essential. The integration gap identified in the Palo Alto Networks research reinforces the importance of shared understanding, clear responsibilities, and coordinated decision-making across IT, security, OT, and engineering teams.

Understanding how to assess OT cyber readiness across these functions helps organizations identify where their procedures, communication, and decision-making may require further attention.

The assessment is intended to support those conversations before an actual incident demands coordinated action.

An assessment can help organizations identify preparedness gaps, but it cannot establish how effectively teams will perform during a real cyber incident.

That requires opportunities to investigate attacks, make decisions, coordinate across functions, and evaluate the results in realistic environments.

Cloud Range helps organizations strengthen critical infrastructure cyber readiness, realistic cloud-based OT/ICS, IT, cloud, and hybrid environments where teams can investigate cyber threats, coordinate incident response, and measure performance. Its critical infrastructure cybersecurity and readiness programs help organizations prepare for attacks that may disrupt industrial processes, equipment, and essential services.

The Cloud Range OT Cyber Range supports flat and Purdue-model industrial network architectures, allowing teams to investigate how connectivity, segmentation, and system dependencies influence attack progression and response. Hardware-in-the-loop capabilities can also connect physical OT laboratory equipment to the cyber range for cyber-physical security validation.

Through OT cyberattack simulations and adversary emulation, teams can investigate ransomware, supply-chain compromise, credential theft, lateral movement, and threats affecting industrial systems.

Performance metrics highlight how teams improve in detecting threats, investigating activity, coordinating decisions, and improving incident response over time.

Across Cloud Range customer engagements, measured improvements have included reductions of up to 66% in mean time to detect and improvements of up to 30% in overall incident response time. These results reflect broader cyber readiness programs and are not specific to OT environments.

As IT and OT environments become more interconnected, organizations face growing pressure to understand both their cybersecurity exposure and their ability to respond to incidents with operational consequences.

The Cloud Range OT Cyber Readiness Assessment provides a structured way to evaluate preparedness across seven critical areas. Organizations can use the findings to prioritize improvements and identify where realistic attack-based validation can provide stronger evidence of readiness.

The objective is not simply to have an incident response plan. It is to build confidence that the people, processes, and technologies involved can work together when an attack affects operations.

Cloud Range is the leader in Cyber Readiness and Validation, helping organizations continuously measure and improve how people, processes, and AI perform under real-world attack conditions. As the creator of the industry's first full-service, cloud-based cyber range, Cloud Range provides realistic IT, OT/ICS, and cloud environments where organizations can safely train, test, validate, measure, and benchmark cyber readiness across people, processes, and AI agents.

Used by enterprise organizations, government agencies, higher education institutions, critical infrastructure organizations, and managed security service providers (MSSPs), Cloud Range helps organizations strengthen cyber readiness through live-fire cyberattack simulations, objective performance measurement, expert guidance, continuous readiness programs, and AI validation.

Cloud Range has received multiple industry awards recognizing innovation and leadership in cyber readiness, cyber defense, and cybersecurity excellence and has been recognized by leading analyst and research organizations for its contributions to cyber readiness, cyber ranges, AI validation, and modern security operations. Learn more at cloudrangecyber.com.

#9764. Jensen Huang's Nvidia Exit Is a Wake-Up Call for Startup Founders

This morning, November 12, 2026, Nvidia's board said Jensen Huang had resigned as President, CEO, and director, effective immediately. CFO Colette Kress is now interim CEO. The board also named Harvey C. Jones as its first-ever chair, which tells you it had been a one-man show for 33 years.

The board's word is "resigned." Most headlines went with "ousted." Days earlier, CBS had reported the board was preparing to remove him. You decide which word fits.

Here's the short version. A New York Times report alleged multiple affairs, including one with a Singapore data-center executive whom U.S. officials reportedly suspected of ties to Chinese intelligence, at a firm that bought billions of dollars of Nvidia hardware. Another alleged affair was with a senior executive who reported directly to him. Huang had already admitted infidelity in a memo to employees on November 9. Then came national-security questions, demands from lawmakers, and a stock that fell roughly 10%, wiping out hundreds of billions in market value. After that, the end came quickly.

Set the morality aside for a minute, because the board didn't need to settle it. What I want founders to notice is the mechanics.

Jensen Huang co-founded Nvidia in a Denny's in 1993. He bet the company on GPUs, then on CUDA, then on AI, and grew it into a company worth more than $4 trillion. He is about as close to a founder-god as Silicon Valley has.

And he had no structural protection whatsoever.

Nvidia has a single class of stock: one share, one vote. Its board was made up of independent directors plus Jensen, and it could remove the CEO with or without cause by simple majority. Mark Zuckerberg can't be fired. Larry Page couldn't be fired. Jensen Huang, the man who made the AI age possible, could be shown the door in a week.

If that doesn't make every founder reading this check their charter, nothing will.

Founders don't usually lose control in one dramatic boardroom scene. They lose it gradually, through a series of small and individually reasonable decisions.

Act I: One share, one vote. For about sixty years the NYSE refused to list companies with dual-class shares. The idea was that voting power should track economic risk. Ford's 1956 IPO, where the family kept super-voting shares, was the famous exception. Media dynasties like the New York Times Company got a pass on the grounds of editorial independence.

Act II: Google changes the rules. In 2004, Larry Page and Sergey Brin took Google public with Class B shares carrying 10 votes each. The public bought it anyway. Facebook, LinkedIn, Snap, and Alibaba all followed. Hong Kong held out, lost Alibaba's $25 billion IPO to New York, and changed its rules in 2018. By 2021–22, about 47% of U.S. tech IPOs were dual-class.

Act III: the slow loss of your majority. This is the part nobody puts in the pitch deck. According to Carta's 2025–26 data, founders typically hold:

Capital intensity makes it worse. If your company works with atoms (chips, robots, biotech), you burn two to three times the cash of a SaaS company and sell more of the company at every round. Jensen is the hardware founder's cautionary tale: decades of capital-hungry growth, and nothing left to vote with when it counted.

The lesson: you don't lose control when the board votes. You lose it, one term sheet at a time, years before.

Every founder knows this story, and every founder assumes it couldn't happen to them.

In 1985, Steve Jobs was 30, a co-founder of Apple, and the person most responsible for its products and culture. He had no super-voting shares. The Macintosh launched to great reviews and disappointing sales. Jobs's "my way or the highway" style wore everyone out. John Sculley, the Pepsi executive Jobs had personally recruited with the famous "sugar water" pitch, moved to take away his operating authority.

Jobs tried to get Sculley removed instead. The plan leaked, the board backed Sculley, and Jobs, with no structural power at all, resigned and went off to start NeXT.

What followed was a twelve-year slide that brought Apple to within about 90 days of insolvency in 1997. The board, out of options, bought NeXT, mostly to get Jobs back. You know the rest: iMac, iPod, iPhone, and the most valuable company on Earth.

Dual-class advocates like to say that if Jobs had held super-voting stock, Apple would have skipped a lost decade.

Maybe. I'll give you the more uncomfortable version. The Jobs who got fired was probably not the Jobs who saved Apple. NeXT and Pixar humbled him and taught him things, and he came back a better CEO. Getting fired may have been the most valuable thing that ever happened to him, though it's hard to see it that way while it's happening.

Adam Neumann got the thing Jobs never had: 20 votes per share. The board couldn't fire him, investors couldn't overrule him, and he ran the company accordingly.

When the S-1 came out in August 2019, public investors saw $47 billion in lease obligations against $4 billion in committed revenue, plus governance that made Apple's 1985 board look like the Federalist Papers. The IPO collapsed and SoftBank had to fund a bailout. Neumann was out, and in 2023 the company filed for Chapter 11.

Here's the lesson I care about most. Super-voting stock does two things: it protects you from the market's panic, and it protects you from your own mistakes. The first is valuable. The second can kill the company. The same structure that would have saved 1985 Jobs from Sculley also saved Neumann from anyone who might have told him no.

So what should you actually do? Here is the playbook, roughly by stage. If you can, negotiate these terms when you have leverage, which means before you need the money.

The academics have a useful framework for this. Agency costs are the damage a founder does when nobody can stop them; that's WeWork. Principal costs are the damage investors do when they're in charge: panic, short-termism, and a buyback where an R&D budget should be. That's 1985 Apple.

Law professors Zohar Goshen and Richard Squire argue the right structure minimizes the sum of the two. A visionary founder in a 20-year bet like AI, VR, or rockets should get more insulation. A mature company with a founder who has drifted should get less.

The data supports this. Dual-class firms trade at a premium at IPO, because markets value the founder's vision. Around seven to ten years later, that premium tends to become a discount as the founder's economic stake shrinks while their votes don't.

So the goal isn't maximum control. It's control that fits where your company is in its life: enough insulation to make long-term bets, with a working mechanism for someone to say "stop" if you lose your way.

Jensen had plenty of the first and none of the second, which was fine for 33 years until this week. Neumann had too much of both. Jobs had none, and it took a lost decade to fix.

Here's what I expect over the next five years.

1. The Jensen effect on fundraising. Founders raising in 2027 will bring up Nvidia in every board-composition negotiation, and investors will bring up WeWork. Both are fair points.

2. Trust-based structures as the new middle ground. Anthropic's S-1 shows a new model. The founders hold a Class F share that gives them 50.1% of ordinary votes, while an independent Long-Term Benefit Trust with no economic stake elects a majority of the board. The founders control the shareholder vote, and the trust controls the board. OpenAI's foundation keeps exclusive power over its PBC's board even though Microsoft owns 27% of the equity. These are deliberate checks and balances in a company charter, and you'll see others copy them.

3. Sunsets become standard. Perpetual founder control is ending. Index providers, proxy advisors, and institutional investors all agree on that. Expect seven-to-ten-year sunsets to become the price of a dual-class IPO.

4. The jurisdiction wars continue. Delaware vs. Texas vs. Nevada. Your state of incorporation is now a strategic decision, not a box your lawyer checks.

5. Character as a governance mechanism. This is the uncomfortable one. As founders gain more structural protection, the remaining risks come from conduct: personal behavior, conflicts of interest, national security. Those risks don't care how many votes your shares carry.

My closing advice to every engineer-founder reading this:

Fight for control early, when it's cheap. Protect it with structure, not just goodwill. Give it an expiration date before someone else does. And above all, build a company and a character that a board would never want to fire.

Jensen Huang built one of the greatest companies in history and still lost it in a week. Your share structure can't fully protect you from yourself, so you'll have to manage that part on your own.

#9763. Checkmarx Appoints Kobi Sivilya as Chief Information Security Officer

Sivilya brings deep cybersecurity and technology leadership to Checkmarx as AI transforms software development.

MOUNTAIN VIEW, CA — November 5, 2026 — Checkmarx, the leader in agentic application security, today announced the appointment of Kobi Sivilya as Chief Information Security Officer (CISO) and Chief Information Officer (CIO). In this dual role, Sivilya will oversee the company’s security, IT and business applications, supporting Checkmarx’s global operations and continued growth.

Sivilya will lead Checkmarx’s corporate security and IT functions, aligning security, technology and business applications with the company’s strategic priorities. He will also help advance Checkmarx’s mission to secure modern application development.

“Kobi brings more than 20 years of experience across cybersecurity and technology, with deep security expertise and practical IT leadership,” said Sandeep Johri, CEO at Checkmarx. “AI is changing how software gets built and attacked, and we need his leadership to keep Checkmarx secure as we protect our customers.”

Related:Risks & Rewards: How AI Is Redefining the CISO's Role

Prior to joining Checkmarx, Sivilya served as CISO and VP of IT at Outbrain, where he led the company’s security and enterprise technology functions. He also served as VP of Security Engineering at Fireblocks, where he helped build and lead security engineering for a blockchain platform that protects digital assets for leading financial institutions in a highly targeted environment.

“As AI accelerates software development, organizations need technology and security capabilities that can evolve alongside it,” said Kobi Sivilya, CISO and CIO at Checkmarx. “My focus will be on ensuring our internal technology and security functions support the way our teams work today while positioning the business to adapt to what comes next.”

About Checkmarx Checkmarx makes security inseparable from how software is built. The foundation is decades of accumulated threat intelligence used to secure trillions of lines of code each year. Checkmarx One now pairs that foundation with frontier AI-powered reasoning, unifying architectures to lead the category in detection accuracy. Checkmarx Assist agents prevent, prioritize, and fix vulnerabilities across software and the AI supply chain, so enterprises never have to trade speed for certainty. The combined result is the Checkmarx One platform, giving enterprises comprehensive application security: capturing risk, eliminating vulnerabilities, and unifying governance. Follow Checkmarx on LinkedIn, YouTube and X.

#9762. U.K. Sanctions Cryptomus for RU Money Laundering

The United Kingdom has issued economic sanctions against Cryptomus, a chameleonic cryptocurrency platform that experts say serves as a major conduit for payments related to ransomware, narcotics, darknet markets, fraud and cybercrime services that are helping Russia circumvent existing financial restrictions.

Heleket’s support agent on Telegram claims, despite all evidence to the contrary, that it is not affiliated with Cryptomus. Image: Richard Sanders.

On October 8, the U.K. issued sanctions (PDF) against Cryptomus — previously known as Certa Payments and Xeltox Enterprises — for processing payments that benefit the Russian government and its financial institutions. The sanctions freeze any Cryptomus assets at U.K. banks, and bar British companies from offering it any business, virtual or otherwise. Also targeted in these sanctions were the virtual payment platforms VexPay, TokenSpot, and the Tsunami Payments service.

As explained in our December 2024 investigation, “How Cryptocurrency Turns to Cash in Russian Banks,” Cryptomus has been a key payment processor for dozens of Russian cryptocurrency exchanges and websites hawking cybercrime services. The company has changed its name several times since emerging in 2022, most recently to “Heleket” last year after Canada levied a record CAD $176 million fine against the platform for anti-money laundering violations.

The blockchain data-crunching firm Chainalysis said the U.K. sanctions target the broader infrastructure supporting Russia’s wartime economy.

“Cryptomus and Heleket have emerged as major payment hubs for illicit activity,” Chainalysis wrote in an October 8 blog post. “Together, these services received more illicit funds across tracked categories than the mixers in our dataset and the number of illicit counterparties surged to more than 900 in a single month in late 2025.”

The Cryptomus support bot on Telegram, responding on Oct. 8 to an inquiry by saying the platform was suddenly unable to process transactions.

In April 2026, the blockchain analysis firm TRM Labs found Cryptomus had processed more than $7 billion in transactions since its inception in 2022, including transactions associated with child sexual abuse material vendors, terrorist financing networks, and human trafficking operations.

TRM noted that Cryptomus’s transaction volume cratered after the platform instituted new “know your customer” or KYC rules, and that the cryptocurrency platform responded to the Canadian fines by launching Heleket as a parallel service that continued to offer no-KYC payment processing.

Richard Sanders is a blockchain analyst and investigator who spent months mapping out Cryptomus’s payment infrastructure and transacting with its customers. Sanders said the U.K. sanctions on Cryptomus are important because Canada’s fine against the platform was ultimately unenforceable and uncollectible.

“A fine doesn’t stop a cryptocurrency payment processor from processing payments,” Sanders wrote on LinkedIn. “Sanctions kill the operation. The distinction matters.”

As our 2024 investigation noted, Cryptomus shared a Vancouver address with dozens of other foreign currency dealers and money transfer businesses — none of which appeared to be physically located there. Following the CAD $176 million fine for alleged money laundering violations, Cryptomus appealed the penalty, launched Heleket as a parallel service, and kept on processing large volumes of sketchy transactions, Sanders said.

Sanders said the sanctions also are notable because they are the first known instance of a “Five Eyes” country (referring to the Australia, Canada, New Zealand, the U.K. and the U.S.) sanctioning a cryptocurrency operation incorporated in another Five Eyes jurisdiction.

Where do entities like Cryptomus and Heleket derive their authority to offer international financial services? The answer appears to involve fake financial institutions overseen by a phony regulatory body positioned in a country that is not widely recognized as a sovereign nation.

Our 2024 investigation found the sole shareholder of Cryptomus’s parent company Certa Payments was a 25-year-old Ukrainian woman who also headed several other firms, including the WS Management and Advisory Corporation, which bills itself as the regulatory body that exclusively oversees licenses for cryptocurrency, foreign exchange and online gaming businesses incorporated in the disputed region in northwest Africa known as the Western Sahara.

That entity’s website — crasadr.com — says it assists applicants with bank setup and formation, online gaming licenses, and the creation and licensing of foreign exchange brokers. One of Certa Payments’ former sites — certa[.]website — also shared a server with 12 other domains, including rasd-state[.]ws, a website for the Central Reserve Authority of the Western Sahara.

The website crasadr dot com, the official website of the Central Reserve Authority of Western Sahara, which lists the entities awarded licenses for cryptocurrencies, gaming and foreign exchange services.

#9761. Build specialized multimodal models with LFM3

LFM3 is our new generation of Liquid Foundation Models (LFMs), built to be the starting point for specialized intelligence. It brings text, vision, audio, omni, and decision models onto one shared backbone, all in the 2B parameter range. This means you can pick the model for your modality, fine-tune it on your own data on a single GPU, and deploy it where your application runs.

LFM3 brings four main changes compared to our previous LFM2 family:

LFM2 showed that a hybrid of short convolutions and attention can run fast on-device without sacrificing quality. For LFM3, we used our hardware-in-the-loop architecture search to redesign that architecture for agentic use cases, which need more capability per parameter and fast inference over long contexts. The search now covers 14 device and backend combinations, from phones and a Raspberry Pi 5 to laptops, cloud CPUs, GPUs, and the Qualcomm Hexagon NPU.

LFM3-1.7B-Base has 24 layers and four main changes:

The payoff shows at long context. Per parameter, LFM3-1.7B matches LFM2-1.2B on short prompts across edge devices, and with 8K tokens in context it is about 25% faster. LFM3-1.7B-Base was pre-trained on 22T tokens with the same 128K vocabulary as LFM2.5-8B-A1B. The final 3.5T tokens are a mid-training stage on curated data with a larger share of agentic traces and tool calls, which also extends the context window to 256K tokens.

Every LFM3 model branches from LFM3-1.7B-Base. Instead of running one large general-purpose model, you pick the one that fits your inputs, customize it, and run it on-device.

The vision and audio models also get two new in-house encoders:

Each model runs in transformers. The snippets below come from the model cards, which also list the other inference engines each model supports.

Reach for LFM3-1.7B when you need local agents, tool calling, structured outputs, or a base for domain-specific fine-tuning. It is post-trained to run in agentic harnesses such as Hermes Agent, Pi, and OpenClaw. It outperforms its predecessor, LFM2.5-2.6B, with 35% fewer parameters, and the biggest gains are on agentic tasks: on WebArena-Verified, it scores 38.42 against 3.02, and it even beats Qwen3.5-9B on long tasks in browsers and business apps. You can find more details in the LFM3-1.7B model card.

To run LFM3-1.7B, install the latest version of transformers:

For local agent setup, see the Agent Harnesses guide.

Reach for LFM3-VL-2B when you need on-device visual understanding. It is the first LFM vision model that takes video as input; it reasons step by step before it answers, and it finds objects and reasons about how they are placed, a strong foundation for robotics. Compared with LFM2.5-VL-3B, it has fewer parameters (1.9B against 3.1B) yet raises the average across 62 vision benchmarks from 57.6 to 71.4, on par with Gemma 4 12B, a model more than six times larger. You can find more details in the LFM3-VL-2B model card.

To run LFM3-VL-2B, install transformers>=5.21.0 with its vision dependencies:

See the LFM3-VL-2B model card for tool calling, tool search, and on-device inference with llama.cpp.

Reach for LFM3-Audio-2B when you need voice chat, speech recognition, speech synthesis, or translation across 18 languages on a laptop or edge device. It takes text or audio as input and responds with text, speech, or both, and it can turn spoken requests into tool calls. Compared with LFM2.5-Audio-1.5B, it uses a new in-house audio encoder and speech codec, speaks with higher quality (UTMOSv2 3.83 against 3.22), and adds audio understanding, general-purpose audio reasoning, and tool calling. You can find more details in the LFM3-Audio-2B model card.

To run LFM3-Audio-2B, install transformers>=5.20.2 with its audio dependencies:

Load the model and processor directly from the Hugging Face Hub:

Then ask a question aloud and get a reply in text and speech:

See the LFM3-Audio-2B model card for live speech recognition, speech synthesis, audio understanding, and tool calling.

Reach for LFM3-Omni-2B when you need one on-device model that sees, listens, and talks back, in place of a separate ASR model, vision-language model, LLM, and TTS model. It can answer spoken questions about an image, watch and listen to a video together, and turn what it sees and hears into tool calls. It is our first omni model, with text, vision, and audio input and both text and speech output, and it keeps the core capabilities of the standalone LFM3 models, including visual question answering, speech recognition, speech synthesis, and instruction following. Like LFM3-Audio-2B, it speaks through LiquidCodec, which turns generated tokens into speech faster than real time, so spoken replies stream as the model generates them. On audio-visual video understanding, it beats models up to 10.7B parameters, such as Qwen2.5-Omni-7B, on Daily-Omni, WorldSense, and AV-SpeakerBench. You can find more details in the LFM3-Omni-2B model card.

To run LFM3-Omni-2B, install transformers>=5.20.2 with its vision and audio dependencies:

Then ask a question about a photo by voice:

See the LFM3-Omni-2B model card for speech output, video with its soundtrack, and tool calling.

Reach for the d1 models when you need fast, structured decisions instead of generated text. Give them a situation (a support ticket, an invoice, an app screen, a photo, a voice note) and a list of questions, and they answer all of them in a single forward pass, each with a calibrated probability. Beyond yes/no, choices, and scores, they can now point at objects, read values from documents, estimate numbers with a range, and pick every option that applies. You can find more details in the model cards for d1-2B and d1-omni-2B.

To run d1-2B, install transformers>=5.19 with its vision dependencies:

Then load d1-2B and ask it several questions about one support ticket in a single pass:

For brevity, we only include the example for d1-2B. See the d1-omni-2B model card for audio clips and spoken questions.

LFM3 is built to be specialized. Frontier models are powerful generalists, but they are not necessarily experts in your use case. LFM3 packs extra capacity into a small, fast model, so a short fine-tune can turn it into a reliable expert on your task, with your data, terminology, and tools. Because it is small, you can deploy the fine-tuned model where your application runs, from devices to private infrastructure to the cloud.

Every model can be fine-tuned on a single GPU, and these notebooks walk you through a complete task for the text, vision, audio, and omni models, from data preparation to evaluation.

We adapt LFM3-VL-2B into three complementary robotics models for orchestration, navigation, and manipulation. The orchestrator operates a robot arm through tool calls: it grounds objects by pointing, measures them with depth tools, invokes motion planners, and checks outcomes in subsequent camera images. The navigator follows route descriptions using recent RGB observations, predicting spatial targets and a waypoint trajectory in just five tokens. The manipulation VLA maps images, language, and robot state to eight-step chunks of continuous actions in a single forward pass. Jointly trained across 15 embodiments, the VLA achieves 96.2% average success across the four LIBERO suites and 45.7% on RoboCasa-GR1 tabletop tasks, generating action chunks in under 50 ms on a Jetson AGX Orin with TensorRT FP16. These results highlight LFM3-VL-2B as a compact foundation for robotics, spanning high-level planning to low-level control with real-time action generation on embedded hardware.

Watch LFM3-VL-2B handle perception, navigation, and manipulation in this demo video.

#9760. F-Secure Identifies 26 Ways AI Can Harm Consumers, and Where to Stop Them

New AI Harms Taxonomy traces how harm moves through AI systems, from misleading chatbot answers to compromised autonomous agents, and identifies where defenses can intervene.

LOS ANGELES (November 10, 2026) — AI now shapes how we search, communicate, decide and run our digital lives. But when it goes wrong, how does it actually hurt people? F-Secure’s new AI Harms Taxonomy maps 26 distinct harms to consumers, tracing the path each one takes to reach a person. The result is a clear view of where protections can step in, and who is in the best position to help.

Developed by Dr. Megan Squire, Principal Threat Intelligence Researcher at F-Secure, the taxonomy tackles a blind spot in how AI risk is discussed. Most frameworks list what could potentially go wrong, but stop short of connecting those harms to the systems and companies that could prevent them. F-Secure’s research goes further by mapping every layer between an AI-enabled threat and its impact on a consumer, then pinpointing where defenses need to go.

“As AI systems become more capable, the consequences of their mistakes can extend well beyond a bad answer,” said Dr. Squire. “The people building them have a responsibility to understand how they can fail and who gets hurt when they do, and to put safeguards in place before that harm happens.”

Related:AI Makes Reverse Engineering Mainstream Software & Malware Far Easier

The taxonomy reflects how the risks themselves are changing. It used to be a criminal going after a person directly, but now AI sits in the middle, which adds new players and new ways for things to go wrong. An assistant acting on someone’s behalf can be manipulated into doing damage, and a chatbot can mislead with complete confidence. Underneath, the trouble often starts in how an AI handles instructions and memory, or in the other services it’s connected to.

The research currently maps 26 harms across five relationship types and 19 intermediary layers, with 24 defenses designed to address risks at different points. Examples range from AI-generated voice and video impersonation to agents making harmful financial decisions, exposing personal information or acting on outdated context. It also examines attacks in which malicious instructions are hidden in content an AI system processes, potentially influencing what an agent does or what a chatbot tells a user.

One of the framework’s central findings is that responsibility for preventing AI harm is spread across several parties. Some risks can be handled by security software on a person’s own device. Others have to be dealt with further upstream, by the companies that build AI products and the systems behind them, including how an AI remembers things and which other services it connects to. Sorting out which is which makes it clear where a defense belongs and who has to build it. It also undercuts the idea that people can stay safe on their own just by spotting suspicious content or double-checking what an AI tells them.

Related:Microsoft Fixes RCE Bug in Windows Paint After Weeks of Confusion

This question of who’s responsible gets more urgent as AI moves from producing information to acting on it. A chatbot that gets an answer wrong can mislead someone, but at least that person is part of the exchange. An agent with access to a person’s accounts and the services linked to them can cause real consequences without that kind of back-and-forth. Protections need to be built around what these systems actually do, which starts with understanding how the two differ.

This research is part of a wider effort at F-Secure to build trust into the AI era. F-Secure Trust, announced alongside a strategic alliance with Quantum AI Lab QuTwo, is the company’s work on protecting people in a world where AI agents increasingly act for them. TrustGuard is designed to help protect people during AI interactions, while TrustPath aims to secure their digital journeys from discovery to delivery. The AI Harms Taxonomy gives that work a research foundation by spelling out the risks the protections need to address, and it makes clear that meaningful safeguards also depend on the companies building and running AI systems.

Related:Critical Rails Bug Threatens to Derail Vulnerable Servers

Today’s digital threats go far beyond just scams. F-Secure’s Illuminate Research team studies people and technology as they actually interact, exploring the messy realities of trust, deception, and online resilience in the AI era.

The AI Harms Taxonomy is available on the Illuminate Research Hub.

F-Secure is a human-first, AI-powered consumer cyber security experience company with 38 years of expertise in tackling digital threats. We help digital service providers turn trust into a high-value growth engine — protecting their customers while enabling them to live their best digital lives in a world of relentless, AI-driven scams. With billions of digital interactions secured each year, tens of millions of consumers protected globally, and over $10bn in partner value created, we deliver proven impact at scale.

#9759. Educational Byte: What Is a Liquidity Pool in Crypto —and Why It Matters

To understand this one, let’s first look at the "traditional" processes for exchanging money via digital platforms. We can commonly see two mechanisms: you exchange your currency directly against the exchange or provider’s own funds, or an order book is used. This order book records all buy and sell orders placed by users and provides liquidity based on that activity. The more orders in place, the more liquidity. Well, liquidity pools have come to replace these models in Decentralized Finance (DeFi) protocols.

A liquidity pool in crypto is a supply of tokens locked inside a smart contract on a DeFi protocol. It has the purpose of offering liquidity to other users for swaps, loans, or any financial activity on that specific protocol. The locked funds come from other users who, in exchange for providing this liquidity to the pool, receive rewards in the form of transaction fees and even governance tokens.

This way, no powerful middlemen are required to safely access financial instruments. It’s the users themselves who provide liquidity in a decentralized environment.

Typically, a liquidity pool holds two tokens, such as GBYTE and USDC. Liquidity providers are the ones who deposit these token pairs—and they could be anyone with the available funds. Then, those funds help to create a big reserve that traders can use for their own operations, like swaps. The smart contract keeps track of those balances and applies the rules that govern each trade.

Price adjustment comes from the reserves themselves. In a classic Automated Market Maker (AMM) model, a simple formula is used: X × Y = K, where X and Y represent the quantities of the two tokens and K is the constant. When someone swaps, let’s say, USDC for GBYTE, the pool receives one asset and releases the other, changing the balances and thus the price for the next trade. Depending on the available liquidity, a larger trade may create more price impact, which implies that the price could drop by a certain percentage for the next swap.

For liquidity providers, the platform may give them LP tokens as proof of their share of the pool. These tokens can be used to track and redeem that share, including the depositor’s portion of trading fees earned by the pool. Their reward is directly proportional to their contribution to the pool.

Some pools may be rewarded with additional incentives. For instance, in the Obyte-based DEX Oswap.io, all liquidity providers to a few selected pools receive 100 GBYTE every seven days, distributed in proportion to their contributed liquidity. That’s an additional incentive on top of fees.

A healthy financial environment needs liquidity, and liquidity doesn’t come out of nowhere. For trades and other operations to actually happen, funds must be available, and someone must put the funds there. In traditional finance, that someone is often a powerful middleman, like a bank. But cryptocurrencies weren’t created to rely on powerful middlemen; they were created to get rid of them. So, we have liquidity pools instead.

By using this model, everyone can access liquidity without cumbersome requirements or censorship risks. Meanwhile, liquidity providers receive rewards for their contributions in what is, without a doubt, a type of investment that can yield a good and frequent passive return. Of course, the specific rules and the censorship resistance vary from network to network.

Obyteuses a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) structure without miners or “validators,” which increases its decentralization and drastically reduces the mere possibility of censorship or blocking. In Oswap.io, each pool has its own parameters and governance, but all are decentralized and open for everyone to participate. That’s the whole idea; that’s why liquidity pools matter: they offer a freedom we can’t enjoy in traditional financial products.

#9757. Feds Suspect Ransom Negotiator Ran ShinyHunters Extortion Site

U.S. federal investigators pursuing the ShinyHunters hacking group that recently stole highly sensitive data from the FBI have identified executives at two different ransomware negotiation firms who maintained unusually close relations with the extortion group, KrebsOnSecurity has learned. Sources close to the investigation say one of the executives in the United States even helped ShinyHunters operate a website that pressured victims into paying a ransom.

Hackers aligned with ShinyHunters have claimed credit for dozens of major data breaches since 2019, when the group was primarily operated by cybercriminals living in France. As those original members were arrested or jailed one by one, control over the ShinyHunters brand eventually passed to “Rey,” identified last year as a teenage hacker from Amman, Jordan. According to the FBI, ShinyHunters has extorted more than $70 million from victims so far this year.

In late September, ShinyHunters hacked the FBI recruitment website fbijobs.gov and taunted the agency by threatening to publish the stolen files, which reportedly included medical and psychological records, Social Security numbers and home addresses, and information about each employee’s unit and specialization.

The FBI jobs site hack has prompted the agency to move with uncommon speed to arrest, detain and question people who had any communications with Rey or other ShinyHunters suspects. Reuters reported on October 3 that Rey had been detained by Jordanian authorities and was cooperating with the FBI.

Rey was able to assume control over the hacking group because one of its alleged senior members had just been nabbed. On the evening of September 15, 2026, authorities in the Netherlands arrested convicted hacker and ShinyHunters suspect Pepijn van der Stap. Dutch police reportedly used flash-bang grenades in an effort to stun and apprehend Van der Stap as he was logged in to various online accounts.

According to a source close to the investigation, the authorities arrested Van der Stap while he was using his Signal instant messaging account, which allowed them to read recent communications with frequent contacts — including ransomware negotiators based in Canada and the United States.

Multiple sources with knowledge of the matter told KrebsOnSecurity that Van der Stap’s messages were the key to unraveling a murder-for-hire plot that emerged immediately following his arrest. The Dutch news outlet RTL reported last month the two murders were allegedly to be committed abroad, and that there are indications Van der Stap gave the order for the attacks (there is no indication those orders were ever carried out).

On October 9, KrebsOnSecurity broke the news that the FBI arrested a 54-year-old Canadian cybersecurity executive named Edward Dubrovsky in connection with the ShinyHunters investigation. Dubrovsky, who recently published a book on handling cyber extortion that recommended always engaging with the hackers, was charged with threatening to disclose stolen or hacked data and interfering with interstate commerce through extortion, according to court records. Politico reports prosecutors have asked that Dubrovsky remain in custody pending trial, and that records related to his case remain under seal.

A source close to the investigation told KrebsOnSecurity that Van der Stap’s Signal messages showed he had frequent conversations with Mr. Dubrovsky and with at least one executive at a large U.S.-based consulting firm, and that these executives often knew the details about new ShinyHunters victims before the victims themselves had even learned of the breach.

That source shared another potentially explosive finding by federal investigators: the Dutch hacker’s chats showed Mr. Dubrovsky knew ShinyHunters had stolen highly sensitive data from FBI servers, and that he never informed the bureau of the data breach prior to ShinyHunters threatening on Twitter/X to publish the agency’s deeply personal personnel files.

KrebsOnSecurity has learned from two sources close to the ShinyHunters probe that FBI investigators believe at least one executive at a U.S.-based consulting firm played an active role in operating the now-defunct ShinyHunters victim extortion website “shinywire[.]com.” KrebsOnSecurity is not naming the U.S. company or the suspected executive(s) for now because they have not yet been charged with a crime, but it is a prestigious firm with more than 1,000 associates.

A section of the homepage for the now-defunct Shinywire website.

The Shinywire website was active from approximately May 3, 2026 until October 16 and had entries for nearly 100 organizations hacked by ShinyHunters. Each entry urged victims to engage with the cybercrime group and discuss terms for payment. The pages also included samples of stolen files and promised those files would be published online if the victim ignored their demands.

The following screenshot shows a cached portion of the Shinywire extortion page for Intuitive Surgical, an American medical technology company that was breached in March 2026 after an employee fell for a targeted phishing email.

The Shinywire website, as indexed by urlscan.io. This listing is an extortion demand targeting Intuitive Surgical, an American medical technology company breached in March 2026 by a targeted phishing email attack that compromised an employee’s credentials.

Victim organizations that refused to engage or negotiate after seven days would find all of their stolen data published on the ShinyHunters victim shaming blog (a website that is only reachable via the anonymity network Tor).

In a story published October 15, The Globe and Mail wrote that a few months before Edward Dubrovsky was arrested by the FBI, the Canadian cybersecurity executive alleged in court documents he had become collateral damage in a campaign by a former business partner to “destroy” another industry executive.

The story noted that Dubrovsky filed the lawsuit in Ontario this year against Daniel Tobok, the former chief executive of Cypfer, a cybersecurity firm founded in Toronto with offices in the U.S., Britain, the Netherlands, the United Arab Emirates, and Mexico. The two first became business partners in 2017 and later developed Cypfer together, where Mr. Dubrovsky was a managing partner and chief operating officer. But by 2024, the two had a falling out, with Dubrovsky accusing Tobok of gradually excluding him from business matters and making “increasingly capricious business decisions.”

Mr. Tobok reportedly denied the allegations and filed a counterclaim, accusing Mr. Dubrovsky of accessing confidential information and unfairly competing with Cypfer through work at another firm called CyberSteward Inc. He also said Mr. Dubrovsky has misrepresented himself as a Cypfer founder, and is not a shareholder.

According to interviews with several former colleagues of Mr. Tobok, as far back as eight years ago he was known to ransomware purveyors by a particular nickname: Ghostbyte. In 2018, a Canadian company was hacked by Dharma, a prolific Russian-language ransomware affiliate program that first surfaced in 2016. The victim company told the Dharma ransomware representative they were leaning toward paying because some of the files were unrecoverable after being locked, but that they needed a better guarantee that Dharma would keep their word if paid.

A redacted copy of the Dharma rep’s reply is pictured below, and it shows the ransomware group urged the victim to contact a person at a Canadian IT firm that helps companies seeking such guarantees. The Dharma rep recommended the victim contact the email address ghostbyte@tutanota.com.

“If you want guarantees, you can write to the IT company,” the Dharma reply advised. “Take the phone and negotiate with them. This IT company often solves such problems in Canada. You can contact them and sign a contract for services. You’ll still have to pay.”

An email reply from the Dharma ransomware group to a victim, recommending they contact an email address that is connected to Mr. Tobok.

It’s unclear if Mr. Tobok ever used that Ghostbyte address offered by the Dharma representative, and he has not responded to multiple requests for comment. However, the breach tracking service Constella Intelligence finds an email address Mr. Tobok has frequently used — dtobok@me.com — is associated with two online accounts where the chosen username was “ghostbyte,” including a Snapchat account.

Incidentally, Constella also finds the Dharma rep’s email address luckygoodlucky@tuta.io is associated with a cryptocurrency address that processed 38 transactions totaling 43 bitcoin, ~$3.5 million at today’s value (the most recent transaction for this wallet is dated February 2019).

In a statement shared on October 14, Cypfer said the company’s business does not include making or facilitating ransomware payments, and that Cypfer learned of Dubrovsky’s arrest when the news first broke in the media.

“We had no prior knowledge of Mr. Dubrovsky’s arrest,” a spokesperson told KrebsOnSecurity via email. “CYPFER has not received any outreach from law enforcement and, to our knowledge, is not the target of any law enforcement investigation.”

The statement said CyberSteward and Cypfer are separate companies with no officers, directors or employees in common, and that Cypfer was recently acquired by the Apros Group, a holding company led by Jason Hogg, a former FBI special agent and former CEO of Aon Cyber Solutions Group. In 2020, Aon aquired Cytelligence, a security consulting firm where Mr. Tobok was founder and CEO and Mr. Dubrovsky was a managing partner.

It is not illegal in the United States to pay hackers for an encryption key to unlock servers infected with ransomware, or in exchange for a promise to delete any stolen files and refrain from publishing them online. While victim organizations can land in legal hot water if they pay a ransom to a group that is sanctioned by the U.S. Treasury Department, ShinyHunters is not among the ransomware groups currently sanctioned by the United States or by any other government.

Experts say ransomware victims are typically directed by their insurance provider to work with a specific incident response firm. But not all cyber forensics and breach response companies will agree to facilitate payments to ransomware groups on behalf of their clients. As a result, once victim firms make a decision to pay, the firms that eschew rewarding extortionists are invariably replaced by companies that have no such qualms.

In December 2024, ShinyHunters began extorting the education technology company PowerSchool, stealing private information on 62 million students and 9.5 million teachers in the U.S. and Canada. PowerSchool reportedly paid a $2.85 million ransom demand, and a “frequently asked questions” statement (PDF) about the breach says PowerSchool was assisted in that effort by CyberSteward (ShinyHunters affiliate Matthew Lane, 20, of Sterling, Mass., was sentenced in November 2025 to four years in prison for his admitted role in the PowerSchool hack).

But that ransom payment did not stop future extortion attempts using the same stolen data. By May 2025, individual school districts were reportedly receiving separate ransom demands using samples of the same stolen files. While nobody has alleged ShinyHunters was behind the second wave of extortion against PowerSchool users, the incident drives home the reality that there is no technical way to verify the threat actors have deleted the stolen data as promised, or prevent others from abusing the same records.

A number of leading cyber incident response firms, including Coveware and Unit 221B, have consistently warned victims against paying ShinyHunters, noting that “destroyed” victim data is often kept, resold or used to extort the company’s clients directly later on.

The FBI echoed those sentiments in an alert on May 15, 2026 advising victims against paying the ShinyHunters group. Meanwhile, ShinyHunters members have been harassing and threatening employees at Coveware and Unit 221B for offering this advice.

The following screenshots show just how annoyed the ShinyHunters leaders were with Coveware’s relentless advice against paying the group. The first image is from a conversation on May 6, 2026 that took place between the group’s main account on Telegram and a co-conspirator. In that chat, snippets of which were shared with KrebsOnSecurity by a trusted source, ShinyHunters complained that Coveware was harming the group’s payment rates.

The operator of the ShinyHunters account on Telegram speaking privately with a co-conspirator and complaining that Coveware was harming their business.

“Go on my website, majority of those companies would’ve paid if it weren’t for Coveware giving them misinformation,” the ShinyHunters account wrote. “Someone (100% Coveware) is going out of their way to make sure i am not paid.”

In another conversation on April 11, 2026, the ShinyHunters Telegram account privately said they were trying to “eliminate the problem,” which they said was Coveware. Coveware declined to comment for this story.

“I’m sure the company will pay but in this specific case I am aware of Coveware and their involvement, and I’ve probably been not getting a lot of other negotiations mostly likely because Coveware keeps getting involved,” the ShinyHunters account bemoaned.

The operator of the ShinyHunters account on Telegram telling a co-conspirator they were “trying to eliminate the problem,” which they identified as Coveware advising victims not to pay the cybercrime group.

Mark Camillo is chief executive at CyberAcuView, an industry group founded in 2021 by a consortium of major cyber insurance carriers. Camillo said some firms charge a flat retainer fee, while those that specialize in helping companies negotiate a ransom payment tend to charge a percentage of the total ransom amount paid.

That latter dynamic, he said, is an inherent conflict of interest, as the negotiator has every incentive to make things more favorable to the attackers because they are financially incentivized to negotiate and pay out, and to not negotiate down on the price.

“It has come to the industry’s attention that many of the ransomware payers charge a percentage of the final payment which may or may not be disclosed,” Camillo said. “This makes no sense if they are also the negotiator. There needs to be more transparency in the process as no one in the ecosystem should be profiting purely on the size of the ransomware transaction or payment itself.”

Camillo said the firms doing this work would argue the fees are needed because there may be unexpectedly higher costs to secure larger quantities of cryptocurrency or more risk carrying the float, and because cryptocurrency exchanges may charge higher fees for high risk transactions.

“There definitely needs to be more visibility around the transaction and clarity on the increasing value of the crypto and the exchange’s percent in the transaction to get to the bottom of this and remove any misaligned incentives,” he said.

In recent months, the U.S. Department of Justice has prosecuted a number of ransomware negotiators alleged to have conspired with cybercriminals to defraud their clients. On October 7, the DOJ charged MonsterCloud CEO Zohar Pinhasi, 50, with wire fraud and conspiracy for allegedly charging customers to remediate ransomware attacks without paying the hackers. According to charging documents, Pinhasi secretly went behind his customers’ backs and paid hackers anyway, paying ransomware groups $8 million while charging customers $19 million.

In July, Angelo Martino, a 41-year-old ransomware negotiator from Land O’Lakes, Florida, was sentenced to 70 months in prison for conspiring with the Blackcat/ALPHV ransomware group to extort multiple victims. According to the DOJ, Martino was paid by BlackCat attackers to provide confidential information about the negotiating position and strategy of his employer’s clients and enable the ransomware actors to maximize the ransoms paid by the victims.

#9756. Artex: The AI Pen-Test Tool Hackers Turned Into a Weapon

Forks of the open source Artex framework, along with 45 similar pen-testing tools, remain capable of executing credential attacks and cloud breaches at machine speed across multiple industries.

AI penetration-testing tool Artex has proven to be a boon for threat actors large and small, taking familiar attacker playbooks and deploying them at machine speeds — ushering in a potentially new era for defenders looking to get ahead of AI-enabled threats.

In July, independent developer Autumn-27 published Artex to GitHub, an open source, multiagent AI penetration testing framework written in Go. It is, by intention, a legitimate tool. However, as is so often the case with pen-test tools (such as, famously, Cobalt Strike), threat actors found a way to take advantage of it for malicious use. By late summer and early fall, a range of threat actors were using it as part of their toolkit.

Artex is capable of brute-forcing passwords, dumping databases, enumerating and abusing APIs, and more. This positions it for credential compromise and lateral movement in its own right, but the agentic element means Artex can operate at inhuman speeds. Microsoft saw an AI agent move from scanning GitHub for secrets to exfiltrating data from an Azure Key Vault in five minutes, for example.

Related:Inside an AI Attack Against a US Retailer

Steve Winterfeld, advisory CISO for Akamai, tells Dark Reading that while legitimate tool misuse is a known quantity, AI reduces the effort and expertise required to execute complex attacks. "What is particularly noteworthy about the Artex campaigns is the acceleration in speed, coordination, and autonomy," he says. "Activities that previously required deliberate integration can now be chained together and executed with limited hacking skills."

At the end of October, Artex's creator deleted the original GitHub repository due to rampant abuse, but many forks of the tool remain, so the threat remains. But even if all the forks went offline and Artex was no longer a going concern, the underlying threat of frameworks like it is far from over.

GitGuardian yesterday, for instance, detailed 45 different agentic attack frameworks (Artex "siblings" as the researchers called them) that are all capable of conducting attacks autonomously with the help of an AI model. Depending on the tool, these pen-testing frameworks are capable of end-to-end attacks against a network, Web application targeting, and/or autonomous coding. Some even include built-in command-and-control functionality. That's not to say these tools are inherently bad — pen-testing tools have many legitimate use cases — but it does illustrate the wide range of options for today's attacker.

The best-known incident to date involved China's Storm-0940, which adapted Artex source code into its own offensive infrastructure. Last month, around Oct. 10, the actor used the Artex framework to launch a massive password-spraying and credential-stuffing campaign against more than 300 specific user accounts at eight critical organizations, making more than 151,000 authentication requests in the process. On average, this represented 2,900 attempts per minute without triggering automated lockout or alert.

Related:CISA Announces Enhanced Reporting Form for Cyber Incidents

When this largely failed, Storm-0940 pivoted to target ConnectWise's internal infrastructure. Attackers exfiltrated trusted OAuth application credentials belonging to ConnectWise's Cloud Backup application, allowing them to compromise more than 2,250 downstream Microsoft 365 and Azure environments within three hours of initial targeting.

Abuse extends far beyond a single threat actor or objective. Microsoft last week published a blog post discussing how a financially motivated Cambodia-based threat cluster tracked as Storm-3358 started using Artex in its attacks against financial organizations primarily (but not exclusively) in Southeast Asia. Microsoft said it observed Storm-3358 using Artex in combination with conventional automated tools to scan systems connected to the public Internet, exploit vulnerabilities, and install open source remote access Trojans (RATs).

Related:Operação de influência russa tem como alvo generalizado a América Latina

Microsoft added that other threat actors have used Artex agents "to scan and exploit vulnerabilities in Web applications, use Web shells for persistence on compromised Web servers, compromise credentials from public sources and compromised systems, and use compromised cloud identities for persistence and data exfiltration."

CrowdStrike on Oct. 29 connected Artex-powered espionage activity to a threat actor it tracks as Vapor Panda, India's CERT (CERT-In) tracked a financially motivated threat actor hitting financial institutions, and as of Nov. 4, Censys observed more than 1,400 internet-exposed Artex console deployments. That said, because Internet exposure is not required for use, Censys estimated actual global use to be higher.

Recent Artex activity stands out because much of the story involves things security practitioners have seen time and time again. Pen-test tool abuse, nation-state tooling moving downstream to financially motivated attackers, password spraying, supply chain attacks, AI — it's a threat intelligence greatest hits album. But Guillaume Valadon, head of cybersecurity research at GitGuardian, tells Dark Reading what stands out to him most is the fast pace of attacks and the agent's initiative to accomplish the user's goals.

"At GitGuardian, we wanted to see how Artex handles secrets, so we ran it in a sealed lab," he says. "Artex ships no secret scanner, yet in every run where it acted, it found eight of the nine secrets. This included an AWS key recovered from git history. The model improvises on its hunt to reach the Artex user's goals."

Matt Snyder, Aviatrix head of security operations and threat research, says he was most surprised at how, despite the sophisticated nature of Artex's framework, the operational maturity of many threat actors deploying it appears to be low (given how many hosts remain Internet-exposed).

"AI is lowering the skill floor for offensive operations without improving operational discipline. The framework may be sophisticated, but the operational security surrounding many deployments is not," Snyder says. "This creates a dangerous combination in which more people can launch capable attacks, while poor security leaves their infrastructure, tooling, and potentially victim information exposed to anyone on the Internet."

Increasing sophistication for lower-grade attackers means, as always, defenders should be ready. Microsoft's Storm-3358 blog includes extensive indicators of compromise and recommends considering tools like defensive honeypots, which trick attackers into thinking they netted a valuable target.

Check Point advised in a blog post last week that organizations should expect greater automated pressure against exposed infrastructure. "Internet-facing systems should be continuously tested and hardened, with particular attention paid to weak authentication, exposed APIs, credential leakage, remote code execution (RCE) vulnerabilities and cloud storage permissions," the blog post read.

Censys principal security researcher Silas Cutler offered encouraging words. Because the underlying tradecraft is conventional, the fundamentals still hold, he said, "Enforce MFA, monitor your attack surface, and practice good credential hygiene."

Alex is an award-winning writer, journalist, and podcast host based in Boston. After cutting his teeth writing for independent gaming publications as a teenager, he graduated from Emerson College in 2016 with a Bachelor of Science in journalism. He has previously been published on VentureFizz, Search Security, Nintendo World Report, and elsewhere.

At Dark Reading, he covers a variety of cybersecurity topics, including the cybercrime ecosystem, open source security, and the intersection between AI and threat actors. In his spare time, Alex hosts the weekly Nintendo podcast, "Talk Nintendo Podcast," and works on personal writing projects, including two previously self-published science fiction novels.

He has received numerous awards, including TechTarget's Writer of the Year in 2022 as well as more than 10 Azbee awards for his reporting between 2022 and today.

#9755. The Digital Euro: Solving Problems You Didn’t Have, With Rules You Don’t Write

Do you actually need a digital euro because payments weren’t convenient enough already?

I pay for everything with my phone. Instantly. Even when I’m abroad. To be fair, I’m still glad we actually get to live in the 21st century.

And no, it’s not because they want to ban cash. Cash is already quietly fading out of daily use in Europe. It’s certainly not because someone at a central bank suddenly developed a burning passion for transparency and democratisation.

So let’s look at what’s actually being built, who gets to set the rules, and most importantly, why it’s being built at all.

(It’s just the rehearsal where nobody gets to leave)

According to ECB Executive Board member Piero Cipollone’s speech on 5 November 2026, they plan a 12-month pilot in the second half of 2027.

It will involve 36 payment service providers, including Deutsche Bank, UniCredit, Revolut, Stripe, and Adyen. Testing will cover ordinary situations: purchases, transfers, and refunds.

According to the ECB, the target for a possible first issuance is 2029, but only if the necessary legislation is adopted by the end of 2026. Only then would the Governing Council decide whether to issue it at all.

Preparing a system and approving its use are two separate decisions. News headlines tend to treat them as the same thing.

It might come as a shock, but the balance you see in your banking app isn’t actually your money. It’s a promise from your local bank that they’ll repay it one day. A digital euro would move that promise even further away, all the way behind the walls of the ECB headquarters in Frankfurt.

Apart from that minor detail, your brand-new digital euro would be almost identical to what you already use.

It would still be worth one euro. It would still appear on your screen as if you owned it. And it would still not be immune to money printing, inflation, or devaluation.

Under the proposed design it wouldn’t even pay the princely 0.05% interest some accounts currently offer. And there would be a limit on how much you could hold. Roughly €3,000 was one of the options analysed, not a final rule.

Now, to be fair, there is one legitimate point in favor of the digital euro.

For card payments, Europe still depends heavily on non-European companies, in practice, mainly Visa and Mastercard. A shared European payments infrastructure makes sense as a political and economic objective. The real test is whether regular people actually get enough out of the digital euro to bother switching.

Good luck convincing 450 million people to just switch up their daily habits. Especially when the new system arrives with holding limits, no interest, and a few extra questions about why you’re using it.

That does not mean the entire wallet would operate anonymously like cash. Anti-money-laundering checks would still apply when depositing, transferring or withdrawing funds.

In other words, the ECB says it will not monitor everything you buy. Your local bank will.

The ECB says the digital euro would not be programmable money. The issuer wouldn’t dictate where, when or on what you could spend it. That’s different from a conditional payment you choose to arrange yourself.

So there’s no need for panic about your money expiring or a sudden ban on steak purchases.

There is a good reason to check whether protection against such restrictions remains firmly written into the final rules. A press release is no substitute for a legal safeguard.

The same applies to cash. The ECB says the digital euro would complement it, not replace it. What matters is whether people can actually keep using cash, and whether pulling it out of your wallet is still treated as normal rather than vaguely suspicious.

The digital euro and Bitcoin serve different purposes.

A digital euro would remain a euro, governed by monetary and public institutions.

As I learned the hard way after a single copy-paste mistake sent a test transfer straight into oblivion: with Bitcoin, I don’t need a central issuer to hold or send my money. The catch? If I hold my own keys, protecting them is entirely on me.

Bitcoin isn’t magically anonymous, either. Its public ledger and wild price swings don’t vanish just because we’re fed up with central banks.

I judge the digital euro on whether it actually fixes payments without chipping away at our rights. I judge Bitcoin on its own merits and risks. They’re playing entirely different games.

The digital euro isn’t about easier coffee purchases.

Once the rules are written and the system is live, complaining that “this wasn’t what we signed up for” will be largely irrelevant.

The real question isn’t whether the digital euro happens.

It’s whether we wake up in time to realize our right to use our own money is being quietly rewritten. Politely, step by step, and backed by world-class PR.

Bitcoin Is Not Just an Investment. It’s an Escape Hatch From the Financial Gulag
