#9744. Postgres not using your index? It's counting pages, not rows

Full-stack Developer TypeScript, Golang, Rust | WEB3 fomo.moe

Full-stack Developer TypeScript, Golang, Rust | WEB3 fomo.moe

Full-stack Developer TypeScript, Golang, Rust | WEB3 fomo.moe

Slow Postgres, part 1 of 8. The SQL and raw numbers for every test are on GitHub.

You add an index on status, run EXPLAIN, and Postgres reads the whole table anyway. ANALYZE doesn't change the plan. Someone suggests SET enable_seqscan = off, the plan finally shows your index, and the query gets slower.

Usually the planner is right. It prices a plan by the 8 KB pages it has to read and by whether it reads them in order or jumps around between them, and once you count pages the same way, you can answer most "why is it ignoring my index" tickets yourself.

This series started as my notes from an open lesson on slow Postgres queries by balun.courses. The tests and numbers are my own.

One note before the numbers: the AlphaVPS link at the end is a referral link, so I may get a commission at no extra cost to you, and the netcup vouchers come from my own account.

A regular B-tree index keeps only keys, the values it is sorted by, and next to each key a TID: the row's address in the heap, which is the table's main storage.

A TID is a page number plus a slot on that page. You can see it as the hidden ctid column:

Row 1000 is slot 48 on page 7. An index lookup for 'chargeback' returns a list of addresses like these, and Postgres then visits each of those heap pages to fetch the row and check that your transaction can see it.

The second step is the one people forget. To fetch one row, Postgres has to read the whole 8 KB page it sits on.

The lab runs on PostgreSQL 17.11 in Docker with default settings. My numbers come from a 4-vCPU, 8 GB cloud VM, but any small VPS or a laptop will do.

136 rows fit on a page, so 30,000 rows take 221 pages. I picked 30,000 because ANALYZE samples 300 × default_statistics_target rows, which is 30,000 at the default. On this table it reads every row, so the statistics are exact and your plans should come out the same as mine.

Ask for the most common value and the index goes unused:

Cost has no unit you can convert to milliseconds. It only means something next to another plan's cost.

The value you filter on appears nowhere in that formula. Ask for 'chargeback' with the index paths switched off and the Seq Scan still costs 596. Only the index path's price moves with the value, so the planner is choosing between a fixed price and a sliding one.

For 'paid', every one of the 221 pages holds paid rows, so the index path would read the whole heap plus the index. Force it with enable_seqscan = off and you get a Bitmap Heap Scan at cost 872.

Selectivity is the share of rows that pass the filter. The usual rule of thumb goes: one row, use the index; 1%, usually; 20%, it depends; 70%, Seq Scan. Here is the same table counted by pages as well as by rows:

The rule of thumb says index failed, and Postgres agrees: Index Scan at cost 235 against 596. Run both with EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS), though, and the index path touches 209 buffers to the Seq Scan's 221, a saving of twelve page reads.

It still finished faster, 0.19 ms versus 0.93, because checking 270 rows is less CPU work than filtering 30,000. For 'chargeback', 30 rows on 30 pages, the index path needs 32 buffers instead of 221.

Two things decide how rows land on pages. Row width sets how many fit on one, and at 136 rows per page any value much more common than 1 in 136 ends up on nearly every page. Physical order is the other. I spread failed evenly on purpose. If your failed orders came from one bad deploy on one afternoon, they'd sit on a few neighbouring pages and the index would look great.

On 221 pages everything finishes in a couple of milliseconds, so for timings I built a bigger table: 5 million rows, 326 MB, about 120 rows per page.

A bucket column holds a random number from 0 to 999,999, so WHERE bucket < 10000 matches 1% of the rows. I loaded the same rows twice, once in random order and once sorted by bucket, and forced each plan with the enable_* settings at shares from 0.01% to 50%. shared_buffers was 2 GB, which kept the whole table in memory.

For scattered rows Postgres picked a bitmap scan, which collects all the TIDs first and then reads each heap page once, in page order. Up to 10% of the rows it beat the Seq Scan, 98 ms to 124. At 25% it lost, 174 against 139, and the planner still chose it. A plain Index Scan, one heap visit per row, lost from 5% on.

By 10% the scattered matches sit on every single page, and the bitmap scan still won. It reads all 41,667 pages but checks only the 499,000 rows the bitmap points to, while the Seq Scan checks all 5 million. With the table in RAM a page read costs next to nothing, and the time goes into checking rows.

For clustered rows the index won at every share I tried, even 50%: 123 ms against 142.

RAM is the friendly case. For the cold runs I restarted Postgres and dropped the OS page cache before every run, so every page came off the VM's disk.

The Seq Scan got about twice as slow, 250 to 350 ms at every share. The clustered index won everywhere again, 23 ms versus 263 at 5%.

The scattered bitmap scan took 748 ms at 0.5% of rows, to the Seq Scan's 349. At 1% it took 1.27 seconds against 255 ms, five times slower, and that's the plan Postgres picks.

The bitmap scan at 2% read more heap pages than at 1%, 37,939 versus 29,143, and still finished more than six times faster, 190 ms against 1,275. From 2% to 10% it beat the Seq Scan again.

The 2% run touched 91% of the pages, so it was close to one long sequential read. The 1% run touched 70%, with holes in between. My best guess is OS readahead, which prefetches reads that look sequential and gives up when they're full of gaps. I haven't confirmed it yet.

The planner has no way to see that difference. All it has is random_page_cost = 4, a single guess at how much a jump costs next to a sequential read, and it used the same guess for both runs.

A 200-row copy shows the other end of the scale, where the table is too small for any index to win.

Only 2 of the 200 rows match, but reading two pages and checking 200 rows costs just 2 + 2 + 0.5 = 4.50. Turn off enable_seqscan and the cheapest index plan costs 6.19, because its one index page alone is priced as a random read at random_page_cost = 4. If you check plans on a 200-row test fixture, this is the arithmetic you're looking at, and it tells you nothing about the same query on 30 million rows in production.

"We're on SSDs, set it to 1.1." Fair, and on this table that flips the plan to an Index Scan at cost 2.77. Both versions finish in 10 microseconds or less, so on a table this size it makes no difference.

The one place for enable_seqscan = off is a scratch session, where it shows you what the other plan would cost. It applies to every query in the session, so in app code it also overrides the plans that were right, like 596 against 872 for 'paid'.

If the queries you care about only ask for the rare values, say a failed-payments dashboard or a chargeback queue, index only those rows:

It holds 3,000 entries instead of 30,000 and takes 5 pages, where the full index takes 28. Paid orders, 90% of the inserts here, never touch it.

Postgres only uses it when it can prove your filter implies the index's WHERE, and a literal status = 'chargeback' does. With only the partial index in place, a prepared status = $1 under a generic plan falls back to a Seq Scan, because the planner can't prove anything about a value it hasn't seen. Generic plans get their own part later in the series.

Before adding an index, look at the column in pg_stats:

That's what the planner believes about status as of the last ANALYZE. If most of your queries filter on paid, at 0.9, they get a Seq Scan, and no extra index will change that.

A negative n_distinct means a fraction of the row count. On tables bigger than the 30,000-row sample these numbers are estimates; you can raise the sample with ALTER TABLE ... ALTER COLUMN ... SET STATISTICS.

The same view has a correlation column, the planner's idea of physical order. On my 5-million-row tables it was 0.01 for the scattered copy and 1 for the clustered one, and that difference in physical order is what separates the scattered and clustered lines in both charts.

Before CREATE INDEX, run the pg_stats query, relpages and the rows-versus-pages count on your own table. If the value you care about sits on most of the pages and the table doesn't stay in memory, the index won't save you reads.

All the numbers above come from one 4-vCPU AMD EPYC cloud VM with 8 GB of RAM, so yours will differ. The SQL, the scripts, the raw output and the chart code are on GitHub. Run them on your own server, and if you get a different picture or think I got something wrong, open an issue or a PR.

My own projects run on netcup (VPS from €2.21 a month) and AlphaVPS (VPS from €2.54 a month). If you need a box for this, either works.

For netcup I have a few €5 vouchers for new customers. Each one works once, so take one and leave the rest for the next person:

Paste it into the "Redeem voucher" field at the bottom of the netcup cart. If they're all gone, message me on LinkedIn and I'll send you a new one.

Good luck with your plans. Part 2 is next: how to read Postgres EXPLAIN ANALYZE.

#9743. Attackers Say 'Hello' to a Different Scale of Cloud Attack

Researchers dubbed an attack chain "Greeter" after discovering that attackers deliberately covered their trail by leaving "hello" messages in logs.

What began as an exploratory Shodan search for exposed cloud instances has led to the discovery of a broad-ranging AI infrastructure attack campaign that researchers have christened "Greeter." The campaign, which started life as an organized, multistage, systematic attack across cloud providers, reinforces why defenders need to shift their thinking about cloud security to include a layered model built around network access control, data protection, and identity security.

Era Security researchers kicked off the research when the Shodan search engine revealed open Amazon DynamoDB instances where anyone could download data or delete it entirely. They dug a little deeper and found Flowise, a connected open source GenAI development platform, where users can build AI agents powered by large language models (LLMs).

Roughly 90% of the nearly 3,000 scanned Flowise deployments were running unpatched versions vulnerable to a critical code-injection vulnerability, CVE-2024-58351 — and if the researchers could see it, so could attackers. So, Era Security deployed AI-powered honeypots, mostly on Amazon Web Service (AWS), to catch them in action.

Related:LLMjacking Emerges as Thriving Cybercriminal Enterprise

Honeypot technology is "not like it was before," and attackers don't recognize it's a decoy until they're much further into the environment, according to the Era Security research team. In the past, it took three or fourth months to build a realistic honeypot. Today, it's two hours.

"The most important finding wasn't the exploitation technique itself, but it was what happened after," Naor Talmor, chief technology officer (CTO) at Era Security, tells Dark Reading. What ensued was a repeatable, staged methodology where attackers mapped out privileges and the environment, hunted for credentials, exploited cloud metadata services across multiple providers to escalate access, and then locked in persistence, he explains. Attackers also obfuscated their activity by leaving seemingly benign and fleeting "hello" messages in the logs, making detection much more difficult because it requires team to spend time searching for specific indicators of compromise in the logs. Thus, the researchers gave the campaign the "Greeter" moniker.

The sophisticated techniques and persistence show that Greeter isn't an opportunistic smash-and-grab attack, a script kiddie, or someone who had merely stumbled upon the honeypots, the researchers noted. And, the campaign was deployed across several AWS regions at once, which indicates broader scale and intent.

Related:External Teams Chats Anchor 15-Minute Malware Delivery

Era Security warns of the potential scale the campaign could reach, confirming 46 real-world victims so far, based on the number of unauthenticated instances that mirrored the honeypot conditions. The team estimates that at least 50% of those remain connected to the Internet and visible, suggesting at least 20 organizations are currently exposed. The sophistication levels of the the threat actors also speaks to how how valuable the cloud and AI attack surface has become, given the effort required to launch Greeter; this wasn't low-hanging fruit.

The Greeter campaign signals a few shifts across the cloud landscape, including how much easier it's gotten for attackers to go unnoticed in workflows. Much of that is due to AI, which threat actors are using to assist in writing code or orchestrating attack steps, according to the Greeter attack logs.

A decade ago, cloud attacks targeted the Docker API. Threat actors then began exploiting workloads, escaping containers to reach the cloud's metadata server underneath, and exploiting service accounts from there, the researchers explain. While attackers are following a similar pattern, they are now using AI infrastructure as the new way to establish persistence.

Related:TiDB Breach Exposes Flawed Cloud Security Assumptions

Researchers agree that the end goal on each instance was to grab cloud credentials and perform lateral movement within a targeted organization.

Meanwhile, attribution remains quite challenging. When the researchers drilled down to the code and techniques, they started to see Chinese characters, though that could be a false flag. Still, a nation-state culprit would make since, because the notion of seeing an "entire orchestration, not even a big cybercrime group could execute that," according to Era Security.

The current velocity of vulnerability exploitation is nothing like the researchers have seen in the past, which puts immense pressure on organizations' traditional patching cycles. This played out just over the past few weeks alone, as security teams raced to fix PHP2Shell and OpenSSH, searching workloads one by one for flaws. However, the Greeter campaign shows a defense challenge for cloud security that's bigger than fixing any specific vulnerability.

Everyone needs to assume a breach now, warns Talmor, adding how if it's not a vulnerability, it may be leaked credentials or an exposed API. Organizations need to design security programs around the cloud to be ready for all of the above, he advises, adopting defense-in-depth.

"A lot of companies adopt that, but they don't really practice it," he notes.

The researchers say organizations can detect this kind of attack much faster if teams monitor for enumeration activity to close gaps before attackers find them. When applications or chat tools are installed, logging can be activated and streamed to a separate location so that even if attackers do delete a device's local history, the logs remain stored in the cloud.

Researchers also noted that this should be monitored closely in critical environments, especially where crown jewels or critical applications are involved, adding that organizations can have dozens or hundreds of accounts depending on the size.

"To be clear, we aren't saying, 'Stop caring about misconfigurations or stop caring about vulnerabilities," Talmor says, warning that patch management is a game "we are losing" that requires organizations to secure their environment layer by layer.

Arielle spent the last decade working as a reporter, transitioning from human interest stories to covering all things cybersecurity related in 2020. Now, as a features writer for Dark Reading, she delves into the security problems enterprises face daily, providing context and actionable steps. She looks for stories that go past the initial news to understand where the industry is going. Her coverage areas include identity and access management, cyber risk and operations, industrial control systems, operational technology, and ransomware trends.

She previously lived in Florida where she wrote for the Tampa Bay Times before returning to Boston where her cybersecurity career took off at TechTarget SearchSecurity. When she's not writing about cybersecurity, she pursues personal projects that include a mystery novel and poetry collection.

#9742. Granite Switch 4.1.1 — Update models like you update software

Just over a week ago, we released Granite Switch 4.1, showing that our modular Switch architecture lets you configure a language model with specialized, cache-efficient adapters — adding new expertise on a single endpoint.

Granite Switch 4.1.1 is a patch release. The version number means what it means in software: fully backwards compatible with 4.1, no migration, incremental improvements under the hood.

While we are excited about these new features, what is notable is the speed and efficiency with which our teams could release this update. Apart from training the new ASR model and Decision adapter, nothing was recomputed: the base model is untouched. You compose the latest adapters you want and deploy.

This pattern can power far more than patch releases to an IBM-provided model. We're working on tutorials and an Adapter SDK so developers and third-party providers can build their own adapters — iterate on versions, test features, and ship updates the way you ship software. More soon.

Until then, test out our latest models, and try out the new multilingual and punctuation capabilities powering our Speech-to-Decisions demo.

#9741. AIを活用したサイバー攻撃の増加を受け、日本がサイバーセキュリティへの緊急資金拠出を推進

Breaking cybersecurity news, news analysis, commentary, and other content from around the world, with an initial focus on the Middle East & Africa, the Asia Pacific, Europe, and Latin America.

この対策パッケージには、官民合同のサイバー対応チーム、経済省が主導するAI専門チーム、および政府の新たな能動的サイバー防衛権限の行使に関する裁量の拡大が含まれている。

Translation provided by Dark Reading's internal AI translation tool.

日本においてサイバー攻撃や情報漏洩が急増していることを受け、日本政府は、攻撃に迅速に対応し、インフラのセキュリティを強化するための産官の専門家チームを設立することを目的とした、100億円（6,300万ドル）規模の緊急サイバーセキュリティ対策パッケージを可決した。

この戦略の4つの柱には、サイバー防衛へのAI導入を含む基礎的なサイバーセキュリティ対策の全国的な徹底、国内のサイバー捜査能力の強化、サイバー攻撃の被害者への支援拡充、そして民間企業と連携してサイバー攻撃に共同で対応することが含まれている。

高市早苗首相は、国のサイバーレジリエンス（回復力）を高めるため、これらのサイバーセキュリティ対策を「迅速かつ効果的に」実施するよう求めた。

「今この瞬間も、不正アクセスや情報漏洩の事案が後を絶たず、人々の日常生活や企業活動に多大な影響を及ぼしている」と、高市早苗首相は11月6日に緊急対策パッケージを発表した際の声明で述べた。「政府のあらゆる資源を動員し、サイバー攻撃への対応能力を全面的に強化していこう。」

サイバー攻撃の急増は、日本企業や政府機関に甚大な被害をもたらしている。サイバーセキュリティ企業（旧トレンドマイクロ）であるTrendAIのデータによると、2026年の最初の9か月間で600件以上のサイバーセキュリティインシデントが公表され、2025年通年の594件を上回った。公表されている報告数は控えめな推計に過ぎない。日本の個人情報保護監督機関は、4月から10月中旬にかけて2,094件の情報漏洩事案を記録しており（原文は日本語）、これも2025年度通年の総件数を上回っている。

他の地域ではAIが攻撃者を支援しているものの、サイバーセキュリティ企業TrendAIの脅威調査共同責任者であるライアン・フローレス氏は、脅威に関する声明の中で、インシデントの増加と攻撃者によるAIの利用との間に明確な関連性は確認されていないと述べた。

Related:Japan Pushes Emergency Funding for Cybersecurity as AI-Assisted Breaches Rise

「サイバー攻撃は世界的に増加しており、その結果として侵害やデータ漏洩も増加しています」と同氏は述べた。「AIが直接関与しているわけではないかもしれませんが、攻撃者が標的を見つけたり、操作を自動化したりするのを支援するAIの能力により、サイバー攻撃は大規模化しています。組織は、被害に遭う確率を下げるために、サイバーリスクを低減し、脆弱性を解消する必要があります。」

最近の侵害事例には、冷凍食品大手のニチレイやビール・食品大手のアサヒに対するランサムウェア攻撃、およびGMOインターネットグループを標的としたデータ侵害などが含まれる。これらの攻撃の多くは犯罪的な性質を持つが、盗まれた情報が他の犯罪グループや国家主体のアクターによって、日本の国民に対して悪用される可能性があることが懸念されていると、日本の通信大手NTTのチーフ・サイバーセキュリティ・ストラテジスト、松原美穂子氏は指摘する。

「攻撃者が十分な個人情報を収集・集約できれば、個人の嗜好から経済活動に至るまで、日本国民の詳細なプロファイルを構築できる」と同氏は述べる。「そのデータは、世論を操作したり、日本の機関に対する信頼を損なわせたりするための標的型偽情報キャンペーンなど、日本に対する影響工作に利用される可能性がある」

日本政府は、緊急資金を活用して、サイバーセキュリティ体制全体を強化するための4つの広範な取り組みを推進する意向だ。閣僚会議の公表された議事録によると、政府は、最近の多くの情報漏洩は適切なセキュリティ対策によって防ぐことができたはずだと指摘し、最初の取り組みとして、各組織が基本的なサイバーセキュリティ対策を確実に実施するよう促すとしている。

2つ目の主要な取り組みは、調査および情報収集能力を向上させ、より精度の高い分析を可能にし、その結果を国民に提供することで、攻撃への備えを強化することである。第三に、政府はサイバー攻撃への対応を強化し、国際的なパートナーシップを構築するとともに、積極的なサイバー防衛措置を実施する。最後に、政府は被害者を支援する能力とインフラを整備し、市民が損害を回復し、企業が事業を継続できるようにする計画だ。

「被害を受けた組織や個人が迷うことなく支援を受けられるよう、利用しやすい相談窓口や専門家による直接的な支援を拡充し、二次被害を防ぐための情報共有を強化する」と、日本の議事録には記されている。「また、官民の専門家を柔軟に派遣するための全国的な仕組みの構築にも着手する」

10月1日、日本の「積極的サイバー防衛法」が施行され、警察や自衛隊（SDF）に対し、日本の国家安全保障にリスクをもたらすあらゆるサイバー攻撃に対して強力な措置を講じる権限が与えられた。

「多くの国が、日本がいかなる種類のサイバー攻撃に対して、どれほどの速さで、どの程度の強度で対応できるのかを知りたがっているだろう」とNTTの松原氏は述べ、次のように付け加えた。「この緊急対策パッケージは……法律の枠組みを経済全体にわたる実用的な能力へと転換し、攻撃の可能性が高まる中、あらゆる規模の組織が攻撃を予防、検知、対応できるよう準備するために必要である。」

しかし、この資金はあくまで第一歩に過ぎず、日本がサイバーセキュリティへの投資を継続するには、さらなる資金が必要になると同氏は指摘する。

「この対策パッケージの重要な点は、サイバーセキュリティを個々の組織に完全に任せておくことはできないという認識が示されていることだ」と松原氏は述べる。「セキュリティ評価やインシデント対応、復旧支援といった形の政府による支援が、大きな違いを生むことができる。」

Rob also analyzes data on various trends using Python and R for both his reporting and his clients. Recent reports include analyses of the shortage in cybersecurity workers, annual vulnerability trends, and annual threat reports.

#9740. Tech Firms Dismantle Botnet That Turned 1.3M TV Boxes Into Proxies

Google said today it worked with industry partners to dismantle a botnet made up of more than 1.3 million Android TV set-top boxes that ship with malicious software which secretly rents the user’s Internet connection out to strangers and conducts advertising fraud. Experts involved in the takedown say the action is likely to sever the botnet’s access to more than 10 million additional compromised systems, including other Internet of Things (IoT) products such as Android-based healthcare devices and karaoke machines.

A report from the Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) said Google has severed ties with Videostrong Technology Co., a TV box manufacturer in China that GTIG and other industry experts concluded was responsible for including malware that enrolled more than 1.3 million set-top boxes in a botnet dubbed “XCPE” (named after one of the malware’s core code components).

The global distribution of XCPE botnet infections. Image: Google Threat Intelligence Group.

The report said the XCPE botnet loaded the user’s device with software that makes their Internet address available for resale by multiple “residential proxy” services, which allow customers to rent Internet addresses as a way to anonymize their web traffic or spoof their true location. As detailed in several stories here over the past year, residential proxy services are a major source of unwanted and often malicious traffic, including account takeover activity, advertising fraud, and mass content scraping for AI projects.

“Videostrong monetized the backdoor by selling access to criminal affiliates and loading those affiliates’ malware modules onto infected devices,” the GTIG post reads, noting that Google took legal action to take down the domains and servers Videostrong used to control the botnet and install additional malware. “A device manufacturer intentionally infecting their users with malware is an unacceptable breach of trust, and represents a serious risk to those users. Without users’ knowledge or consent, infected devices were offered as a distribution mechanism for a wide array of criminal actors.”

The report notes that while TV boxes made up the the majority of the botnet, the same XCPE malware was found in other Android-based IoT products, including telehealth devices, karaoke machines, and even digital signage systems.

Google said it requires all Android device makers to pass compatibility and security tests to ensure their products don’t harm users, but that Videostrong nevertheless found a way to load their malicious software immediately after a user boots up one of these devices for the first time (Google says it has since addressed that weakness).

The GTIG report calls out a number of residential proxy providers whose software development kits were routinely downloaded by devices infected by the XCPE botnet. Those include AppSalt, also known as Honeygain, which was developed by the Vilnius, Lithuania-based Oxylabs. In October 2026, Oxylabs and Honeygain were reorganized as independent platforms under an umbrella entity called Source, which received $130 million in funding from private equity firm Warburg Pincus that reportedly valued the business at $3.6 billion.

Another provider linked to the botnet was NetNut, a once sprawling residential proxy company operated by the publicly-traded Israeli company Alarum Technologies. In July 2026, the FBI worked with industry partners to seize hundreds of domains associated with NetNut, saying the company was responsible for operating a separate botnet called Popa that enslaved TV boxes as residential proxies. Other proxy providers named in the GTIG report include EarnFM, Traffmonetizer, Jaguar, LINKFOG, BMW/IPWeb and GaGaNode.

Google’s announcement credits a number of industry partners, including Synthient, a startup that tracks proxy providers. In January 2026, Synthient published research into the rapid spread of the Kimwolf botnet, which at the time was hammering networks worldwide with record-smashing DDoS attacks. Synthient documented how Kimwolf infected millions of Android set-top boxes virtually overnight, using a widespread vulnerability in these residential proxy services to compromise other Android-based devices inside the local networks of unsuspecting TV box users.

Synthient’s research caused dozens of residential proxy providers to patch their networks, which helped to fragment the Kimwolf botnet into much smaller pieces that made its incessant and disruptive DDoS attacks far easier for network operators to manage. It also attracted the attention of the Motion Picture Association (MPA), a trade group representing the major Hollywood studios, which partnered with Synthient to purchase and tear apart a number of popular Android TV set-top boxes — including some that were being infected by Kimwolf and other IoT botnets.

In a report published today, Synthient examined a popular, pre-infected TV box sold under the brand MECOOL by a publicly traded company in China called Skyworth Technology, concluding that MECOOL also bundled the malware from Videostrong Technology Co. and likewise installed AppSalt/Honeygain and other proxy components.

The MECOOL storefront and marketing. Image: Synthient.com.

Synthient founder Ben Brundage told KrebsOnSecurity that Videostrong’s malware also distributed software for the proxy service Grass. In our November 2025 story, “Is Your Android TV Streaming Box Part of a Botnet?” we quoted a researcher from Censys who found the popular Superbox TV streaming device bundled Grass’s residential proxy software. We also quoted the Grass founder, who denied any affiliation with the TV box maker.

That November 2025 story noted that Superbox and similar Android TV set-top boxes gain new customers primarily by engaging influencers on Tiktok and other social networks who praise the product’s ability to offer hundreds of (pirated) pay TV streaming services for a one-time fee.

The popular Youtube channel Linus Tech Tips discussing MECOOL TV streaming boxes.

The GTIG report estimates the XCPE botnet takedown should sever access to at least 10 million additional compromised devices, noting that the various proxy and ad fraud affiliates of Videostrong “each have diversified distribution channels for their modules beyond XCPE.”

Synthient’s Brundage echoed that conclusion, calling the 1.3 million number “highly conservative.”

“The scale of affected devices is likely way higher,” he said. “This is probably the largest operation against backdoored TV boxes that we’ve seen.”

Update, Nov. 5, 11:07 a.m. ET: In a statement shared post-publication, Oxylabs said that while its system is built so that a device can’t be used as a proxy exit node unless they receive a signal that it has consented, the developer faked these signals.

“We have been conducting regular audits of the applications provided by our partners,” the statement reads. “However, following this incident, we will improve the application and application’s build fingerprinting logic to better detect cases where the SDK is running on an unapproved build of an originally authorized application.”

The statement said Oxylabs has no record of any company called Videostrong Technology Co., but it did find between is suppliers the domain “com.abc[.]nexus,” mentioned in the GTIG report as an external malware loader.

“As soon as we saw that, we suspended the relationship and sent them a formal legal inquiry,” the statement reads. “This supplier accounts for less than 1% of our IP address pool. We had a signed contract with them, they assured our QA team that users had given consent, and we saw the consent flow ourselves.”

Further reading: Plume Security Labs white paper on the XCPE botnet (PDF) Black Lotus Labs writeup on LinkedIn TrendAI’s analysis Synthient’s list of affected devices, broken down by model number

You got the channel name wrong. its “Linus Tech tips” and not “Linux Tech tips”

Linus probably reads any ad from a company that gives him money. That’s a common thing for most YouTubers. And that’s how we got LastPass and similar products.

It’s comforting to know that they could ship 1.3 million smart TVs with malicious code and never know it. The consumer is lucky it was just botnets and not something much more personal and damaging.

I have no intention of *ever* buying a “smart” home appliance. 100% of them are spying on you – no, not an exaggeration – and I’d appreciate anyone naming *ANY* OEM who knows what the phrase “firmware/software security update” means, or one single one that has pushed one out.

[“I heard you got robbed.”](https://en.wikiquote.org/wiki/Chris_Rock)

I would really appreciate a little less journalistic “neutrality” than I’m seeing these days. It’s not just you, Brian, but the larger spectrum of non-investigative news reports that just repeat what the talking heads say. A better framing to my thinking (and why I gave that Chris Rock excerpt from 1996) is that Google *enabled* this abuse and then sat on their hands as it grew and grew to well over a million devices! They are in no way the good guys here. The deeper story to be uncovered and disclosed is why have they only acted now?

> residential proxy services are a major source of unwanted and often malicious traffic

Which is why they all need to be blocked by firewalls. That includes the networks of ISPs who *host* the devices and do not act to end their customer’s abuse. None of them are network peers whose traffic should be routed; the record DDoS attacks would be over if the Internet were just managed around that one sane principle.

For real, there’s no way Google was completely unaware of what was happening until now. In a similar vein, why does Google allow so many junk apps in the Play Store that can hijack the Android home launcher for even more advertising fraud? Does Google lack the ability to lock the home launcher to prevent it from happening? If Apple’s App Store can be so closely controlled, so could the Google Play Store.

I will now offer the exceptional advice you all need and will likely ignore them regret it if you connect the dots:

Do not put your AI apps on any app stores or share the distribution of any software other than that. Dedicated app store for ONLY that. Dedi servers. Dedi IPs. Heavily DMZed. Encrypted. No cohabitation with any of your other products or any one else’s and definitely don’t let them all distro like they live in the impossibly priced imaginary apartment in Friends.

But I mean that won’t fix the problem. Just ameliorate some of your psychological issues for a brief time.

The same lesson holds one level up, with people instead of devices. Before I let anyone near what I cannot afford to lose, I check three things: whether their story changes once the details get boring, whether they volunteer the part that makes them look bad, and what they did the last time nobody was watching. Nobody ever asked who that box belonged to. That question is cheap, and almost never asked about a person who wants your money.

What makes this class of compromise nasty is that the abused resource produces no symptoms: outbound traffic from a set-top box relaying someone else’s requests looks identical to a firmware update checking in. Owners had no reason to suspect anything, which is how the count reached 1.3M. The downstream cut-off of 10M more systems is the part worth watching – if proxy-rental demand simply migrates to other weak-identity IoT segments, the same playbook repeats somewhere quieter.

#9739. GITEX GLOBAL 2026 Puts AI Security, Cyber Resilience and Post-Quantum Readiness in Focus

As artificial intelligence moves from experimentation into critical business and government infrastructure, cybersecurity is facing a new set of challenges. Autonomous AI agents, increasingly interconnected systems, and growing concerns around data sovereignty are changing how organizations approach digital security. These developments will take center stage at GITEX GLOBAL 2026, taking place December 7–11 in Dubai, UAE. The growing adoption of AI is creating new opportunities for businesses, but it is also expanding the attack surface.

Organizations must account for how AI systems access information, interact with other applications, and operate within critical business environments. #9738. Transformers Model Integration Contracts

On July 30, 2026, Transformers enabled PyTorch's scaled dot-product attention (SDPA) for T5. As a side effect, UMT5's decoder could attend to future tokens. During training, it could peek at the answer it was supposed to predict. Nothing crashed, and the bug stayed in main for almost two months.

When we later replayed those commits, a small UMT5 model running on CPU flagged it on every one of them. This post is about that model and the tests built around it.

Transformers supports over 750 model types, and its test suite is big: 88,000+ CPU tests on main, plus 200,000+ GPU tests in a daily run. Model tests are only part of it: we also test pipelines, training, distributed execution, quantization and attention kernels.

The integration tests load real checkpoints and exercise the model's API on real hardware. Running all of that on every PR would mean keeping a lot of GPUs busy all day long, which isn't practical. By the time a scheduled run finds a regression, it may already be in main.

Our approach is to shrink the model instead. We build a fixture: a small model made from the real checkpoint's configuration, with fewer and narrower layers but every kind of layer it has, and its tokenizer and processor files unchanged. It is published once, then reused. We run "fast integration tests" against it on a cheap CPU runner. In our CPU study, the experimental UMT5 fixture used 66 MB of weights; the source checkpoint is 1,227 MB.

This also covers very large models: some don't fit on our standard GPU runners, but their fixtures run on CPU.

Model integrators already build tiny test models (Transformers' tiny-random-* checkpoints). We wanted a common recipe, and checks that go beyond loading the model and running a forward pass. The UMT5 bug would have passed a forward pass just fine.

Fixtures won't replace full integration tests, but on PRs they give us a chance to catch bugs before they reach main.

transformers-mic is a proposed standard for packaging these tests. A Model Integration Contract (MIC) has three parts:

The contract holds if running the usage path on the fixture still produces the baselines.

A contract covers an architecture and a usage path, not a single checkpoint: compatible checkpoints can share a fixture, while each keeps its own expected results. We publish them in huggingface-mic.

For example, the SmolLM contract generates from prompts such as "The capital of France is" and compares its token IDs with a recorded answer. After loading the model and tokenizer, the generation code is, simplified to one prompt:

It also compares training loss, checks that gradients are finite and verifies that an optimizer step changes the weights. See the full usage.md.

A fleet dataset on the Hub pins each MIC to a frozen revision, along with the package versions used to record its baselines. Each CI run records the fleet revision it used, so we can reproduce it later.

On a PR, we pick MICs based on the files the patch changes.

We replayed frozen MICs over five months of Transformers commits. The small UMT5 fixture flagged the regression from its introduction on July 30, 2026 until its fix on September 28. Label log-probabilities differed from the reviewed baseline by 1.22 and training loss by about 0.20.

One detail mattered: the contract used SDPA, the default attention path. Running only the eager attention variant missed the bug. A fixture only helps if it goes through the same code as the real checkpoint.

We then reverted the fix on a proof branch in Transformers' CI. The check failed with the same differences, and the selected T5 contract's runner step took 13.4 seconds on CPU, excluding setup.

The replay results and the CI demo have the measurements and reproduction details.

The first recipe was simple: make the dimensions smaller and keep fewer layers. That wasn't enough for mixed architectures. Keeping two layers is no use if both use sliding attention and the full-attention layers disappear.

We also keep the original weights file format. Otherwise we would skip the conversion code that runs when a user loads the real checkpoint. The full recipe has more detail.

The Llama 4 Scout shrink report shows what this looks like on a big model. 108.6 billion parameters become 44.7 million. The vision stack goes from 34 layers to 2 and the language stack from 48 to 4, keeping the checked layer kinds and MoE routing style.

Our CLI, tmic, creates the contract and builds the fixture. For a new model, an LLM drafts the usage code and manifest, and CPU and GPU runs measure the candidate baselines. The LLM drafts; it doesn't approve. Changed expectations require human review.

To try it on your machine, use your source checkpoint in place of org/model:

It drafts the contract, builds the fixture and records its baselines on your machine, asking you to review each step, and stops before uploading anything. For a new model, the draft comes from an LLM through Inference Providers, billed to your own account (--bill-to ''). The CLI docs cover the individual steps.

We used agents to build MICs across model families. When they hit an edge case, we fixed the recipe itself rather than the one fixture, with help from model experts. The published models and remaining gaps are in the coverage space.

With random weights, our Whisper fixture barely responded to changes in the audio. It ran, but that made it a poor test of the audio path.

So we trained it on a few tones paired with words such as "red" and "green". We weren't teaching it speech recognition, just making audio changes visible in its outputs. In our weight-initialization study, the random Whisper fixtures caught 18 of 24 injected faults. The overfit fixtures caught all 24.

That gives us two ways to build the weights:

The Whisper result doesn't settle which is better. Those were synthetic faults, and we haven't found a real regression caught only by the overfit version. Both versions missed an assisted-decoding bug that the real Whisper checkpoint exposed.

So we keep random weights when they pass the checks, and overfit when we need better sensitivity or readable answers. Training takes seconds, but it is one more step that can fail to converge, and one more thing to maintain. The comparison has the results for both.

As of November 1, 2026, the MIC job in Transformers CI reports failures without blocking PRs. Whether it should block depends on things we haven't measured yet:

We also don't know how many bugs, like the Whisper assisted-decoding one, only show up with real weights, or whether overfitting catches real bugs that random weights miss.

Coverage is still partial, across model families and the APIs people use. When a regression slips through, we can add the missing usage path and replay it on the broken and fixed versions. We'll keep existing tests until their coverage is accounted for.

Finally, we'd like to link original Hub model pages to their MICs, so a developer or an agent using a checkpoint could start from an example tested on that checkpoint, its environment and its expected outputs.

Want to help? Pick an uncovered model from the coverage space, try the tmic workflow, and contribute a usage path or review a generated contract.

#9737. Japan Pushes Emergency Funding for Cybersecurity as AI-Assisted Breaches Rise

Breaking cybersecurity news, news analysis, commentary, and other content from around the world, with an initial focus on the Middle East & Africa, the Asia Pacific, Europe, and Latin America.

The package adds public-private cyber responders, an AI-focused team run by the economic ministry, and more leeway to use the government's new active cyber-defense powers.

To read this story in Japanese, please click here (translation by our internal AI tool).

With Japan facing a surge in cyberattacks and breaches, the Japanese government has passed a ¥10 billion ($63 million) emergency cybersecurity package aimed at establishing teams of industry and government experts to quickly respond to attacks and better secure its infrastructure.

The four pillars of the strategy include thoroughly implementing basic cybersecurity measures country-wide, including adopting AI for cyber-defense, strengthening the nation's cyber-investigations capabilities, better supporting the victims of cyberattacks, and partnering with private industry to jointly respond to cyberattacks.

Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi called for the cybersecurity measures to be implemented "promptly and effectively" to enhance the nation's cyber resilience.

"Even at this very moment, incidents of unauthorized access and information leaks continue to occur, significantly affecting people's daily lives and business activities," Takaichi said in a published statement announcing the emergency package on November 6. "Let us mobilize the full resources of the Government to strengthen Japan's overall capabilities to respond to cyberattacks."

Related:AIを活用したサイバー攻撃の増加を受け、日本がサイバーセキュリティへの緊急資金拠出を推進

While AI has aided attackers elsewhere, TrendAI has not established a firm link between the increases and the use of AI by attackers, Ryan Flores, co-lead for threat research at TrendAI, a cybersecurity firm, said in a statement on the threats.

"Cyberattacks are increasing globally, and so are the breaches and data leaks as a result," he said. "While AI might not be directly involved, its ability to help the attackers find targets and automate their operations makes cyberattacks scalable. Organizations need to shrink their cyber exposure and close the vulnerabilities in order to lower the odds of being victimized."

Recent compromises include ransomware attacks on business, such as frozen food giant Nichirei and brewery and food giant Asahi, and data breaches targeting GMO Internet Group. While many of the attacks are criminal in nature, the worry is that the stolen information could be used by other criminal groups and nation-state actors against the Japanese public, says Mihoko Matsubara, chief cybersecurity strategist for Japanese telecom giant NTT.

Related:UK Wades Into Tech Sovereignty Amid AI Policy Changes

"If attackers can collect and aggregate enough personal information, they can build detailed profiles of Japanese citizens, from personal preferences to economic activities," she says. "That data could potentially be used for influence operations against Japan, such as targeted disinformation campaigns to manipulate public opinion or undermine trust in Japanese institutions."

The Japanese government intends to use the emergency funding to pursue four broad initiatives to improve its overall cybersecurity posture. Pointing out that many recent breaches could have been prevented by good hygiene, the government's first initiative is to ensure organizations are implementing basic cybersecurity measures, according to the published Japanese notes of the ministerial meeting.

The second major initiative is to improve investigation and information collection capabilities, allowing better analysis that can then be delivered to the public to better prepare them for attacks. Third, the government will strengthen its response to cyberattacks, establishing international partnerships and implementing active cyber-defense measures. Finally, the government plans to create the capability and infrastructure to support victims so that citizens can recover damages and businesses can remain operational.

Related:UK Warns Its Critical Infrastructure Faces Grave Risk

"Accessible consultation points and direct expert support will be expanded so that affected organizations and individuals can connect to support without confusion, and communication to prevent secondary harm will be strengthened," the Japanese notes stated. "Work will also begin on building a nationwide mechanism for flexibly dispatching public- and private-sector specialists."

On October 1, Japan's Active Cyber Defense legislation came into effect, authorizing the police and the Self-Defense Forces (SDF) to take strong measures against any cyberattacks that pose a risk to Japan’s national security.

"Many countries would be keen to learn how quickly Japan could respond to which kind of cyberattacks, and with what level of intensity," says NTT's Matsubara, adding: "This emergency package is ... necessary to translate the law’s framework into practical capabilities across the broader economy, preparing organizations of all sizes to prevent, detect and respond to attacks as they become increasingly likely."

However, the funds are only enough to get started, and more will be necessary to continue Japan's investment in cybersecurity, she says.

"The important aspect about this package is that it recognizes that cybersecurity cannot be left entirely to individual organizations," Matsubara says. "Government assistance, in the form of security assessments and incident response or recovery support, can make a difference."

Rob is an award-winning, veteran technology journalist of more than 30 years, reporting on global cybersecurity issues, the latest offensive and defensive technologies, malware incidents, cyber conflict, and AI's impact on software and cybersecurity.

A former research engineer, Rob has written for more than two dozen publications, including CNET News.com, Dark Reading, MIT's Technology Review, Popular Science, and Wired News. He has received five awards for journalism, including Best Deadline Journalism (Online) in 2003 for his coverage of the Blaster worm. Rob also analyzes data on various trends using Python and R for both his reporting and his clients. Recent reports include analyses of the shortage in cybersecurity workers, annual vulnerability trends, and annual threat reports.

Rob holds degrees from Cornell University in Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (double major).

#9736. Packaging Innovation for Good

Founder @ NowSourcing & Innovate Summit | Contributor @ Hackernoon | Advisor: Google Small Biz, SXSW

Founder @ NowSourcing & Innovate Summit | Contributor @ Hackernoon | Advisor: Google Small Biz, SXSW

Founder @ NowSourcing & Innovate Summit | Contributor @ Hackernoon | Advisor: Google Small Biz, SXSW

The European Union has declared an ultimatum against unsustainability: all consumer packaging placed on the EU market must be designed for recycling by 2030.  This mandate was announced by the Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation (PPWR) and formally became law in all 27 EU member states on Aug. 12, 2026.  Since then, the mandate has placed restrictions on synthetic “forever chemicals” (PFAS) in food packaging as part of the “Design for Recycling” (DfR) framework, which will become the baseline by 2030.  It is significantly reshaping how companies design, import and sell products globally.

All packaged products must meet these regulatory changes, not just those manufactured in the EU.  Because many brands prefer to standardize packaging across different nations’ markets, it is probable that PPWR’s influence will reach well beyond Europe as brands change their designs to streamline operations.

Under PPWR, materials will be graded based on their recyclability performance rates through the DfR framework.  Grade A materials are __≥95% recyclable__and meet the highest circular life cycle standards.  Grade B materials are ≥80% recyclable and are still considered to be highly efficient.  Materials graded as C are ≥70% recyclable.  Any material rated below 70% is deemed unrecyclable and will be banned from all markets.

The new rules imply that paperboard is one of the best materials for long-term reuse, reducing and recycling because it combines a high recyclability rate and excellent compatibility with set content targets.  This paper-based material can be recycled 5-10 times into innovative packaging for consumer retailers and their customers.  After it is responsibly disposed of, the cycle starts again for this valuable material.  European waste systems reportedly recover 87% of paper and paperboard packaging for reuse.  This significantly outperforms plastic, which has just a 42% recovery rate.  Other fiber-based materials help companies adjust to the tightening restrictions and mandates on single-use plastic packaging while simultaneously supporting enduring goals made for resource efficiency and overall recyclability.

The first rising concern about single-use plastics began in the 2010s.  By 2022, the European Commission proposed PPWR to replace the outdated Packaging and Packaging Waste Directive (PPWD) of 1994.  By February 2025, PPWR went into full effect.  In the coming years, the development of secondary legislation will start.  By 2028, mandatory standardized labels will appear on consumer packaging and on all waste sorting receptacles. Later on in the early 2030s, all packaging in the EU, whether locally produced or imported, will officially meet DfR criteria.  Most plastic packaging and plastic parts will meet initial minimum recycled content requirements.  By the end of the decade, all packaging must meet even stricter criteria for recyclability to ensure an even more sustainable world.

The PPWR intends to set a binding packaging waste reduction target of 15% by 2040.  Brands that adapt to the DfR mandates from the start by adopting paperboard material and designing for a circular material lifecycle will be better prepared for decades to come.  Additionally, they will also gain an advantage in a competitive market where environmental sustainability is rapidly becoming the criterion.

#9735. Chinese AI Project Scouts Spies in Taiwan Chip Industry

Breaking cybersecurity news, news analysis, commentary, and other content from around the world, with an initial focus on the Middle East & Africa, the Asia Pacific, Europe, and Latin America.

The CCP built a Big Data system to scrape reams of information and learn about individuals abroad, to potentially target and exploit them. Think Alice Huang Lite.

The Chinese government is keeping tabs on ethnic Chinese people abroad via an AI-powered Big Data mining program. In some cases, the program is helping the government design influence operations targeting high-ranking individuals in the artificial intelligence (AI) industry.

Since the AI boom began, world leaders have been feeling out how to exploit it to cement their power. While Washington's emphasis has been on shorter-term AI ventures — tracking immigrants and political protestors, identifying social services to cut, etc. — the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) has been building something more durable: a data center that facilitates gargantuan Web scraping from social media and other public sources, feeds the results into machine learning algorithms, and outputs actionable intelligence for the apparatchiks in Beijing.

That's according to documents leaked to China watchdog NetAskari. In a report shared with Dark Reading and Sky News UK ahead of publication, NetAskari detailed a program that balances straightforward government PR with unsavory surveillance. Sometimes the data gathering has been designed around Cambridge Analytica-style targeted propaganda campaigns. In more nefarious cases, it has been used to identify individuals in political and economic spheres of interest who might one day make good spies or unwitting assets in spy campaigns.

Related:Malicious Linux Implants Mimic Asian Mail Security Products

"A foreign nation with rather undemocratic tendencies is running an extensive, AI-charged analysis and information-scraping operation to find ways to influence other nations' internal social, economic, and political landscapes," a NetAskari analyst explains in an interview with Dark Reading over Signal. "That this system is particularly aiming at the Chinese diaspora, to see if [foreign citizens] can be used to further these ambitions, even if they might not be aware of it, is rather shocking."

On Nov. 8, NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang — one of the few most important people in the most important industry in the world — emailed his staff, admitting to an affair with a newly outed spy. The Ministry of State Security (MSS) agent, Alice Huang, redirected Nvidia semiconductors to China, where they're banned, and translated intelligence from the CEO to the CCP.

While the MSS ran Huang, the United Front Work Department (UFWD) took its own, less dramatic approach to the challenge of breaching Taiwan's semiconductor industry.

The UFWD's main game is influence operations, at home and abroad, according to NetAskari. Its mission includes gauging and shaping media narratives about China abroad, engaging Chinese diaspora communities — to their benefit or detriment, depending on the situation — and, in certain cases, attempting to gain influence over powerful or otherwise useful individuals and organizations in China and abroad.

Related:UAE, Saudi Arabia Face Onslaught of Increasingly Complex Cyberattacks

In this instance, the UFWD appears to have been scoping out ethnic Chinese individuals involved in the semiconductor industry. A leaked report titled "Profiles of Ethnic-Chinese Leading Talent in the Chip Field, Their Circle Characteristics, and Work Recommendations" identifies executives of the Taiwanese AI company Skymizer, high-performing students at a top Taiwanese research university, and an AI research center director at Microsoft, among others, as individuals of note. It then details strategies for getting closer to these VIPs, like "leverage non-official organizations — hometown associations, alumni associations, professional societies — for relationship-building and cooperation."

The system used to generate this report is called the "Overseas Chinese Affairs Big Data Platform."

The platform's brain is a 500-square-meter Big Data laboratory at Jinan University in Guangzhou, built to comfortably house rows of server racks and at least 100 employees.

Related:Cybercriminals Hack Brazilian Government Servers to Host Phishing Sites

Basically, it's built to ingest massive amounts of online information about overseas Chinese communities, identify people, relationships, and public sentiments, and convert it all into actionable reports for CCP leadership, according to NetAskari.

Social media provides much of the content. The platform scrapes liberally from platforms like Instagram, Facebook, and X, plus Chinese platforms like Weibo and WeChat. As a rule, the actual scrapers are run on machines located in foreign countries. As with Chinese hacking campaigns more broadly, the machines doing the crimes are also shielded behind rotating proxy networks. The goal of this obfuscation, one leaked document explains, is to “ensure the security of data collection and prevent the collection system from being traced and discovered" by targeted platforms.

The data then makes its way to China for processing. Foreign languages are translated into Chinese, keywords are extracted, and meaningful links are drawn. UFWD then cross-references these data with preexisting records of notable people identified as being involved in the media, sciences, politics, etc., as well as blacklisted and "two-faced people." These two sources feed a "business system" — the layer that seems to draw meaningful connections about public sentiments, the results of influence operations, and more.

Sometimes, the final reports outputted by this multitiered system simply concern public relations trends. Sometimes they've been used to identify ethnic Chinese individuals of note around the world — be they Taiwanese engineers, social media influencers, or something in between — and unearth strategies for how to utilize them to further the ends of the Chinese Communist Party.

Overall, the NetAskari analyst describes the Overseas Chinese Affairs Big Data Platform as "a worldwide dragnet that uses open source intelligence (OSINT) and Big Data analysis to identify and find potential collaborators, partners, and affiliates that the UFWD can work with to further their goal [of] extending the Communist Party's influence abroad and creating a 'China-friendly' environment in other nations' political, economic, and social settings."

It's nothing the UFWD wasn't doing before, to be sure. Instead, the analyst adds, "What used to be done manually, at a much slower speed, is now supercharged via AI and modern technology."

That, ultimately, is the rub. The leaked documents contain only outdated references, from 2021, about how machine learning (ML) and natural language processing (NLP) algorithms fit into this picture. It's unclear whether, and how, more modern large language models have been incorporated into — and potentially supercharged — the system. The better the AI gets, the more wide-ranging and granular the Overseas Chinese Affairs Big Data Platform can become, with real consequences for people who may not know they are being targeted by a foreign nation.

"A surveillance state can't accept that its own citizens are escaping to other nations, outside the reach of Beijing's grasp. For the best part of the last 20 years, most people had the luxury to ignore this part of the Chinese state. Often practical and physical limitations restricted Chinese organiations to expand too quickly abroad or even get a foothold. But with remote methods like the ones we have seen applied in the Big-Data center of Jinan University, these 'natural boundaries' don't apply anymore," the analyst laments.

"Pair it now with ever-growing globalization, China's stepping out onto the world stage, and crises of democracy in many Western nations, and it is not hard to see why such operations should concern even average citizens in the US or Europe," he says. "Even if they have no personal ties to China."

Nate Nelson is a journalist and award-winning scriptwriter. In addition to Dark Reading he writes for Darknet Diaries, the most popular show in cybersecurity across all media.

He began his career as a freelancer, ghostwriting Forbes and CNBC op-eds for executives in tech and finance. Then he transitioned to journalism at Threatpost, where he covered cybersecurity news and trends. Throughout those years he co-created a cybersecurity podcast, Malicious Life, which in its day climbed into the Top 20 technology podcasts charts on Apple Podcasts and Spotify.

He holds degrees from New York University and Bard College. As a born and bred New Yorker, he enjoys a superiority complex, but is polite enough to keep it to himself.

#9733. Inside an AI Attack Against a US Retailer

When hand-typed commands failed to breach a US retailer, the attacker turned to AI-generated scripts, achieving lateral movement in minutes.

A threat actor deployed an AI model during a stalled cyberattack and rescued the campaign, achieving lateral movement in the process.

The attack, detailed today by Symantec, targeted an unnamed US retail organization in September. The threat actor's hand-typed commands were repeatedly blocked, so the attacker switched to what appeared to be AI-generated commands and rapidly broke through the retailer's defenses. The attacker ultimately harvested credentials and achieved lateral movement within minutes.

Symantec believes AI was used because the timing between commands was more indicative of automation than direct hands-on keyboard. That said, the timing was such that investigators believe this activity was "more consistent with an operator relaying output to an AI tool than with an autonomous agent."

The security firm said this incident is one of dozens of AI-assisted attacks Symantec has investigated since May, though it added that activity was heavily concentrated around September.

Related:Artex: The AI Pen-Test Tool Hackers Turned Into a Weapon

Threat actors have utilized large language models (LLMs) in their attacks as long as the technology has been widely available. Early applications involved generating convincing phishing lures or conducting basic data reconnaissance, but recent evidence shows attackers deploying AI to execute end-to-end attacks, assist with malware development, and more. More recently, attackers have abused — and continue to abuse — agentic penetration testing tools to break into target environments at machine speed.

In this attack specifically, Symantec said it did not identify the initial access vector, focusing more on the timeline it was able to glean from its post-incident investigation. According to the blog post, the attacker worked at first by hand, which investigators determined due to artifacts like typing errors.

When every staged payload was terminated by security software, indicators suggest attacker tactics changed when they tried again the next day. "For almost two hours," Symantec said, "the attackers submitted long, error-free PowerShell scripts with labelled output sections and, in places, comments that read as a model's reasoning." Approximately 10 minutes after querying the victim's SolarWinds Orion monitoring software, attackers managed to laterally move to a second server.

The blog post hypothesizes that the attackers behind the attack were likely financially motivated, as they searched point-of-sale scripts for passwords, and one address they contacted was linked to an operation that stole card data from online retailers.

Related:CISA Announces Enhanced Reporting Form for Cyber Incidents

During the second-stage activity, the threat actor gained initial access to a Web server and stole credentials from configuration files tied to the SolarWinds Orion monitoring software. And while the idea of AI speeding up or improving attacker tradecraft is nothing new, the attack is its deployment of AI to a hands-on keyboard attack in progress and possibly seizing victory out of an apparent defeat. It presents LLMs as a difference-maker for a less skilled threat actor.

Dick O'Brien, principal intelligence analyst on the Symantec Threat Hunter Team, tells Dark Reading this incident is one of several the team has seen in recent weeks where AI revived an attack. While he calls this a game-changer for attackers, "defenders can potentially leverage that pattern" as AI behaves in a particular kind of way, such as testing variants of a technique in quick succession.

"The retry pattern is a signal itself," he says. "Blocking on behavior rather than file names or exact commands matters much more. Treating a blocked attempt followed by a variant as a high-priority alert is worth considering."

Although no vulnerability was exploited and no patching was required, O'Brien believes this trend of AI accelerating attacks is and will continue to affect the patching race. "Our view is that defenders need to start looking at mean time to mitigate rather than mean time to patch. Patching is still important, but it can’t be the only countermeasure."

#9732. CWE-bench v2: More coverage, quality, and transparency

CWE-bench is designed to test the limits of frontier cyber capabilities. In our continued pursuit to push the horizon at Collinear AI, CWE-bench v2 opens up a public set of 100 tasks that anyone can run and evaluate their models on. The setup is the same as before. An agent gets a checkout of a real open-source repository and a short instruction, with the goal of finding and fixing a security weakness without breaking existing functionality. Scoring is fully programmatic, so results are deterministic and anyone can reproduce them without extra cost. All our programmatic checks have been curated with the help of LLM judge panels that shape them towards the direction of hardness and fairness. We also maintain a held-out set, so that we can keep tracking progress on tasks no model has seen. To evaluate your model on the held-out set, contact cyber@collinear.ai.

Our goal is to be exhaustive. A defender has to anticipate the ways an attacker could get in, and get it right every single time. These 100 tasks cover 91 different CWEs, spanning a wide range of vulnerability classes. A model that does well here has to understand the multiple weakness surfaces that a potential attacker can exploit. Recognising a familiar pattern is not enough.

As part of our meticulous effort to keep improving quality, for every task we checked that the following questions were true:

Every task was also reviewed by hand. Open-sourcing the set is part of the same effort to improve quality. We welcome feedback on any task, and contributions to the public set.

Results are tracked in two places on the Hub. The leaderboard on the CWE-bench dataset page covers open-weight models and updates on its own: labs and the community add a result by opening a PR on the model's repo with a results file (how). For the full comparison, including API-only models such as Gemini, Claude and GPT, see the CWE-bench leaderboard Space, where new models are added through a PR on the Space.

Open-weight models, from the dataset page:

All evaluated models, including API-only ones:

Of the 11 models evaluated, Gemini 4 Argon leads with 67.8% pass@1 and 81.0% pass@4, just ahead of Claude Opus 5.5 (67.3% pass@1, 78.0% pass@4). 95 tasks are solved by at least one model, an indication that the tasks are indeed solvable. However, even the leader fails 19% of the set on every attempt, so the long tail is far from solved. The public set, the grader and the harness are open. Run your model, and tell us where it stands.

On cost, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (1017), Claude Opus 5.5 and Gemini 4 Argon form the Pareto frontier: DeepSeek reaches 57.0% pass@1 at $0.04 per rollout, Opus adds ten points at $1.83, and Gemini edges ahead at $3.92.

Every task is a self-contained Harbor task (a Dockerized environment, an instruction, and a deterministic verifier), and the dataset ships a registry.json. Harbor can therefore run the whole benchmark straight from the Hugging Face repo, without cloning anything yourself:

-k 4 runs 4 attempts per task, and the reported score is the mean reward over all 400 trials. The dataset is gated: accept its access conditions on the dataset page first. Harbor fetches the tasks with git, so also save your HF token to git's credential helper once:

The tasks are also tagged rl-environment: the same environments and verifiers can provide rewards for training defensive agents, not just for evaluating them.

#9731. Want to Rent an Internet Address at the White House?

Several staffers at the White House are using computers or mobile devices equipped with residential proxy services that render their internet address available for others to rent, security experts warned today. One of the proxy services is a Russian company whose founder’s web hosting business was ground zero for cyberattacks against election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016.

The security firm Layer3 Intel said it detected multiple residential proxy nodes beaconing out from the internet address network reserved for the Executive Office of the President (AS2650). Layer3 said the proxy activity was relatively persistent between October 5 to November 3, and that a review of the proxies available from AS2650 showed they exited from the White House network 236 times during that period.

The proxy tracking company Synthient said on Twitter/X that the activity it saw coming from AS2650 was related to multiple Windows 11 installations of a service called Infatica, a proxy program that is often integrated into “free” mobile and desktop applications. Infatica’s founder Vladimir Fomenko is a Russian man whose hosting firm King Servers was home to six of the eight internet addresses used by Russia’s state security services to compromise databases for election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016.

Synthient’s depiction of the outgoing proxy traffic from the dedicated White House network (AS2650). Click to enlarge.

There are dozens of residential proxy providers with varying degrees of legitimacy, many of them based in China or Russia. But at a minimum, they all make it simple for customers to rent someone else’s internet address as a way to anonymize their web traffic or spoof their true location. From a website’s perspective, the traffic from a proxy network user appears to originate from the rented IP address, not from the proxy service customer.

Layer3 Intel said the proxy exit nodes at the White House came from six internet addresses, on 26 of the 30 days, and that most of the activity happens in the evening, between 5 p.m. and midnight.

Incredibly, Infatica was not the only proxy service that reportedly has been reselling access to White House internet addresses: Layer3 Intel said it found 28 separate residential proxy services were able to exit through this network.

“This is public access,” the Layer3 Intel team wrote. “Anybody can obtain it by signing up to a public residential proxy service, paying a few dollars and sending requests through it. We did not selectively target this network or try to make our probes exit from it. We caught this by chance, simply by requesting global rotating access through these services.”

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

As detailed in several stories here over the past year, residential proxy services are a major source of unwanted and often malicious traffic, including account takeover and other cybercrime activity, advertising fraud, and mass content scraping for AI projects.

They can also introduce serious security risks. In late 2025, it was discovered that cybercriminals were mass exploiting a widespread vulnerability in these services that allowed them to probe each proxy endpoint’s local network for vulnerable systems to infect with malware. In January 2026, dozens of proxy services were forced to patch their networks after Synthient Founder Ben Brundage showed how cybercriminals were abusing a vulnerability in these residential proxy services to seize control over devices inside the local networks of unsuspecting users.

“Some of these resellers sell bandwidth for as low as 60 cents a Gigabyte, that means for less than a dollar you can gain access into some of the most confidential and trusted networks,” Brundage told KrebsOnSecurity. “The reseller ecosystem further enables this with any criminal able to buy access while skipping KYC [Know Your Customer] processes.”

All too often, these proxy services are beaconing out from employee devices brought into the workplace. App developers can embed software development kits (SDKs) provided by the residential proxy networks to monetize their software, allowing them to receive a small amount of money on each installation.

As risky as residential proxies can be for unsuspecting end users, they are all too commonly found on government and corporate networks. In a webinar in January 2026, the proxy tracking service Spur found residential proxies in nearly 300 government owned and operated networks, 318 utility companies, 166 healthcare companies or hospitals, and 141 companies in banking and finance. In a blog post earlier this year, the security firm Infoblox said it discovered that fully 65% of its customer base was querying one or more residential proxy related domains.

#9729. Extortion Group Luna Moth Flits Into Law Firms a Second Time

The cybercriminals are retargeting law firms that refused to pay its first ransom, with a social engineering con aimed at stealing Microsoft access tokens.

A data extortion outfit has returned to previously targeted law firms for a second go, via a "vishing"-based social engineering campaign where they purport to be IT staff.

That's according to the ReliaQuest Threat Research team, which today published a blog post disclosing that Luna Moth, a threat extortion group that has targeted law firms since at least mid-2023, has for now abandoned remote-management tools and manual exfiltration to steal data, instead looking to swindle victims out of access tokens. Then, they're using these tokens to access and steal information.

Joseph Keyes, author of the blog post and cyber threat intelligence analyst at ReliaQuest, wrote that this latest wave of targets are "likely" those that didn't pay Luna Moth's first extortion demand, with this second hit coming weeks-to-months later.

A ReliaQuest spokesperson tells Dark Reading that these firms were targeted a second time because the group knows these organizations can be socially engineered (so it tries again with different tactics), for a second set of data. Moreover, as fewer organizations are paying, law firms make a good fit to target, because "their client data is highly sensitive and the reputational hit from exposure is severe, so repeated leverage is worth the effort."

Related:3AM Affiliate Embraces AI-Like Loops in European School Attack

In the initial variants of the attack, Luna Moth would reach out as IT support and trick victims into connecting to Windows' built-in remote assistance tool. It would then download data directly. This time, the group sent blank-subject emails from a free email address with a broken PDF masquerading as a business report; the "report" would then fail to open. The attacker would use this pretext to reach out soon after, posing as IT support responding to a malicious alert, while at the same time offering to fix the PDF.

Once on a video call, the "IT support" directs the target to turn on screen-share functionality so they can direct the target through a "fix." The attacker then tells the target to open Microsoft Copilot from the Web browser on their work laptop, open the browser's developer tools, find the request Copilot sends to Microsoft Graph, and copy the application's access token.

The attacker instructs the target to paste the token into a public text-sharing site the attacker can access. Finally, the attacker gives the token to its own folder and downloads files through the Microsoft Graph API.

This social engineering tactic requires no malware and no vulnerability. It relies solely on tricking a target into giving an access token, effectively a master key into the front door of an organization. The use of IT support to "fix" a technical issue evokes ClickFix, as both techniques rely on human problem-solving tendencies to trick an end user.

Related:'AdFection' Turns Ad Impressions Into Zero-Click Spyware Delivery

The ReliaQuest spokesperson says the firm considers this attack representative of a gap in how controls are scoped within an organization. Because the token is issued to the victim's compliant device and handed over "willingly," security red flags do not go off.

"A token is a bearer credential, so it works from anywhere until it expires, unless CAE [Continuous Access Evaluation] with strict location enforcement (or token binding) applies," the spokesperson says. "Similar to device code phishing, the user completes a legitimate flow, so MFA is satisfied. The weakness is the assumption that authentication equals ongoing trust. Microsoft's defaults, such as the 60- to 90-minute lifetime and CAE not being enforced by default, make it easier."

ReliaQuest recommends that organizations turn CAE on by default, block browser developer tools and token-inspection pages on managed browsers, and restrict remote-support and screen-sharing tools where there's no business need. Additionally, it may be wise to inform employees of the ways threat actors attempt to steal credentials from employees.

Related:Biomemory Launches DNA Shield, First Commercial Product Built on Its Molecular IT Platform

As the blog post put it, "Tell users that IT will never ask for developer tools or tokens and that they should verify IT requests by callback."
