#9728. Cyber Experts Weigh In: How to Fight Artex & AntiFox

Cybercriminals using agentic pen-testing tools is a proverbial genie out of the bottle at this point, so enterprises need to get a defense plan in place right away.

A month since it went closed-source, the Artex agentic penetration testing framework is spreading faster and causing more havoc than ever. Still, cyber defenders tell Dark Reading that defending against it is largely a matter of willingness, not capability.

To recap: In August, a Chinese open source (OSS) developer released a cybercrime-grade agentic red-teaming tool called "Artex." In the months that followed, attackers and cybersecurity researchers have gradually realized just how effective Artex is at probing for vulnerabilities and turning initial access into meaningful compromise at so-called machine speed.

"Artex is what the perpetual conflict era looks like," says Yuval Itzchakov, co-founder and chief technology officer (CTO) of A Security. "When our research team ran it against our open source benchmark, it found eight vulnerabilities in about 45 minutes, including a critical privilege escalation to admin, and chained them into a full attack path through a WAF, CAPTCHA, and MFA. All it took was a download, an install script, and a model key."

Related:Attackers in Binance Breach Targeted Known Weakness, Missing Controls

Nothing about it is so complicated, he says, "And that's the point. Take the guardrails off an AI hacking tool, and anyone can run agentic attacks at scale. In Artex, scope is just a suggestion to the model."

Though its author de-listed the original Artex on Oct. 8, new variants continue to cause trouble. The variant du jour, "AntiFox," was recently weaponized by attackers to exploit Internet-facing Web services and their associated Amazon Web Services (AWS) environments. According to researchers at Arctic Wolf Labs, threat actors used their new agentic toy to breach, deploy Web shells, and execute operating system (OS) commands on compromised Microsoft Internet Information Services (IIS) servers, as well as enumerate services, expose production secrets, and manipulate Simple Storage Service (S3) buckets across AWS environments.

Notably, Arctic Wolf Labs offered relatively banal advice for organizations defending against this quite new threat: hunt for indicators of compromise (IoCs), rotate and revoke relevant credentials and sessions. In fact, researchers say, there's little more to defending against Artex or AntiFox than basic cybersecurity hygiene. However, it's also important to avoid making assumptions; as GitGuardian pointed out in a blog post on AntiFox, "Blocking scanner tools won't stop these agents, and a leaked key stays dangerous until someone revokes it."

The prospect of every Tom, Dick, and Harry having an agentic attack framework in their pocket might be intimidating, but cybersecurity defenders still possess some distinct advantages.

Related:Getting Past the Post-Quantum Cryptography Discovery Phase

First off, Itzchakov points out that "Artex stops at the front door. It has no lateral movement, no Active Directory testing, and no view inside. Defenders can see their whole environment and test it continuously with the same speed and autonomy, under guardrails no one can switch off. The organizations that come out ahead will treat this as permanent and build their security around it."

In a profile of a recent incident response (IR) effort against an Artex attack, Eye Research noted another serious weakness of agentic tools in general: They're loud. "The agents left their name in pod names and probes, hammered endpoints no human would touch, and tripped detections on systems with EDR installed," it explained. "Where we had visibility, we saw them immediately."

"If you want to be positive, there are a lot of small steps you can put together in order to protect networks and organizations," says Guillaume Valadon, lead cybersecurity researcher at GitGuardian. To catch Artex or AntiFox's loudness, for example, "blue teams must have in place a security information and event management (SIEM) platform and a really good detection system, to make sure that they will detect these tools in the noise."

Related:Japan Pushes Emergency Funding for Cybersecurity as AI-Assisted Breaches Rise

Besides active detection, organizations would be well advised to focus on secrets management. Artex and AntiFox have proven adept at finding secrets, in part because they use ordinary commands like "git" and "grep" to find what they're looking for, instead of shipping a more easily identifiable and blockable secret scanner.

"Defenders need to be looking for exposed and dormant keys, checking Git repos for exposed secrets, and heavily implementing a defense-in-depth posture," adds Justin Moore, Arctic Wolf's director of adversary operations. "What makes these frameworks so effective is not that they’re conducting novel attacks; they’re just doing what we already know, just faster than we have seen before. Good cyber hygiene is exactly what prevents these types of attacks from being so successful, whether they’re agentic or not.”

Despite all of the positive steps organizations can take, Valadon says, "If I'm being negative, I would say that it's too late."

"For years we have been telling people that they should not output secrets — that we're finding really important hardcoded secrets everywhere, publicly. On Docker, GitHub, and so on. Now, because we have these tools that can go fast from nothing to discovery to weaponization, that makes it more difficult for blue teams," he says.

"The agentic capacity for the attacker is already here, and they're going faster and faster and faster," he notes. "So if you didn't do the right stuff before, it will be difficult for you to catch up."

The cybersecurity industry has been waiting for AI-driven cyberattacks for years now. Product marketing campaigns have hinged on agentic attacks being right around the corner. Stories of lightly AI-influenced tactics, techniques, procedures (TTPs), and malware have kept food on cyber reporters' plates. Most of the discourse has been, at best, theoretical, at worst, misleading.

A meaningful, if incomplete, turning point seems to have occurred around midyear, if not among the most sophisticated attackers, then at least in the world of middling cybercriminals.

"When we all started using ChatGPT, at that time, we were just asking it simple questions. It was fun, but it was not possible to code," Valadon explains. "And then we had agents that were more capable at coding and syncing. This year you can do it all, from end to end. You just give [an agent] a rough idea, and it will do some planning, syncing, it will build the code for you, and deploy it for you. It's getting better and better at doing the whole cycle."

He also points to Anthropic and OpenAI's warnings about OSS AI earlier this fall: "Some people are saying that we are seeing these [attack] frameworks because of Chinese open-weight models. Because if you have a big GPU, you are able to run your own offensive models with Artex."

"It's getting more and more dangerous," he says. "It's all fitting into the HuggingFace, OpenAI, Anthropic narrative [warning against attackers] having access to real offensive tools."

Nate Nelson is a journalist and award-winning scriptwriter. In addition to Dark Reading he writes for Darknet Diaries, the most popular show in cybersecurity across all media.

He began his career as a freelancer, ghostwriting Forbes and CNBC op-eds for executives in tech and finance. Then he transitioned to journalism at Threatpost, where he covered cybersecurity news and trends. Throughout those years he co-created a cybersecurity podcast, Malicious Life, which in its day climbed into the Top 20 technology podcasts charts on Apple Podcasts and Spotify.

He holds degrees from New York University and Bard College. As a born and bred New Yorker, he enjoys a superiority complex, but is polite enough to keep it to himself.

#9727. Most Frequently Asked Questions About NFTs(Non-Fungible Tokens)

Non-fungible tokens (NFTs) are the most popular digital assets today, capturing the attention of cryptocurrency investors, whales and people from around the world. People find it amazing that some users spend thousands or millions of dollars on a single NFT-based image of a monkey or other token, but you can simply take a screenshot for free. So here we share some freuently asked question about NFTs.

NFT stands for non-fungible  token, which is a cryptographic token on a blockchain with unique identification codes that distinguish it from other tokens. NFTs are unique and not interchangeable, which means no two NFTs are the same. NFTs can be a unique artwork, GIF, Images, videos, Audio album. in-game items, collectibles etc.

A blockchain is a distributed digital ledger that allows for the secure storage of data. By recording any kind of information—such as bank account transactions, the ownership of Non-Fungible Tokens (NFTs), or Decentralized Finance (DeFi) smart contracts—in one place, and distributing it to many different computers, blockchains ensure that data can’t be manipulated without everyone in the system being aware.

The value of an NFT comes from its ability to be traded freely and securely on the blockchain, which is not possible with other current digital ownership solutionsThe NFT points to its location on the blockchain, but doesn’t necessarily contain the digital property. For example, if you replace one bitcoin with another, you will still have the same thing. If you buy a non-fungible item, such as a movie ticket, it is impossible to replace it with any other movie ticket because each ticket is unique to a specific time and place.

One of the unique characteristics of non-fungible tokens (NFTs) is that they can be tokenised to create a digital certificate of ownership that can be bought, sold and traded on the blockchain.

As with crypto-currency, records of who owns what are stored on a ledger that is maintained by thousands of computers around the world. These records can’t be forged because the whole system operates on an open-source network.

NFTs also contain smart contracts—small computer programs that run on the blockchain—that give the artist, for example, a cut of any future sale of the token.

Non-fungible tokens (NFTs) aren't cryptocurrencies, but they do use blockchain technology. Many NFTs are based on Ethereum, where the blockchain serves as a ledger for all the transactions related to said NFT and the properties it represents.5) How to make an NFT?

Anyone can create an NFT. All you need is a digital wallet, some ethereum tokens and a connection to an NFT marketplace where you’ll be able to upload and sell your creations

When you purchase a stock in NFT, that purchase is recorded on the blockchain—the bitcoin ledger of transactions—and that entry acts as your proof of ownership.

The value of an NFT varies a lot based on the digital asset up for grabs. People use NFTs to trade and sell digital art, so when creating an NFT, you should consider the popularity of your digital artwork along with historical statistics.

In the year 2021, a digital artist called Pak created an artwork called The Merge. It was sold on the Nifty Gateway NFT market for $91.8 million.

Non-fungible tokens can be used in investment opportunities. One can purchase an NFT and resell it at a profit. Certain NFT marketplaces let sellers of NFTs keep a percentage of the profits from sales of the assets they create.

Many people want to buy NFTs because it lets them support the arts and own something cool from their favorite musicians, brands, and celebrities. NFTs also give artists an opportunity to program in continual royalties if someone buys their work. Galleries see this as a way to reach new buyers interested in art.

There are many places to buy digital assets, like opensea and their policies vary. On top shot, for instance, you sign up for a waitlist that can be thousands of people long. When a digital asset goes on sale, you are occasionally chosen to purchase it.

To mint an NFT token, you must pay some amount of gas fee to process the transaction on the Etherum blockchain, but you can mint your NFT on a different blockchain called Polygon to avoid paying gas fees. This option is available on OpenSea and this simply denotes that your NFT will only be able to trade using Polygon's blockchain and not Etherum's blockchain. Mintable allows you to mint NFTs for free without paying any gas fees.

The answer is no. Non-Fungible Tokens are minted on the blockchain using cryptocurrencies such as Etherum, Solana, Polygon, and so on. Once a Non-Fungible Token is minted, the transaction is recorded on the blockchain and the contract or license is awarded to whoever has that Non-Fungible Token in their wallet.

You can sell your work and creations by attaching a license to it on the blockchain, where its ownership can be transferred. This lets you get exposure without losing full ownership of your work. Some of the most successful projects include Cryptopunks, Bored Ape Yatch Club NFTs, SandBox, World of Women and so on. These NFT projects have gained popularity globally and are owned by celebrities and other successful entrepreneurs. #9726. Microsoft Fixes Nearly 1,100 Security Vulnerabilities

Microsoft did another four-digit patch drop today, releasing updates to fix almost 1,100 security vulnerabilities in its Windows operating systems and supported software. This month’s Patch Tuesday addresses 63 critical flaws — including a zero-day in Microsoft Outlook — and comes amid important security updates from other software makers, including Adobe, Apple, Google and Mozilla.

Image: Shutterstock.com. Diorama by @zepp1969.

November’s patch release from Redmond tackles 1,093 vulnerabilities, fixing 63 “critical” flaws that can be exploited to seize control over a Windows system with little or no help from users. Nearly half of those critical bugs are remote code execution vulnerabilities. Overall, 535 of the flaws addressed this month allow an attacker to elevate their privileges on a vulnerable device.

This latest round of updates means Microsoft has shipped more than 5,100 security patches so far this year, a staggering number considering that a year ago Microsoft was averaging around 100 patches per month. Microsoft credits advances in artificial intelligence for helping to find (and fix) such a large volume of security bugs in recent months. Last month, Microsoft pushed more than 1,400 fixes.

According to Redmond, just one of the flaws is already seeing active exploitation: CVE-2026-124194, a spoofing bug in Outlook. The advisory for CVE-2026-124194 says it affects Microsoft 365 Apps for Enterprise and editions of Microsoft Office.

Several other major software makers pushed security updates this week to fix critical weaknesses in their products. Apple on Monday released out-of-cycle security updates to fix at least nine vulnerabilities in iOS/iPadOS, macOS, watchOS and visionOS. Among the weaknesses reportedly fixed in Apple’s release include an iMessage flaw that could let a remote attacker join a group chat and receive its messages; the updates also fix a separate iMessage flaw that could let someone added to a group access messages sent before they joined.

Lee Neely, an instructor at the SANS Institute, noted that Apple backported the fix to iOS 18.

“I take notice when Apple releases fixes to more than two versions,” Neely wrote in a SANS newsletter today. “You really need to get to version 27.2.1 of their OSes and push folks who are holding onto devices which cannot run the current version. The best plan often involves setting an upgrade date for old hardware. Run through all your Apple devices and make sure everything is up to date, don’t assume the fixes went out automatically.”

Google this week released Chrome version 157.0.8103.50, which resolves nine security holes, including CVE-2026-125350, the sixth zero-day vulnerability this year for Chrome (this bug also is being patched in Chromium-based browsers like Edge). The latest Chrome version follows its November 3 release, which fixed 213 vulnerabilities. A new version of Mozilla Firefox out today (Firefox 160) resolves almost 100 CVEs, about half of them high severity.

Adobe today released patches for at least 110 vulnerabilities across a range of products, with nearly half of the flaws rated high severity. Adobe said there is no evidence any of the security holes it addressed this month are being actively exploited.

Chris Goettl, vice president of product management at Ivanti, said it’s easy for security teams at large enterprises to feel overwhelmed by the volume and criticality of patches from Microsoft lately. But he notes that while some 95,000 vulnerabilities have been assigned CVEs this year across all vendors, only 217 have so far this year been added to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) list maintained by the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA).

“Roughly four in ten of this year’s exploited vulnerabilities sit in operating systems, endpoint software, browsers, and server platforms, which a continuous patch strategy can close quickly,” Goettl said.”The rest calls for exposure management alongside patching, especially the 44% that sit in edge devices and IT management or remote access tools, the internet-facing systems that hold privileged access. Teams that can quickly identify those assets, confirm exposure and act on confirmed exploitation can focus on the small slice of vulnerabilities attackers are actively using, while the rest stays on the normal patch cadence.”

Please don’t neglect to back up any important data if you haven’t recently; generally speaking, this is a task best accomplished before applying operating system updates. As ever, if you experience any issues installing this month’s bundle of love from Microsoft, please drop a comment about it in the space below.

#9725. Getting Past the Post-Quantum Cryptography Discovery Phase

News, news analysis, and commentary on the latest trends in cybersecurity technology.

Most organizations haven't sorted out their cryptographic estate enough to even know where they'd start with post-quantum cryptography (PQC).

The pressure is mounting for security leaders to get serious about their post-quantum cryptography (PQC) transition plans, but most organizations aren't even ready to get ready for PQC.

Studies show that, yes, CISOs today do see PQC as a priority they've got to plan for. However, the bulk of organizations don't have a detailed enough cryptographic inventory to help them sketch out a roadmap of where to get started.

"When it comes to post-quantum cryptography, every company, no matter which ones you talk to are kind of stuck in the discovery phase," says Dr. Anurag Swarnim Yadav, founder and CTO of the startup QubitAC.

Recent numbers back up his observations. According to a July study by DigiCert, while 87% of organizations say they're planning, testing, or implementing PQC, only 44% have developed transition plans or created inventories. That mirrors another study by Ponemon Institute that found only 43% of organizations have full visibility of their cryptographic estate. Those respondents reported that their inability to discover those assets and improve that visibility is their number one greatest concern about PQC migration.

Related:Attackers in Binance Breach Targeted Known Weakness, Missing Controls

Cryptography sits in web servers, certificates, VPNs, code signing, vendor products and all nature of assets in between. Getting every encryption use case ready for a post-quantum world will be a sweeping transition, and the latest research suggests developments in quantum computing are proceeding on a much faster timeline than originally anticipated. If an enterprise can't enumerate all the cryptography impacted, it means they're not toeing the start line for this footrace.

Getting all of those assets into post-quantum readiness will be a generational effort easily on par with the Y2K effort. Unlike with Y2K, however, there's no set-in-stone deadline for post-quantum.

The closest thing is Q Day, the point when a cryptographically relevant quantum computer (CRQC) can break the public-key cryptography behind key exchange and digital signatures. The big problem with building a widespread sense of urgency is that nobody knows exactly when Q Day will arrive.

Yadav says estimates for when Q Day will come run from 2030 to 2040 and beyond, but his own bet is that attackers could pull it off by 2029 based how the research is shifting. The expected window until Q Day arrives keeps compressing as quantum researchers perfect their craft. Last year, Google researchers calculated that breaking 2048-bit RSA encryption would take a quantum computer 20 times smaller than they had estimated in 2019. And in March Google set a 2029 target for its own PQC migration, influenced by such research and recent progress in quantum hardware.

Related:Investors Dish on New Startups & What They'd Back Next

Global governments are also starting to get firm about their own timing expectations for PQC transition in the run-up to Q Day. NIST finalized its PQC transition roadmap in late October, and a June executive order requires federal high-value assets and high-impact systems to move key establishment to post-quantum algorithms by 2030 and digital signatures by 2031. The United Kingdom’s National Cyber Security Centre recommends that large organizations complete discovery and assessment and build an initial migration plan by 2028, then finish migrating by 2035.

Even if we don’t know exactly when Q Day will come about, the math behind what will happen after that day is well understood. Public-key cryptography lets two parties who have never met agree on a secret and prove who they are. It works because some math is easy to run forward and impractical to reverse. RSA relies on the difficulty of factoring huge numbers, while elliptic curve cryptography and Diffie-Hellman key exchange rely on a related problem called the discrete logarithm.

Quantum computers use subatomic particles instead of transistors to represent data. This gives them an edge in how they process the ones and zeros of computing. Cryptography experts for years have warned that a sufficiently advanced enough quantum computer could use that edge to factor huge numbers and solve discrete logarithms at a rate of efficiency unheard of from even the most advanced classical super computers.

Related:AI Agents as Insider Threats: Inside Microsoft's Bet on a Unified Security Stack

There's also a more immediate deadline that's brewing from what attackers are likely doing today to prepare for Q Day. It's fairly trivial for the bad guys to vacuum up high-value encrypted traffic today with the promise that they might have a chance to decrypt it at a later date. For long-lived information like financial or health details, or secret sauce intellectual property, the long-game of this harvest now, decrypt later (HNDL) is worth the effort for future-minded criminals.

"The data is worthless to attackers right now, but becomes priceless later," Yadav explains. He offers credit card numbers as a classic example. They stay valid for years, so a cache of encrypted numbers harvested now could still be good if Q Day lands inside that window.

In its recently finalized roadmap, the National Institute of Standards and Technology named HNDL as one of the main reasons the transition is so urgent. NIST mathematician and cryptographic expert Andrew Regenscheid says HNDL reframes the whole PQC timeline for critical information stores across industry and government systems.

"This information may need to remain secret for years, or even decades, into the future," he explained in a NIST Q&A this summer. "For that kind of information, waiting until a cryptographically relevant quantum computer arrives is waiting too long."

Considering that the most isolated cryptographic migrations can still linger for upwards of a decade or longer, even a conservative 2040 estimate for Q Day should be enough to have security experts scrambling to plan PQC transitions. The scale of changes needed will take significant planning and prioritization that will need to be phased in.

"Changing these algorithms is something that’s been done before. It’s a complex process that takes years," Regenscheid said. "Based on our experience and the challenge of navigating the post-quantum world, we expect this process to be the most challenging one yet. The breadth of these systems and the complexity of the change will dwarf what we’ve done before."

The destination, at least, is defined. In 2024, NIST finalized three post-quantum standards, one for key exchange (ML-KEM) and two for digital signatures (ML-DSA and SLH-DSA), built on math that's expected to hold up against quantum computers. The harder job is finding every place RSA and elliptic curve cryptography still run, and planning how and when to swap out each use case. Because of HNDL, NIST suggests the first transition phases should be prioritized around data that is particularly sensitive or has to stay secure for a long time.

In a September study on PQC readiness, Frost & Sullivan analysts emphasized how important risk-based prioritization like this will be for PQC readiness.

"A non-compliant cryptographic asset supporting a low-value application may represent limited immediate risk, while the same technology supporting sensitive information or a critical business process could require urgent remediation," they wrote.

Sorting through all the assets and ranking them depends on having a solid inventory on hand, though. This is why the discovery is so crucial. Frost &Sullivan concurred that the discovery process is proving to be trickier than many thought it would be.

"The inventory needs to extend beyond simply identifying algorithms to understanding the dependencies between cryptographic assets and business-critical applications," they explained.

Tools — commercial and open source — designed to assist organizations in their PQC journey are already available. These tools have their own approaches and have varying levels of maturity. One such tool is AC Scanner, which Yadav and QubitAC co-founder Joseph Wilson demoed at Black Hat Arsenal last August. The free open-source tool is purpose-built to kickstart the inventory process, Yadav says. It's a fast, lightweight tool that runs from command line, scans for outward facing TLS and SSH services, and creates an inventory for the IP range it's pointed at.

"You start with nothing but a domain name and by the end you get a complete cryptographic bill of materials (CBOM)," Yadav says. The CBOM is an inventory of the algorithms, keys, certificates and protocols in use, and the scanner pairs it with two scores, one for overall security health and one for post-quantum readiness based on NIST's post-quantum standards.

It also doubles as an outside check on HNDL exposure. Every encrypted session starts with a key exchange, where the two sides agree on a secret. If a public-facing endpoint still uses a classical exchange, traffic an attacker records today could be unlocked later by a quantum computer. A hybrid exchange that adds post-quantum math protects that traffic, provided the client uses it too, and the scanner reports which kind each endpoint offers.

Classical endpoints are the ones most exposed to HNDL, and Yadav sees AC Scanner as giving organizations a starting point for making HNDL-aware transition plans.

Of course, any security professional will be quick to point out that a scan is just an informational snapshot. It's what happens after that information is in hand that really counts. Scanning tools can kickstart discovery, but organizations need to follow up what they find with a migration plan and start executing on it. NIST’s Regenscheid says the sooner organizations can get to these plans, the better.

"Given how long these transitions take, the organizations that start planning and begin moving to post-quantum products and services now will be in a far stronger position later," he says, stating that this is an opportunity to modernize a lot of the process. "Many steps must occur in sequence, which is why an early start is crucial."

An award-winning freelance reporter with nearly two decades of experience covering B2B cybersecurity, Ericka Chickowski has tackled every angle of security and risk for Dark Reading since 2009. Her coverage has spanned the full range of cyber topics important to every kind of cybersecurity stakeholder, including cybersecurity practitioners, CISOs, security-minded business managers, and security-aware board directors. She specializes in going deep on topics, breaking down how the technology trends affect real people, and how risk impacts the bottom line.

Some special areas of focus include: adversarial AI; AI risk and resilience; AI and agentic governance; application security (AppSec); governance, risk, and compliance (GRC); cloud security; network security; software supply chain risk; cyberinsurance; DevSecOps; enterprise risk management; and CISO career development.

In addition to Dark Reading, Ericka has written for many different IT and business publications over the years. This helps inform her stories on software risks and business resilience.

Ericka is also a prolific executive ghost writer, with experience helping cybersecurity and IT leaders bring their ideas to life. She's helped them craft important position pieces for respected publications like the Financial Times and The Wall Street Journal.

Prior to beginning her freelance career, Ericka served in a number of editorial staff roles, including West Coast Bureau Chief for SC Magazine. Before that position, she was editor-in-chief for a cluster of regional technology and lifestyle magazines in the Seattle area, as well as a beat reporter for a regional business newspaper. She holds a bachelor's degree in English from the University of Washington. Her work is well-regarded and has won multiple awards from the Society of Professional Journalists.

#9724. Palette: teaching a small model to build decks in your design language

Ask a frontier model for a slide deck and you'll get a good one. Ask for ten and they start to look alike: the same tasteful defaults, the same house style, a faint "AI-generated deck" look. That's fine until you want the deck to look like your template. Frontier models have their own house style, and no amount of prompting stops them drifting back to it. And sometimes the content is confidential and can't leave your systems at all.

Both of those point to a model you own: open weights, running on your own infrastructure, trained on your own design language. The catch is that small open models, the kind you'd actually self-host, are bad at this. Their decks come out broken: titles that vanish into the background, text running off the slide, shapes stacked on top of each other.

Palette tests one bet: that a small open-weight model, trained on synthetic data in your design language and checked by a harness, can compete with frontier systems while you keep ownership of the result. We fine-tuned a 20B model to build decks the way people do: a designer plans the deck and a coder draws each slide. Its training data follows the IBM Design Language, and on PresentBench it ranks first on two of the three domains we measured. This post covers how we synthesized the data, trained the model and built a harness around it.

A slide deck looks simple, but making one asks a model to do three things small models are bad at.

It lays out the slide without seeing it. The model doesn't draw slides; it writes code that places every element at an x, y, width and font size. Whether a 75-character title fits on two lines at 56pt is arithmetic the model does in its head, and it only finds out it was wrong after the code renders. Small models get this wrong often, which is where overlapping shapes and text running off the slide come from.

It makes two kinds of decisions at once. Deciding what each slide says and how to show it (a chart or a table? what to cut?) is editorial judgment. Placing it precisely is geometry. A single pass has to do both across 10–20 slides, while keeping the palette, type and layout consistent.

There's no data showing how decks get made. Plenty of finished decks exist, but not the rationale behind the design choices or the code that produced them.

Nobody makes a deck in one pass. You decide the story first (how many slides, what each one says, which gets a chart and which gets a table) and only then build each slide. Palette splits the work the same way, into two roles served by a single LoRA adapter:

Each role now makes one kind of decision: the designer handles the editorial judgment, and the coder handles the geometry. The brief between them is readable and editable, so a person or an agent can change one slide's layout without regenerating the deck. And because every slide's context is fixed before any code is written, the coder calls run in parallel, one per slide, which makes the coding stage about 6–7× faster.

We trained the adapter with LoRA rather than full fine-tuning: it teaches a format and a skill on top of a capable base without disturbing what the base already knows, and it made each experiment cheap. One lesson: coder examples are about 5× longer than designer examples, so a naive mix undertrained the designer until we oversampled its examples 5×.

There's no public corpus of plans, design decisions and slide code, so we generated one with a large open teacher. Each deck starts from a recipe that sets its genre, length, layouts and any user directives, so we control what the data covers. Plans range from tidy outlines to raw content dumps, so the model learns to cut and condense. We generated around 1000 decks covering roughly 10,000 slides.

Every example also carries the reasoning behind it, written as a counterfactual: the trace weighs an alternative and says why it was rejected, so the model learns the rule behind a choice, not just the choice. The designer reasons about content and form. For example:

"Revenue for four quarters, with one clear upward trend. I considered a table, but the point of this slide is the trend, not the exact figures, so a bar chart makes it visible at a glance."

"The title is 62 characters. At 44pt it would wrap to three lines and run into the chart below, so I set it at 36pt, which fits on two lines and leaves room above the chart."

The teacher alone doesn't make the data good; the loop around it does. Every synthesized deck is rendered and checked for overlaps and overflow by the same checker the harness uses at inference. Broken slides are repaired, and their reasoning is rewritten as the same kind of counterfactual, covering what the original layout got wrong and why the fix works. Each mistake the checker catches becomes a better training example.

The hardest problem was faithfulness. The worst failure is a slide with facts that weren't in the input, and we found that a prompt rule can't prevent it. If a brief asks for a six-by-five table but carries only three bullets, the coder has to invent the rest.

What fixed it was reference decks, not the rules: fixing a reference reliably changed the teacher's output, while adding a rule rarely did. The teacher sees a few reference decks in its prompt and copies them far more than it follows instructions.

Users often want finer-grained control over specific design choices: a chart instead of a table, a particular color, a darker cover. Palette lets them ask for these with directives, short instructions written directly in the plan and wrapped in [[ ]]:

The designer builds each directive into the brief, and the coder follows it when drawing the slide. Without the directive, the model would reasonably show these milestones as a table; with it, the model draws a timeline instead.

The model follows directives because it was trained to. The data recipes include directives from 12 categories, a few of which are shown below, each phrased several different ways, so the model learns the intent rather than a fixed phrase.

Figure 1. An illustration of the same plan without (left) and with (right) the [[make this a timeline]] directive.

Even a well-trained model sometimes produces a broken slide: a title in the same color as the background, or two boxes stacked on top of each other. So Palette doesn't return the model's output directly; every deck goes through a harness first.

Figure 2. The designer drafts the brief, the coder writes each slide's code in parallel, and the harness checks and repairs every slide before the deck is returned.

First, simple rules fix known mistakes, such as a malformed color code that would otherwise turn every slide black. Then each slide is rendered and measured: a geometry checker flags text that overlaps, gets clipped or runs off the slide. Flagged slides go to a separate editor model, which rewrites that slide's code.

The key rule is that a rewrite is kept only if the checker confirms the slide improved; otherwise the original stays. That makes the harness safe to run on every deck. It can fix a slide, but it can't make one worse.

Figure 3. An illustration of a repair. As generated (left), each card's title is stacked on top of its description; the harness detects the overlaps and reflows the cards into a 2×2 grid (right).

To measure its effect, we generated each PresentBench deck once and scored it with and without the harness. Across 131 decks, the harness adds 3.5 points on average.

We evaluate on PresentBench, which scores generated decks on five criteria: fundamentals, visual design, completeness, correctness and fidelity. PresentBench provides a source document rather than a plan, so for these runs a separate frontier model drafted each plan from its document, and Palette built the deck from that plan. We report three domains; baseline numbers are from the PresentBench paper.

Figure 4. PresentBench scores by domain. Palette (blue) against NotebookLM, Manus 1.6 and five other systems (gray). Palette ranks first on Economics and Education, third on Talk, and second on the three-domain mean.

Palette does best where structured content and numeric accuracy decide the score, ranking first on Economics and Education. On Talk, where decks are narrative and speech-driven, two closed systems score higher and Palette places third. Across the three domains it places second, 1.1 points behind NotebookLM (59.7 vs 60.8) and ahead of the rest of the field, as a single 20B open-weight model.

PresentBench measures whether a deck is good, but not whether it follows a specific design language. We're not aware of a benchmark that does, and it's a gap we hope to help close.

The harness already computes cheap, verifiable signals: does the slide render, does anything overlap or overflow, does every fact trace back to the brief. Today we use them to repair output after generation. Next, we want to use the same checks as rewards for reinforcement learning, so the model stops making these mistakes in the first place. Because the coder works one slide at a time, each slide is a short, independently checkable rollout, a natural fit for GRPO-style training.

We also want to close the gap on figure-heavy decks by extracting figures from source documents (e.g. with Docling) and placing them with the harness. And we're exploring a lighter way to bring your own templates: re-skinning output from one or two of your existing .pptx files, without retraining.

Building Palette taught us a few effective methods that extend naturally to other tasks whose output has a structure you can check in code, from charts and diagrams to UI layouts:

#9721. Attackers in Binance Breach Targeted Known Weakness, Missing Controls

News, news analysis, and commentary on the latest trends in cybersecurity technology.

Blockchain complexities, such as attacker-deployed sweepers, hobble security controls designed to limit the damage of an exchange compromise.

On Oct. 29, cyber thieves transferred around $6.34 billion in various cryptocurrencies from at least 11 wallets owned by exchange Binance to attacker-controlled addresses. Binance seemingly had not put in place security controls to quickly detect malicious authorizations and disable them through a pretested kill switch, experts say — which should put other crypto firms on notice.

While Binance's internal security systems issued an alert in minutes, the attackers exploited a feature of Ethereum smart accounts — a relatively new type of account abstraction introduced to Ethereum with the EIP-7702 proposal in 2025 — to essentially install malicious code, known as a "sweeper." The sweeper code transferred all the funds held in a primary treasury wallet at Binance — consisting of more than five dozen cryptocurrencies totaling approximately $2.5 billion — to the attacker's address created minutes before.

Related:Getting Past the Post-Quantum Cryptography Discovery Phase

In the end, the wallet was left with a single ETH coin, according to an analysis by blockchain security firm BlockAid.

Large transactions from other wallets to the same address, initiated by the attackers, triggered internal alerts at Binance. The company took countermeasures, but the smart-account authorization continued to function for about four hours, siphoning additional funds.

"An EIP-7702 authorization [is] a standing delegation," says Ido Ben-Natan, co-founder and CEO of BlockAid. "Once it is on-chain, attacker-controlled code can move that hot wallet's funds, and anything later deposited to it, until the same wallet ... [revokes the authorization]. It carries no amount and no destination, so withdrawal controls never see it."

Despite a sweeper function enabled through EIP-7702 authorization being a known threat, Binance noted in a Nov. 3 post-mortem report that the authorization hobbled the companies efforts to stop transactions from flowing out onto the blockchain.

"Once established, these authorizations enabled the attackers to continue moving assets independently of Binance's normal withdrawal infrastructure," the company stated in a post-mortem report. "Binance needed additional transactions to revoke these on-chain authorizations ... suspending withdrawals and shutting down hot wallet services did not automatically invalidate existing on-chain authorizations."

Developers were the initial weak point, enabling the EIP-7702 authorization attack to occur. One developer downloaded a compromised version of Homebrew, an open source package management tool for Macs, while a second developer fell for a fake job interview, during which they were given a software "assignment" that compromised his system, according to Binance's post-mortem.

Related:Investors Dish on New Startups & What They'd Back Next

In the end, the attackers used their compromise of the two developers' systems — as well as a third developer's system — to gain signing privileges, creating 50 presigned authorizations to flood the targeted wallet, known among blockchain analysts as "Binance 14," at the right time.

The same targeting of developers happened during the ByBit Ethereum heist on Feb. 21, 2025, says Avi Sambira, vice president of North America at incident-response firm Sygnia. In that case, cyber thieves compromised the Mac of a Safe{Wallet} developer nearly three weeks before the actual theft, according to Sygnia's analysis of that incident. Safe{Wallet} is used by Ethereum and other decentralized autonomous organizations (DAOs) to enforce multisignature security.

"[A]n AWS token was used and attackers operated inside Safe{Wallet}'s cloud environment for roughly two weeks before modifying the signing interface," Sambira says. "Binance's disclosure appears consistent with the same model, with initial reporting indicating endpoint and internal-tool compromise preceded credential, token, and[/or] container access to wallet signing."

Related:AI Agents as Insider Threats: Inside Microsoft's Bet on a Unified Security Stack

Like that incident, the FBI placed blame directly on North Korean cybercriminal operators, releasing a list of more than 600 Ethereum addresses, 19 Bitcoin addresses, and 1 SOL address linked to TraderTraitor, a moniker for the group behind the attacks.

Exchanges and crypto-finance firms need to treat their developers, vendors, and suppliers as critical elements of their infrastructure. Attackers are increasingly looking to compromise developer identities, repositories, CI/CD pipelines, cloud control planes, and third-party integrations, Sambira says. Those assets sit only one or two trust boundaries away from withdrawal authority.

"TraderTraitor's evolution is less about abandoning old techniques than combining them into a more sophisticated trust attack," he says. "Fake recruiters and malicious coding assignments establish the foothold, [while] stolen sessions, cloud credentials, and trusted interfaces turn that foothold into transaction control."

When the cyberattackers used their pregenerated authorizations, they sent 50 at the same time because every transaction needs a valid nonce — a sequential counter — so the attackers used a window of 50 authorizations and needed only a single one to match.

The nonce spray to install a malicious sweeper is a new, but known, threat. In a paper presented at the USENIX Security conference in August, researchers from Hong Kong University of Science and Technology and two other Chinese schools revealed that at least 924 malicious smart contracts had been enabled through the EIP-7702 mechanism, leading to at least $2.3 million in losses.

In its own research, BlockAid saw at least $1.1 million in losses across four instances. It predicted that the first 10-figure attack would arrive before the end of 2026. The firm was off by a factor of 100.

The attacks can be stopped — or at least blunted — by a combination of controls. Any company processing cryptocurrency transactions in real time should use simulations to detect malicious rules, enforce policies on the allowed size of transactions and their destinations, issue alerts based on detecting a burst of large transactions, and deploy a fast kill switch that has been prebuilt to pause signing and stop wallet refills, says BlockAid's Ben-Natan.

Binance seemingly had none — or only some — of those controls in place. In the end, it took nearly four hours — the attack started at 20:05 UTC and the last transaction was recorded at 23:56 UTC — for the company to stop transactions from being recorded on the blockchain, subsequently freezing and recovering about $2.85 billion in attempted stolen assets. The company did not respond to requests for comment.

Binance highlights the importance of having good monitoring and the ability to detect anomalous transactions.

The difficulty in responding to the attacks underscores the problems that cryptocurrency exchanges and infrastructure firms face to combat theft and fraud. In many ways, Binance had created an overlapping set of controls to detect attacks and block transfers in near real time. However, the state-sponsored attackers found a way to bypass those controls through the EIP-7702 sweeper.

The pressure on cryptocurrency firms will only rise because attackers can exfiltrate the funds quickly, says Ari Redbord, global head of policy at TRM Labs and a former federal prosecutor and US Treasury official.

"For years we've seen hacks against large financial institutions, tech companies, and even government agencies — the difference is that in crypto you can steal funds in real time," he says. "There's no clawback window, and the money is gone in minutes."

Crypto-finance firms need to have visibility across four domains: identity and authority governance, infrastructure and execution integrity, custody and transaction authorization, and on- and off-chain detection, says Sygnia's Sambira. Companies that only monitor transactions on the blockchain are seeing changes too late, he adds.

In addition, crypto firms should rigorously track all identities and systems that can initiate, approve, modify, or execute transactions and be ready to suspend those accounts' privileges, he says.

"Controls with the greatest containment value involve the preauthorized ability to revoke identities and tokens, pause transfers, isolate wallets, and rebuild affected infrastructure within minutes," Sambira says. "Those capabilities must be tested before a crisis hits and retested regularly."

Testing and practicing these controls are critical because companies need to know that they will work in real time, says TRM Labs' Redbord.

"The actionable part for any company touching crypto is that these patterns are recognizable. If you watch in real time, you can act in the first moments, when it matters most," he says. "This is all about speed."

Monitoring transactions can detect suspicious activity quite quickly and, in the case of the cryptocurrency thefts targeting Binance and ByBit, can stop attacks before too much value is lost. The keys to adequate responses are speed and relationships to the various stakeholders, says Redbord.

"Issuers like Tether and Circle can freeze the addresses holding stolen tokens and then burn those tokens and reissue the same amount to the rightful owner," he says. "The funds don't have to be chased down. They can be made whole on-chain."

Nearly all issuers, exchanges, blockchain intelligence firms, and many global law enforcement agencies are part of the Beacon Network, created by TRM Labs and other industry players, for early detection of and intelligence sharing about cryptocurrency incidents. In addition, cryptocurrency-reliant businesses should ensure that any exchange with which they do business has withdrawal limits and allowlists, isolates their signing systems on computers reserved for that purpose, and constantly trains their engineers against social engineering, Redbord says.

Organizations should also reduce measures of time to detect, time to contain, and time to freeze to seconds. The approval of major transactions should require multiple signatures from systems that are used for only that purpose, and businesses need to have a response plan that keeps them operational while they recover.

Binance has taken some of these steps, including identifying the affected systems, cleaning or replacing them, and replacing wallets, it stated in its initial incident report. It has also completed "enhanced" security scans across employee devices, rotated credentials, and deployed enhanced AI-based behavioral anomaly detection, the company stated.

"There are a number of security measures we have implemented and are implementing that will remain private to prevent malicious actors from compromising our security," the company stated.

#9720. Dharma Field Extractor: Any Document In, Structured Fields in JSON Out

A 2-billion-parameter model that extracts exactly the fields you ask for, from any document type, outperforming every frontier LLM we tested, at a fraction of the cost.

In April, we released DharmaOCR-LITE, a model specialized for OCR across a wide range of documents, from contracts and court filings to invoices, IDs and forms. The paper behind it made a narrow, well-measured case for domain specialization: a smaller model trained closer to its task beating general-purpose frontier APIs on that task.

OCR gives you the text on a page, faithful to the original formatting. That's exactly what you want when the job is the whole document, like a contract you'll read end to end or a manuscript you're digitizing.

However, there's a different use case: you don't want the page, you want specific fields out of it, in a shape a system downstream can consume. Every line item on an invoice, as a list. The patient name, exam type and date from a medical requisition, ready to schedule. The fields off an ID, mapped to the columns of an employee record.

Run that document through OCR and you get back everything printed on it, line by line, with no indication of which string is the exam type, which is the date or which number is the total. Someone still has to write the code that maps each value to the right field before it reaches the database.

A general-purpose LLM can do this work today, with careful prompting. At frontier API pricing and latency, on a task many businesses need to run at high volume, that quickly becomes the expensive way to solve a well-defined problem.

So we built a model for it instead. The Field Extractor takes a document image and either a request for everything it can find, or an exact schema to fill, and returns structured JSON: typed, field by field, nested where the document nests. An invoice comes back with every line item as an ordered list, each with its own quantity and value, alongside the totals. An ID comes back as the fields you'll store, under the names your system already uses for them. The same checkpoint handles all of it, with no per-type fine-tuning.

Say a batch of supplier invoices lands every morning, and you need four things off each one to push into your system: the supplier, the invoice number, the due date, the total. Same story for medical requisitions going into a scheduler, or contracts feeding a compliance system, where what matters is the parties, the term, the penalties and the fine amounts. You don't need the page, you need certain fields. With the Field Extractor there are two ways to ask for them:

The choice comes down to what you already know. Send an open request when you don't know what the document holds. Send a schema when the output has to match a shape that already exists somewhere else.

Either way, what comes back is JSON: the fields as keys, the values typed as requested, and null where the document didn't have what you asked for. When you send a schema, the output follows it exactly, with the same keys and no extra fields, so it can go straight into the next system.

The base model is DharmaOCR-LITE v1.1, a new 2-billion-parameter version optimized from the one in the paper and already specialized for OCR through supervised fine-tuning and DPO. On top of that checkpoint we trained a LoRA adapter on 43,384 training examples covering both request modes.

The data is organized into three streams:

All three streams are annotated at the field level. The mix is deliberately multi-domain: receipts, commercial invoices, forms, bank statements, ID documents and synthetic documents, rather than one filing type.

The full benchmark covers 546 documents across three request scenarios, for 1,638 total cases: extracting every field with no schema, a partial schema naming only real fields, and a schema that also includes deliberately nonexistent fields. The score is field-level F1 (matched by path, including position inside a table), multiplied by the Levenshtein similarity on the values that matched and by the share of outputs that come back as valid JSON.

We ran the same benchmark against four general-purpose frontier configurations.

Against general-purpose LLMs, the quality gap runs from 1.8 points (Claude Opus 5, the closest) to 9.3 points (GPT-5.6 Luna, the widest).

Cost runs from roughly 6 times lower (GPT-5.6 Luna) to roughly 147 times lower (GPT-5.6 Sol). The two sides are priced differently. The frontier figures come from measured average input and output tokens per page, reasoning tokens included, against each provider's published list pricing. Every frontier model ran with reasoning set to low; Claude Opus 5 used adaptive effort, which can skip reasoning on simpler pages while staying at the low level. Ours isn't billed per token: the model runs self-hosted, so the figure is GPU time on a single L40S at $2.24 per hour.

This is not a sales price. Self-hosted cost depends on the hardware, the volume and the latency each deployment needs. The comparison is here to show that a sovereign SSLM, deployed on your own infrastructure, is a real alternative to frontier APIs.

SROIE and FUNSD are two public datasets in our benchmark, not used in training. Below is one example from each.

On a SROIE receipt, we asked for all 18 fields printed on it, with no phantom fields this time, and every one comes back correct: the multi-line, unlabeled billing address captured as a single field, the two blank fields (salesperson and ref) correctly returned as null, and every number on the receipt matching to the cent.

On a FUNSD photocopying variance form, a checklist of twelve boolean fields with one nested group of five sub-options, the model marks exactly the one box that's checked (poor quality original, with a handwritten "faded" note beside it) as true, and the other eleven as false, matching the form exactly. It also reads the handwritten Bates ID off the page correctly, and returns null for the two fields left blank.

A 2-billion-parameter model scored 0.834, above every frontier configuration we tested, from Claude Opus 5 at 0.816 to GPT-5.6 Luna at 0.741, while running on a single L40S at a lower cost per extraction than every API in the comparison. Higher quality and lower cost, measured on the same benchmark, in the same run.

This isn't the first time we've measured it. Our OCR paper put the first DharmaOCR-LITE, a 3-billion-parameter model, above every commercial frontier API tested on Brazilian Portuguese; three months later, newer and better-resourced models arrived, and the gap held. Now a 2-billion-parameter model does it on field extraction. Each result adds evidence for the thesis we started Dharma-AI with: on a bounded task, a small model trained close to that task beats a frontier model asked to do the same thing in general. In this benchmark, it also cost 6 to 147 times less to run.

Parameter count sets the ceiling; training decides how much of it a model reaches on your task. Your business doesn't need the biggest model available. It needs one trained for your problem.

Try it on your own documents here. To learn more about Dharma-AI and the specialized models we build, visit dharma-ai.com.

#9719. ArcticRAT Cybercrime Gang Profiles Victim Finances With AI

The Android malware has expanded from focusing on crypto theft to full device control, and the attackers have added advanced analysis of stolen information.

Android cryptocurrency stealer ArcticRAT has evolved into a sophisticated remote access Trojan (RAT) capable of taking control of victim devices, harvesting sensitive information, and using AI to identify valuable financial data.

Researchers at Zimperium who are tracking the malware described it as representing a "dangerous escalation" in the mobile threat landscape. The newer versions, according to the vendor, give attackers the ability to interact with infected devices in real time, rather than relying purely on hardcoded actions.

The malware uses multiple techniques, including a "completely black, un-dismissible" screen overlay to conceal attacker activities from victims. Most significantly, the operators of ArcticRAT are now using large language model (LLM) services to automatically sift through stolen text messages and other data from infected device for financial information worth exploiting.

Related:APT29's Watering Holes Target Thousands of Mobile Users

"ArcticRAT uses AI to read through user information such as SMS messages to filter for financial information that could be used perform fraud," Nico Chiaraviglio, chief scientist at Zimperium, tells Dark Reading. "One particularly challenging technique is hidden remote control combined with a black-screen overlay. Attackers abuse legitimate Android features while making the device appear locked or powered off."

Defending against threats like ArcticRAT requires organizations to deploy AI-powered, on-device threat detection, enforce controls over application installation and permissions, and use runtime application protection to identify suspicious screen-sharing activity and malicious overlays, he adds.

Early versions of ArcticRAT targeted users of 11 specific cryptocurrency applications. Its primary purpose was to harvest sensitive information from infected Android devices that attackers could use to gain access to victims' cryptocurrency accounts.

In contrast, the newer versions that Zimperium is tracking pack considerably more capabilities. These include remote device control and surveillance, credential and keystroke theft, screen capture, live screen streaming, microphone monitoring, and the theft of SMS messages, contacts, and call logs. Another feature allows attackers to steal or change device lock-screen credentials, potentially locking victims out of their devices.

Since July, Zimperium analysts have identified 78 unique malware samples, 42 dropper samples, 36 payloads, and 21 IP addresses that the malware operators have been using for command-and-control communications. The researchers also identified 129 distinct commands that attackers can use to remotely control infected devices, steal information, monitor user activity, and manipulate device functions.

Related:Indonesia Hit by Android Banking App-Cloning Campaign

The operators of ArcticRAT 2.0 are using malvertising, smishing, and third-party forums to direct visitors to malicious websites in which the malware is embedded, "The primary attack vector," according to Zimperium, "relied on a landing page that convincingly impersonated Google Play to trick targets into downloading a malicious application." In some instances, the researchers observed the attackers using Amazon Web Services storage buckets to deliver the payload directly on Android devices.

Once installed, the latest version of ArcticRAT — like prior versions — abuses Android Accessibility Services permissions to connect with its command-and-control (C2) servers, giving attackers remote control over the device. The malware first collects information about the compromised device, including its location, battery status, screen state, Wi-Fi connectivity, and currently active applications.

It sends the information to the cyberattackers, who can then select which functions to activate based on the victim's device and installed applications. This can include actions as varied as capturing keystrokes, taking screenshots, recording screen activity, monitoring microphone audio and extracting sensitive information from messages and applications.

Related:ToxicPanda Banking Trojan Matures Into Enterprise Threat

One of the more significant additions to ArcticRAT is its use of artificial intelligence to analyze information stolen from compromised devices and identify data of potential financial value. Zimperium found the malware featuring an API connection to xAI's Grok model, which attackers can activate remotely to examine the victim's installed applications and identify banking, cryptocurrency, and trading platforms.

The new AI capabilities allow ArcticRAT to process stolen SMS messages, separate routine communications and promotional messages from information such as one-time authentication codes, account balance changes, and transaction notifications. It can even estimate a victim's financial standing before sending the information to its command-and-control infrastructure, according to Zimperium.

This allows attackers to automate much of the work involved in sorting through large volumes of stolen information and identifying potentially valuable financial intelligence, rather than having to manually examine the data themselves, according to the firm. "As mobile Trojan threats like ArcticRAT become increasingly sophisticated, conventional signature-based security layers are no longer sufficient to protect enterprise mobile endpoints."

ArcticRAT's transformation from a targeted cryptocurrency stealer into a sophisticated RAT is an example of how quickly mobile threats are evolving, with attackers using AI to make their malware more capable and dangerous. Analysts have noted how the trend underscores the need for users and organizations to stop treating their mobile devices as secondary security concerns and instead apply the same level of threat monitoring, access controls and security protections as they do to traditional endpoints.

Illinois-based Jai Vijayan is a veteran, award-winning technology journalist with more than 25 years of experience covering cybersecurity. His information security reporting has explored everything from ransomware, nation-state threats, and identity security to AI risk, critical infrastructure protection, software supply chain security, cloud security and emerging enterprise technologies.

Over the course of his career, Jai has written news stories, feature articles, survey reports, white papers, and e-books for enterprise and technology audiences. He has also moderated panel discussions and executive roundtables featuring CISOs, security researchers, and industry leaders.

His work has earned multiple industry honors, including a Joint ASBPE Excellence Award for Best Coverage of Government IT, and a Joint Jesse H. Neal Award for wireless LAN security coverage. Jai holds a Master’s degree in statistics from Bangalore University, and studied broadcasting and electronic communication at Marquette University in Milwaukee.

#9718. AARO Solved Iraq's 'Jellyfish' as Balloons. Alaska's Jellyfish UFO Still Lacks the Data

Anomaly Detected. Anomaly Detected. Anomaly Detected. Anomaly Detected. Anomaly Detected. Anomaly Detected. Anomaly Detection.

Anomaly Detected. Anomaly Detected. Anomaly Detected. Anomaly Detected. Anomaly Detected. Anomaly Detected. Anomaly Detection.

Anomaly Detected. Anomaly Detected. Anomaly Detected. Anomaly Detected. Anomaly Detected. Anomaly Detected. Anomaly Detection.

Feature image: still from Sara Jane Osborn's June 15, 2026 recording in Anchorage, Alaska. Credit: Sara Jane Osborn, via GadgetReview (original image).

A June sighting in Anchorage went viral in November. Two witnesses, one camera, a rainbow, a military base somewhere behind the treeline, and far more questions than verified answers.

At about 10:13 p.m. Alaska Daylight Time on June 15, 2026, Sara Jane Osborn was photographing a rainbow from a car on Sixth Avenue in Anchorage when she noticed a dark, black-and-silver shape above the trees. Her husband, Pete, pulled into an empty downtown parking lot so she could shoot unobstructed. Osborn described dangling appendages that seemed to move independently as the shape turned side to side, and said it was visible for roughly three minutes before it "disappeared almost as quickly as it came," according to IBTimes UK, which drew on a November 10 Daily Mail interview.

The couple then searched a nearby park for a kite flyer and drove toward Arctic Valley, looking for about 30 minutes without finding an operator or another witness. That fruitless search is part of their testimony. It is not proof that a kite was impossible. Asked who knows what she saw, Osborn offered: "Only God and the government." She also allowed, "maybe it's a drone-type thing."

Two eyewitnesses are named: Sara Jane and Pete Osborn. Only Sara Jane is credited as the camera operator. Coverage that says the couple "captured" the object does not establish two independently operated cameras.

The defensible public count as of November 12: one witness, one phone, several still photos taken in quick succession, followed by one video, per IBTimes UK. No outlet we reviewed published the video's length or the total number of stills. The clips circulating on X and Instagram, including an X post by Mario Nawfal and a screengrab WION credits to X user @digijordan, appear to be reposts, crops or excerpts of the same encounter. Counting reposts as independent sightings would be misleading.

No verified second-angle recording was located. Nor was an original uncompressed file, complete EXIF metadata, camera specifications, verified geolocation or an authenticated radar track. WION says plainly that it "cannot independently verify the authenticity" of the footage.

Tech editor's note: five months between capture and publication is a long time for a file to travel through messaging apps and social platforms, each of which strips metadata and recompresses video. Provenance standards like C2PA can, in principle, ride along with a file, but provenance metadata is only useful if it survives, and as Paul Krause argues on HackerNoon, records attached to a file can simply be stripped. The single most valuable artifact in this story is still the original file on Osborn's phone.

The couple believed the object sat toward Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson (JBER). Pete estimated it was within about three miles. IBTimes UK notes that neither the distance nor any link to the base or military airspace has been verified. An object visually aligned with military land may be much closer to the camera. Without a reliable range, azimuth and camera position, no one can say whether it entered restricted airspace.

The published still adds a useful constraint. In the frame, the object hangs in front of a sunlit, forested mountainside, not against open sky (see the feature image). Whatever it was, it was nearer to the camera than that slope. That fits a modest-range object at least as well as a giant distant one.

JBER is large. A U.S. Air Force installation document puts it at about 73,157 acres, including roughly 13,375 acres on the Elmendorf side, while an Alaska environmental record rounds the installation to 74,000 acres. Neither figure tells us how much of the actual sightline crossed military land.

Construction at Elmendorf Field began June 8, 1940, and Elmendorf and Fort Richardson were consolidated as JBER in October 2010. The land has a far longer history of Indigenous presence; the base points readers to a cultural-resource history and story map. JBER hosts F-22 Raptor operations, as IBTimes UK notes, but the sighting has no demonstrated connection to any mission.

"10:13 p.m." sounds like night. In Anchorage in mid-June, it isn't. Sunset that week falls around 11:39 p.m. at an azimuth of about 328 degrees, and civil twilight runs all night. Using the standard NOAA solar-position approximation, we estimate the sun sat roughly 6 degrees above the horizon in the northwest at the time of the sighting.

Two things follow. First, a rainbow always forms opposite the sun, so Osborn was facing generally east to southeast, toward the Chugach front range, which is consistent with a sightline toward the eastern reaches of JBER and Arctic Valley. Second, a low sun behind the camera front-lights everything in view. That helps explain a "silver" sheen on a dark object. Reflective fabric, foil or Mylar would flash brightly in exactly that light.

It also rules out one famous lookalike. A "space jellyfish" is a rocket exhaust plume lit by the sun high above a ground observer who is in twilight darkness. Osborn was standing in daylight, and the object was in front of a mountainside, not 100 miles up.

Visually, yes, at a descriptive level. A domed upper mass with thin dangling projections evokes a jellyfish drifting through water, and the resemblance strengthens when the appendages flex and the body rotates. But resemblance is not taxonomy. Helium decorations, show kites, balloon bundles, fabric, debris and compression artifacts can all produce organic silhouettes.

Real jellyfish move by contracting a bell to push water. The Anchorage object has not been shown to pulse in a matching locomotion cycle, and the available clips do not establish its speed, altitude or any controlled acceleration. "It looked alive" is a witness impression, not a biological or aerospace finding.

Kite or line laundry. Long fabric streamers and wind-driven rotation fit the silhouette. Inflatable octopus and jellyfish show kites are commercial products, sold in sizes like an 8-meter octopus. A visible tether, an identified operator or a weather-consistent trajectory would strengthen the case. Note that under the FAA's Part 101 rules, kites flown high or near an airport require notice to air traffic control, and Anchorage has several airports, including JBER and Merrill Field. The couple's failure to find a flyer does not eliminate the explanation, and Osborn's own reasoning ("why would you only fly it for, like, three minutes?") is a fair question rather than evidence.

Balloon cluster or novelty balloon. A buoyant object can drift and rotate while ribbons swing on their own. Close-ups showing seams or strings, or a reconstruction against wind data, would test it. This is the explanation that resolved the most famous previous "jellyfish" (see below).

Drone carrying material. Mechanically possible, but there is no evidence of a drone, operator, motor noise or flight record. Since March 2024, the FAA has fully enforced its Remote ID rule, which requires most drones to broadcast identification and location. A compliant drone would have been detectable by any nearby receiver at the time; no one has reported such a capture.

Digital manipulation or AI generation. Possible in principle, but no forensic analysis of the original file has been published either way. As HackerNoon contributor Matthew of Technology News Australia observes, despite ubiquitous cameras no one has produced one clear, independently verified photograph of an alien craft. Blurry phone footage keeps both the believers' and skeptics' cases unfalsifiable.

Perspective and apparent size. The couple recalled an aircraft that looked much smaller than the object. That comparison cannot establish size unless both distances are known. The Pentagon's AARO paper on forced perspective and parallax explains why apparently huge or fast objects routinely mislead observers.

As of November 12, no aerospace engineer, meteorologist, imaging-forensics specialist or AARO investigator has publicly authenticated or solved this recording. Claims of expert confirmation should be treated with caution. IBTimes UK states explicitly that the object's identity, location and link to the base remain unverified.

The base rate is worth knowing. AARO's FY2025 annual report, summarized by New Space Economy, counted 319 new reports. Of the 114 incoming cases it closed, 60 were balloons and 44 were satellites. The Pentagon's 2024 historical UAP review found no verified evidence of extraterrestrial technology and noted that many unresolved cases simply lack adequate data. Neither is a determination about this video.

Conversely, speculation about "sentient plasmoids" and nonhuman intelligence, aired in a Post Disclosure World episode summarized by UAPDrop, is conjecture, not evidence that the Alaska object was alive or alien.

Al Taqaddum Air Base, Iraq, October 23, 2017. The infrared "jellyfish UAP" that Jeremy Corbell released in January 2024 was filmed from a force-protection aerostat over the base. In September 2025, AARO assessed with high confidence that it was a cluster of fully and partially inflated balloons drifting with the wind at roughly 4 to 14 mph and 850 to 2,200 feet, with no heat signature from motors. It is a separate case with a different sensor and does not corroborate Anchorage, but it is the closest precedent: dangling strings, apparent shape-shifting and a military backdrop, all resolved as balloons once the full footage and geometry were analyzed. The Metabunk forum thread documents how independent analysts reached the same answer.

Stroud area, England, February 10, 1989. Drivers near the A46 reported a jellyfish-like aerial object, according to a recap citing the Swindon Star's front page. The account rests on old newspaper reports, with no comparable imagery.

Fresno area, California, April 2023. A tentacled object drew comparisons to sci-fi creatures until zoomed footage showed strings consistent with a novelty kite, per the same recap. A useful cautionary counterexample, not a debunking of Anchorage.

The useful next steps are concrete: obtain Osborn's original phone files and full photo burst; check capture timestamps and GPS metadata; pin down the exact Sixth Avenue and parking-lot positions; reconstruct the rainbow and mountain sightlines (the solar geometry above is a start); identify the lens focal length; pull wind profiles at several altitudes; check FAA records, Part 101 kite notices and any Remote ID logs; request a JBER public-affairs response; and look for other cameras pointed east that evening.

The open question is not whether the silhouette is strange. It is. The questions are whether the object was near or far, how it moved relative to the wind, whether its disappearance was real acceleration or just loss of visibility, and whether anyone else filmed it. Until those are answered, the most precise description is "an unidentified object in one witness's video," not an alien vehicle over a military base.

The Anchorage jellyfish is real as a reported encounter: a named woman and her husband say they saw something unusual, and her imagery surfaced five months later. The viral claims, including giant size, flight directly over JBER, impossible motion, multiple independent films and extraterrestrial origin, remain unverified. The one still in public view places the object in daylight, front-lit by a low sun, in front of a mountainside. The last famous jellyfish turned out to be balloons. This one deserves the same patient analysis, starting with the original file.

The Basic Reasoning Test That Separates Real Intelligence from AI
